paragraphs: Daurises directed his march to the cities on the Hellespont and took Dardanus and Abydos and Percote and Lampsacus and Paesus—taking one of these on each day. But as he was marching from Paesus against the city of Parium, the report came that the Carians had made common cause with the Ionians and were in revolt from the Persians. He therefore turned back from the Hellespont and marched his army upon Caria. As it happened, a report of this was brought to the Carians before Daurises arrived; and on being informed, the Carians gathered at the place called the “White Pillars,” and at the river Marsyas, which flows from the region of Idrias and empties into the Maeander. When the Carians had gathered there, among many counsels offered, the best, in my opinion, was that of Pixodarus son of Mausolus, a man of Cindye, who was married to the daughter of Syennesis king of the Cilicians. His opinion was that the Carians should cross the Maeander and engage the Persians with the river at their backs, so that the Carians, being unable to flee backwards and compelled to remain where they were, might prove themselves even braver in the fight than they naturally would. This opinion did not prevail; they resolved instead that the Persians rather than themselves should have the Maeander at their backs—clearly so that if the Persians were put to flight and worsted, they might never return home but fall into the river.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 119
paragraphs: After this, when the Persians had come and crossed the Maeander, the Carians engaged them at the river Marsyas and fought a battle that was stubbornly contested and long, but in the end they were worsted by superior numbers. Of the Persians some two thousand fell, but of the Carians ten thousand. Those who escaped were shut up in Labraunda within the sanctuary of Zeus Stratius, a great sacred grove of plane-trees (the Carians are the only people we know of who sacrifice to Zeus Stratius). These men, shut up there, were taking counsel among themselves about their safety—whether they would fare better by surrendering to the Persians or by leaving Asia altogether.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 120
paragraphs: While they were taking counsel in this way, the Milesians and their allies came to their aid. The Carians then set aside the plans they had been considering and prepared to start the war afresh; and when the Persians came against them, they engaged them in battle, and were beaten even more severely than before. Many fell on all sides, but the Milesians suffered worst.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 121
paragraphs: Afterwards, however, the Carians repaired this loss and retrieved their defeat. For being informed that the Persians had set out to march against their cities, they laid an ambush on the road that runs by Pedasus; and the Persians, falling into it by night, were destroyed—both they and their commanders, namely Daurises and Amorges and Sisimaces; and with them died Myrsus son of Gyges as well. The leader of this ambush was Heraclides son of Ibanollis, a man of Mylasa.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 122
paragraphs: These Persians, then, were destroyed in this way; and meanwhile Hymaees, who was another of those pursuing the Ionians who had marched on Sardis, directed his march to the Propontis and took Cius in Mysia. Having taken this city, when he was informed that Daurises had left the Hellespont and was marching against Caria, he left the Propontis and led his army to the Hellespont; and he conquered all the Aeolians who occupy the district of Ilium, and also the Gergithae, who were left as a remnant of the ancient Teucrians. While conquering these tribes, Hymaees himself ended his life from sickness in the land of Troas.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 123
paragraphs: He thus brought his life to an end; and Artaphrenes, governor of the province of Sardis, was appointed together with Otanes, the third of the commanders, to make an expedition against Ionia and the adjoining part of Aeolis. Of Ionia they captured the city of Clazomenae, and of the Aeolians Cyme.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 124
paragraphs: While the cities were being taken in this way, Aristagoras the Milesian, being—as he proved in this instance—not a man of very distinguished courage, since after having stirred up Ionia and set vast projects in motion he counseled running away when he saw these developments (and moreover it had become clear to him that it was impossible to overcome King Darius)—Aristagoras, I say, in view of these things, called together those of his own party and took counsel with them, saying that it was better that a refuge should be prepared for them in case they should after all be driven out from Miletus; and he proposed the question whether he should lead them from there to Sardinia to found a colony, or to Myrcinus in the land of the Edonians, which Histiaeus had been fortifying after receiving it as a gift from Darius. This was the question Aristagoras put to them.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 125
paragraphs: The opinion of Hecataeus, son of Hegesander, the historian, was that he should not take a colony to either of these places, but should build himself a wall of defense on the island of Leros and keep quiet, if he should be forced to leave Miletus; and afterwards, with this as his base, he would be able to return to Miletus.

chapters.title: Book V — Terpsichore, Chapter 126
paragraphs: This was the counsel of Hecataeus; but Aristagoras was most inclined to go to Myrcinus. He therefore entrusted the government of Miletus to Pythagoras, a man of repute among the citizens, and sailed off to Thrace, taking with him everyone who wished to go; and he took possession of the region for which he had set out. But setting out from there to make war, he perished at the hands of the Thracians—both Aristagoras himself and his army—while he was encamped around a certain city and the Thracians wished to come out of it under a truce.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 1
paragraphs: Aristagoras, then, after having caused Ionia to revolt, thus ended his life; and meanwhile Histiaeus, the tyrant of Miletus, having been let go by Darius, had arrived at Sardis. When he came from Susa, Artaphrenes, governor of Sardis, asked him for what reason he supposed the Ionians had revolted; and Histiaeus said that he could not tell, and moreover expressed wonder at what had happened, pretending he knew nothing of the state of affairs. Then Artaphrenes, seeing that he was dissembling and knowing the truth about the revolt, said: “It stands with you, Histiaeus, in this way in these matters: this shoe was stitched by you, and put on by Aristagoras.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Thus spoke Artaphrenes regarding the revolt; and Histiaeus, fearing Artaphrenes because he understood the matter, ran away the next night at nightfall and went to the coast, having deceived King Darius—seeing that he had undertaken to subdue Sardinia, the largest of islands, and was instead trying to assume leadership of the Ionians in the war against Darius. Then crossing over to Chios, he was put in bonds by the Chians, who accused him of working for a change in their government on Darius's instructions. When, however, the Chians learned the whole story and heard that he was an enemy of the king, they released him.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 3
paragraphs: Then, when the Ionians asked Histiaeus for what reason he had so urgently charged Aristagoras to revolt from the king and brought so great an evil upon the Ionians, he did not at all declare to them what had truly been the cause; but he reported to them that King Darius had resolved to remove the Phoenicians from their land and settle them in Ionia, and the Ionians in Phoenicia, and that for this reason he had given the charge. Thus he tried to alarm the Ionians, although the king had never resolved to do anything of the kind.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 4
paragraphs: After this Histiaeus, acting through a messenger, Hermippus of Atarneus, sent papers to the Persians who were at Sardis, implying that he had already discussed revolt with them. Hermippus, however, did not deliver the papers to those to whom he was sent, but took them and placed them in the hands of Artaphrenes. Artaphrenes, perceiving all that was being done, bade Hermippus carry the papers sent by Histiaeus and deliver them to those to whom he had been sent, and to deliver to him in turn the replies sent back by the Persians to Histiaeus. These things having been discovered, Artaphrenes thereupon put many of the Persians to death.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 5
paragraphs: As regards Sardis, then, his plan was thrown into confusion; and when Histiaeus was disappointed of this hope, the Chians attempted to restore him to Miletus at his own request. The Milesians, however, having been glad before to be rid of Aristagoras, were by no means eager to receive another tyrant into their land, having tasted freedom; and indeed, when Histiaeus tried to return to Miletus by force and under cover of night, he was wounded in the thigh by one of the Milesians. Repulsed from his own city, he returned to Chios; and from there, since he could not persuade the Chians to give him ships, he crossed over to Mytilene and tried to persuade the Lesbians to give him ships. They manned eight triremes and sailed with Histiaeus to Byzantium; and stationing themselves there, they captured the ships sailing out of the Pontus, except where the crews said they were ready to do Histiaeus's bidding.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 6
paragraphs: While Histiaeus and the men of Mytilene were acting thus, a large force of both sea and land was threatening to attack Miletus itself; for the commanders of the Persians had joined together to form one single army and were marching on Miletus, considering the other towns of less account. Of their naval force the most zealous were the Phoenicians; and serving with them were also the Cyprians, who had only just been subdued, and the Cilicians and Egyptians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 7
paragraphs: These, I say, were advancing on Miletus and the rest of Ionia; and meanwhile the Ionians, informed of this, were sending representatives chosen from themselves to the Panionium. When these had come to that place and taken counsel together, they resolved not to raise a land-army against the Persians, but that the Milesians should defend their walls by themselves, and that the Ionians should man their fleet, leaving out not one of their ships, and, having done so, should assemble as quickly as possible at Lade to fight a sea-battle in defense of Miletus. Now Lade is a small island lying opposite the city of the Milesians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 8
paragraphs: Then the Ionians manned their ships and came there, and with them also those Aeolians who inhabit Lesbos; and they were drawn up in order as follows. The extremity of the line to the east was held by the Milesians themselves, who furnished eighty ships; next to them were the Prienians with twelve ships, and the men of Myus with three; next to the men of Myus were the Teians with seventeen ships, and after the Teians the Chians with one hundred; after these were stationed the men of Erythrae and of Phocaea, the former furnishing eight ships and the latter three; next to the Phocaeans were the Lesbians with seventy ships, and last, holding the extremity of the line to the west, were stationed the Samians with sixty ships. Of all these the total number proved to be three hundred and fifty-three triremes.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 9
paragraphs: These were the ships of the Ionians; and of the barbarians the number of ships was six hundred. When these too had come to the Milesian coast and their whole land-army was also on hand, then the commanders of the Persians, being informed of the number of Ionian ships, were struck with fear that they would not be able to overcome them, and thus on the one hand would not be able to conquer Miletus for lack of command of the sea, and at the same time would run the risk of being punished by Darius. Reflecting on these things, they gathered together the tyrants of the Ionians who were exiles with the Medes, having been deposed from their governments by Aristagoras the Milesian, and who happened to be then taking part in the expedition against Miletus. Of these men they called together those who were present and spoke to them as follows: “Ionians, now let each of you show himself a benefactor of the king's house—that is, let each try to detach his own countrymen from the alliance. Make your proposals, promising at the same time that they shall suffer nothing unpleasant for their revolt; neither their temples nor their private houses shall be burned, nor shall they have any worse treatment than they had before. But if they will not do so, and persist in entering into a contest with us, threaten them and tell them this, which in truth will happen to them: if they are worsted in the fight, they shall be reduced to slavery; we will make their sons eunuchs, we will remove their maidens to Bactria, and we will hand their land over to others.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Thus they spoke; and the tyrants of Ionia each sent by night to his own people, announcing this to them. But the Ionians, that is those to whom these messages came, remained obstinate and would not accept the idea of treason to their cause; and each people thought that the Persians were sending this message to them alone.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 11
paragraphs: This happened as soon as the Persians came to Miletus. After this, the Ionians, gathered at Lade, held meetings, at which others no doubt also made speeches to them, but especially the Phocaean commander Dionysius, who said: “Seeing that our affairs, Ionians, are set upon the razor's edge—whether we are to be free or slaves, and slaves to be treated as runaways—now therefore, if you are willing to take on hardships, you will have labor for the time being, but you will be able to overcome the enemy and be free. If, however, you continue to be self-indulgent and without discipline, I have no hope that you will not pay the penalty to the king for your revolt. No, do as I say, hand yourselves over to me, and I promise—if the gods grant equal conditions—that either the enemy will not fight us at all, or that if they do fight they will be greatly discomfited.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 12
paragraphs: Hearing this, the Ionians handed themselves over to Dionysius; and he used to bring the ships out every day in single file, so that he might train the rowers by making the ships break through one another's line, and so that he might get the fighting-men on the ships under arms; and then for the rest of the day he would keep the ships at anchor. In this way he gave the Ionians work to do all day long. For seven days they submitted and did what he commanded; but on the next day the Ionians, being unaccustomed to such toils and exhausted by hard work and hot sun, said to one another: “Against which of the gods have we offended, that we so fill up the measure of our misery? For surely we have handed ourselves over to a Phocaean, a charlatan, who furnishes only three ships; and he has taken us into his hands and maltreats us with evil dealing from which we can never recover. Many of us, in fact, have fallen into sickness, and many others may be expected to suffer the same thing shortly; and for us it is better to endure anything else in the world rather than these ills, and to undergo the slavery that will come upon us, whatever it may be, rather than to be oppressed by what we have now. Come, let us obey him no more.” So they said; and forthwith, after this, each refused to obey him, and they pitched their tents on the island like an army, and kept in the shade, and would not go on board their ships or carry out any drills.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 13
paragraphs: Perceiving what the Ionians were doing, the commanders of the Samians then at length accepted from Aeaces son of Syloson the proposals that Aeaces had earlier sent at the Persians' bidding, asking them to leave the Ionian alliance. The Samians, I say, accepted these proposals, seeing that there was great lack of discipline on the Ionians' part, while at the same time it was clear to them that it was impossible to overcome the king's power; and they knew well also that even if they should overcome Darius's present naval force, another would be upon them five times as large. Having found a pretext, then, as soon as they saw that the Ionians refused to be of service, they counted it gain for themselves to save their temples and their private property. Now Aeaces, from whom the Samians accepted the proposals, was the son of Syloson, the son of Aeaces; and being tyrant of Samos, he had been deprived of his rule by Aristagoras the Milesian, like the other tyrants of Ionia.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 14
paragraphs: So when the Phoenicians sailed to the attack, the Ionians put out their ships from shore against them, sailing in single file. When they came near and engaged one another in battle, as for what followed I am not able to record precisely which of the Ionians showed themselves cowards or brave men in this sea-fight, for they throw blame on one another. The Samians, however, it is said, in accordance with their agreement with Aeaces, put up their sails and set off from their station in the line to sail back to Samos—except for eleven ships: the captains of these stayed in their places and took part in the sea-fight, refusing to obey their division commanders. The Samian state granted them, for this reason, to have their names inscribed on a pillar together with their fathers' names, as having proved themselves brave men; and this pillar still exists in the marketplace. Then the Lesbians, too, when they saw those next them in the line taking to flight, did the same as the Samians; and most of the Ionians also did the very same thing.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 15
paragraphs: Of those who remained in their places in the sea-fight, the Chians suffered very severely, since they displayed brilliant feats of valor and refused to play the coward. These, as has been said, furnished one hundred ships, and in each of them forty picked men of their citizens served as marines. When they saw the greater number of their allies deserting them, they did not think it fit to behave like the cowards among them, but, left with only a few allies, they continued to fight and kept breaking through the enemy's line; until at last, after having defeated many of the enemy's ships, they lost the greater number of their own.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 16
paragraphs: The Chians, with the remainder of their ships, fled away to their own land; but those of the Chians whose ships had been disabled by the damage they had received, being pursued, fled for refuge to Mycale; there they ran their ships ashore, left them behind, and proceeded on foot over the mainland. When the Chians had entered the territory of Ephesus on their way—coming into it by night, just at a time when a festival of the Thesmophoria was being celebrated by the women of the place—the Ephesians, not having heard beforehand how matters stood with the Chians and seeing an armed body entering their land, assumed for certain that they were robbers with a design on the women; so they came out in a body to the rescue and killed the Chians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 17
paragraphs: Such was the fortune that befell these men. But Dionysius the Phocaean, when he perceived that the cause of the Ionians was ruined, having captured three enemy ships, sailed away—no longer to Phocaea, for he knew well that it would be reduced to slavery along with the rest of Ionia, but straight to Phoenicia. Having sunk merchant ships there and taken a great quantity of goods, he sailed from there to Sicily. Then with that for a base he became a freebooter, plundering no Hellenes, but only Carthaginians and Tyrsenians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 18
paragraphs: The Persians, then, being the victors over the Ionians in the sea-fight, besieged Miletus by land and sea, undermining the walls and bringing up against it all manner of engines; and they took it completely in the sixth year from the revolt of Aristagoras, and reduced the people to slavery—so that the disaster agreed with the oracle that had been uttered about Miletus.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 19
paragraphs: For when the Argives were inquiring at Delphi about the safety of their city, an oracle was given them that applied to both—that is, part of it had reference to the Argives themselves, while what was added afterwards referred to the Milesians. The part that referred to the Argives I will record when I come to that place in the history, but what the oracle uttered about the Milesians, who were not there present, is as follows:

“And at that time, O Miletus, contriver of evil deeds, you shall be made a brilliant spoil and a feast for many; then your wives shall be compelled to wash the feet of the long-haired; and in Didyma then my shrine shall be tended by others.”

At the time of which I speak, these things came upon the Milesians, since most of the men were killed by the Persians, who are long-haired, and the women and children were treated as slaves; and the temple at Didyma, with the sacred building and the sanctuary of the oracle, was first plundered and then burned. Of the treasures in this temple I have made frequent mention elsewhere in the history.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 20
paragraphs: After this, the Milesians who had been taken prisoner were brought to Susa; and King Darius did them no other harm, but settled them on the sea called Erythraean, in the city of Ampe, beside which the Tigris flows on its way out to the sea. Of the Milesian land the Persians themselves kept the area around the city and the plain, but the heights they gave to the Carians of Pedasa for a possession.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 21
paragraphs: When the Milesians suffered this treatment from the Persians, the men of Sybaris, who were living in Laüs and Scidrus after being deprived of their own city, did not repay like with like. For when Sybaris was taken by the men of Croton, the Milesians all from youth upwards shaved their heads and put on great mourning; for these cities were bound together by ties of friendship more than any other cities we know of. The Athenians, by contrast, were unlike the Sybarites; they made it clear that they were grieved at the capture of Miletus in many ways, and especially in this: that when Phrynichus had composed a drama called “The Capture of Miletus” and put it on stage, the body of spectators fell to weeping, and the Athenians moreover fined the poet a thousand drachmas on the ground that he had reminded them of their own calamities; and they ordered also that no one in future should produce this drama.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 22
paragraphs: Miletus, then, had been stripped of its former inhabitants; but among the Samians, those who had means were by no means satisfied with what had been arranged by their fleet commanders with the Medes. Taking counsel right after the sea-fight, they resolved that, before their tyrant Aeaces arrived in the country, they would sail away and found a colony, and not stay behind and become slaves of the Medes and of Aeaces. For just at this time the people of Zancle in Sicily were sending messengers to Ionia inviting the Ionians to come to the “Fair Strand,” wishing to found a city of Ionians there. Now this so-called Fair Strand is in the land of the Sicels and on the side of Sicily that faces Tyrsenia. So when this invitation was given, the Samians alone of all the Ionians set out, having with them those of the Milesians who had escaped; and in the course of this matter it happened as follows.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 23
paragraphs: As the Samians made their way toward Sicily, they reached Epizephyrian Locri, and at the same time the people of Zancle, both themselves and their king, whose name was Scythes, were encamped around a city of the Sicels, hoping to take it. Perceiving these things, Anaxilaus, tyrant of Rhegium, who was at odds with those of Zancle, communicated with the Samians and persuaded them that they should leave the Fair Strand alone, to which they were sailing, and take possession of Zancle instead, since it was now without men to defend it. The Samians did as he said and took possession of Zancle. The men of Zancle, when they were informed that their city was in enemy hands, set out to rescue it and called on Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela, to help them, for he was their ally. But when Hippocrates too had come up with his army to their rescue, he first put Scythes the ruler of the Zanclaeans in fetters, on the ground that he had been the cause of the city's loss, and together with him his brother Pythogenes, and sent them off to the town of Inyx. He then betrayed the cause of the remaining Zanclaeans by coming to terms with the Samians and exchanging oaths with them; in return for this, it had been promised by the Samians that Hippocrates should receive as his share half of all the movable goods in the city and of the slaves, and the whole of the property in the fields round about. So the greater part of the Zanclaeans he put in bonds and kept as slaves for himself, but the chief men among them, three hundred in number, he handed over to the Samians to put to death—which, however, the Samians did not do.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 24
paragraphs: Now Scythes the ruler of the Zanclaeans escaped from Inyx to Himera, and from there he came to Asia and went up to the court of Darius; and Darius considered him the most righteous of all the men who had come up to him from Hellas, for he was given leave by the king and went off to Sicily, and again came back from Sicily to the king; and finally he ended his life among the Persians in old age, possessed of great wealth. The Samians, then, having got rid of the rule of the Medes, had gained for themselves without effort the fair city of Zancle.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 25
paragraphs: After the sea-battle fought for Miletus, the Phoenicians, at the Persians' command, restored Aeaces son of Syloson to Samos, since he had been of great service to them and had done great things for them; and the Samians alone, of all who had revolted from Darius, had neither their city nor their temples burned, because of the desertion of their ships in the sea-fight. Then, after the capture of Miletus, the Persians at once got possession of Caria, some of the cities having submitted to their power voluntarily, while others they brought over by force.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 26
paragraphs: So it came to pass regarding these matters; and meanwhile Histiaeus the Milesian, who was at Byzantium seizing the Ionian merchant vessels as they sailed out of the Pontus, received the report of what had happened concerning Miletus. Upon this he entrusted affairs pertaining to the Hellespont to Bisaltes son of Apollophanes, a man of Abydos, while he himself with the Lesbians sailed to Chios. When a body of Chians on guard would not let him approach, he fought them at the spot in Chian territory called the “Hollows.” Histiaeus not only killed many of these, but, taking Polichne of the Chians as his base, he subdued the remainder of the Chians too with the Lesbians' help, since they had suffered great loss in the sea-fight.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 27
paragraphs: And heaven, it seems, tends to give signs beforehand whenever great evils are about to fall on a city or a race of men; for to the Chians too, before these events, remarkable signs had come. In the first place, when they had sent a chorus of a hundred young men to Delphi, only two returned home, the remaining ninety-eight having been seized by a plague and carried off. And secondly, in their city at about the same time—just before the sea-fight—as some children were being taught in school, the roof fell in on them, so that of a hundred and twenty children only one escaped. These signs the god showed to them beforehand; and after this the sea-fight came upon them and brought their state to its knees; and since the Chians had suffered great loss, Histiaeus without difficulty effected the conquest of them.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 28
paragraphs: From there Histiaeus made an expedition against Thasos, taking with him a large force of Ionians and Aeolians; and while he was encamped around the town of Thasos, a report came to him that the Phoenicians were sailing up from Miletus to conquer the rest of Ionia. Being informed of this, he left Thasos unconquered and himself hurried to Lesbos, taking his whole army with him. Then, as his army was short of food, he crossed over from Lesbos to reap the corn at Atarneus and also in the plain of the Caicus, which belonged to the Mysians. In these parts there happened to be a Persian named Harpagus commanding a considerable force; and this man fought a battle with him after he had landed, and took Histiaeus himself prisoner and destroyed the greater part of his army.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 29
paragraphs: Histiaeus was taken prisoner in the following manner. As the Hellenes were fighting the Persians at Malene in the district of Atarneus, after they had been engaged in close combat for a long time, at length the cavalry charged and fell upon the Hellenes; and the cavalry in fact decided the battle. So when the Hellenes had been put to flight, Histiaeus, trusting that he would not be put to death by the king for his present offense, conceived a love of life; so that when he was being caught in his flight by a Persian and was about to be run through at the moment of capture, he spoke in Persian and made himself known, saying that he was Histiaeus the Milesian.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 30
paragraphs: Now if on being taken prisoner he had been brought to King Darius, he would not, I think, have suffered any harm, but Darius would have forgiven him the charge against him. As it was, however, for this very reason—that he might not escape punishment and again become powerful with the king—Artaphrenes the governor of Sardis and Harpagus, who had captured him, when he had reached Sardis on the way to the king, put him to death there and then; and they impaled his body, but embalmed his head and brought it up to Darius at Susa. Darius, on being informed of this, found fault with those who had done it, because they had not brought Histiaeus up to his presence alive; and he bade them wash the head of Histiaeus and give it proper care, and then bury it, as that of one who had been a great benefactor both of the king himself and of the Persians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 31
paragraphs: So it happened regarding Histiaeus. Meanwhile the Persian fleet, after wintering near Miletus, when it put to sea again the following year, conquered without difficulty the islands lying near the mainland—Chios, Lesbos, and Tenedos. And whenever they took one of the islands, the barbarians, as each was conquered, swept the inhabitants off it. They do this in the following manner: they extend themselves from the sea on the north to the sea on the south, each man holding the next by the hand, and then pass through the whole island, hunting the people out of it. They took also the Ionian cities on the mainland in the same way, except that they did not sweep off the inhabitants thus, for it was not possible.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 32
paragraphs: Then the commanders of the Persians proved not false to the threats with which they had threatened the Ionians when they were encamped opposite each other; for when they conquered the cities, they chose the most comely of the boys and made eunuchs of them by castration, and the fairest of the maidens they carried off by force to the king. And not only this, but they also burned the cities together with the temples. Thus for the third time had the Ionians been reduced to slavery: first by the Lydians, and then twice in succession by the Persians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 33
paragraphs: Leaving Ionia, the fleet proceeded to conquer all the places of the Hellespont on the left as one sails in, since those on the right had already been subdued by the Persians themselves, approaching them by land. The cities of the Hellespont in Europe are these: first comes the Chersonese, in which there are many cities, then Perinthus, the strongholds of the Thracian border, Selymbria, and Byzantium. The people of Byzantium, and those of Calchedon opposite, did not even wait for the coming of the Persian ships, but had left their own land first and departed, going within the Euxine; and there they settled in the city of Mesambria. So the Phoenicians, having burned these places that have been mentioned, directed their course next to Proconnesus and Artace; and when they had delivered these also to the flames, they sailed back to the Chersonese to destroy the remaining cities that they had not sacked when they had touched there before. But against Cyzicus they did not sail at all; for the men of Cyzicus, even before the time the Phoenicians sailed in, had submitted to the king of their own accord and had come to terms with Oebares son of Megabazus, the Persian governor at Dascyleium.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 34
paragraphs: In the Chersonese, then, the Phoenicians made themselves masters of all the other cities except the city of Cardia. Of these cities up to that time Miltiades son of Cimon, son of Stesagoras, had been tyrant—Miltiades son of Cypselus having acquired this government in the way I shall now describe. The inhabitants of this Chersonese were Dolonkian Thracians; and these Dolonkians, being hard pressed in war by the Apsinthians, sent their kings to Delphi to consult the oracle about the war. The Pythian priestess answered that they should bring into their land as founder of a settlement the man who should first offer them hospitality on their return from the temple. The Dolonkians then traveled along the Sacred Road through the land of the Phocians and Boeotians, and since no man invited them, they turned aside and came to Athens.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 35
paragraphs: At that time in Athens the government was held by Peisistratus, but Miltiades son of Cypselus also had some power. He belonged to a family that kept four-horse chariot teams, and was descended originally from Aeacus and Aegina, though in more recent times his family was Athenian, Philaeus son of Ajax being the first of his house to become an Athenian. This Miltiades was sitting in the entrance of his own house, and seeing the Dolonkians passing by in clothing that was not of the native Athenian fashion and carrying spears, he called out to them; and when they approached, he offered them lodging and hospitality. They accepted, and after being entertained by him they declared to him all the utterances of the oracle; and having declared it, they asked him to do as the god had said. Miltiades, when he heard it, was at once disposed to agree, because he was vexed by Peisistratus's rule and desired to be out of the way. So he set off at once to Delphi to inquire of the oracle whether he should do what the Dolonkians were asking of him.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 36
paragraphs: Since the Pythian priestess bade him do so, Miltiades son of Cypselus—who had already been a victor at Olympia with a four-horse chariot—now, taking with him every Athenian who wished to share in the expedition, sailed with the Dolonkians and took possession of the land; and those who had invited him made him tyrant over them. First he built a wall across the isthmus of the Chersonese from the city of Cardia to Pactye, so that the Apsinthians might not be able to invade the land and do them damage. The number of furlongs across the isthmus at this point is thirty-six, and from this isthmus the Chersonese within is in all four hundred and twenty furlongs long.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 37
paragraphs: Having built the wall across the neck of the Chersonese and thus repelled the Apsinthians, Miltiades first of all made war on the people of Lampsacus; and the people of Lampsacus laid an ambush and took him prisoner. Now Miltiades had come to be a friend of Croesus the Lydian; and Croesus accordingly, being informed of this event, sent and ordered the people of Lampsacus to let Miltiades go—otherwise he threatened to destroy them utterly like a pine tree. When the people of Lampsacus were at a loss in their deliberations as to what this saying meant with which Croesus had threatened them—that he would destroy them utterly like a pine tree—at length one of the elder men with some difficulty grasped the truth, and said that the pine alone of all trees, when it has been cut down, puts forth no further growth but perishes, being utterly destroyed. The people of Lampsacus, then, fearing Croesus, released Miltiades and let him go.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 38
paragraphs: He thus escaped through Croesus; but afterwards he ended his life leaving no son to succeed him, and passed on his rule and his possessions to Stesagoras, who was the son of Cimon, his brother on the mother's side. The people of the Chersonese still offer sacrifices to him after his death, as is customary for a founder, and hold a contest of horse-races and athletic exercises in his honor, in which none of the men of Lampsacus are allowed to compete. After this there was war with those of Lampsacus; and it happened to Stesagoras also that he died without leaving a son, having been struck on the head with an axe in the city hall by a man who pretended to be a deserter but proved himself in fact to be an enemy, and a rather hot-blooded one at that.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 39
paragraphs: Then after Stesagoras had also ended his life in this way, Miltiades son of Cimon and brother of the dead Stesagoras was sent in a trireme to the Chersonese to take possession of the government, by the sons of Peisistratus, who had treated him well at Athens too, pretending that they had had no share in the death of his father Cimon—the circumstances of which I will set forth in another part of the history. When Miltiades came to the Chersonese, he kept to his house, making a show of honoring the memory of his brother Stesagoras; and the chief men among the inhabitants of the Chersonese in every place, being informed of this, gathered themselves together from all the cities and came in a body to condole with him—and when they had come, they were laid in bonds by him. Miltiades then was in possession of the Chersonese, supporting a body of five hundred mercenary troops; and he married the daughter of Olorus king of the Thracians, whose name was Hegesipyle.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 40
paragraphs: Now this Miltiades son of Cimon had at the time in question only recently returned to the Chersonese; and after his return there befell him other misfortunes worse than those he had already suffered. For two years before this he had been a fugitive from the land at the hands of the Scythians, since the nomad Scythians, provoked by King Darius, had joined together in a body and marched as far as this Chersonese; and Miltiades had not awaited their attack but had fled from the Chersonese, until at last the Scythians departed and the Dolonkians brought him back. These things had happened two years before the calamities that now oppressed him.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 41
paragraphs: At this time, being informed that the Phoenicians were at Tenedos, he filled five triremes with the property he had at hand and sailed away for Athens. Setting out from the city of Cardia, he was sailing through the Gulf of Melas; and as he passed along by the shore of the Chersonese, the Phoenicians fell in with his ships, and while Miltiades himself with four of his ships escaped to Imbros, the fifth ship was captured in the pursuit by the Phoenicians. In command of this ship, as it happened, was Metiochus, the eldest of Miltiades's sons—not born of the daughter of Olorus the Thracian, but of another woman. The Phoenicians captured him along with his ship; and being informed that he was the son of Miltiades, they brought him up to the king, thinking they would lay up for themselves a great obligation, because it was Miltiades who had declared his opinion to the Ionians that they should do as the Scythians said, at the time when the Scythians asked them to break up the bridge of boats and sail away to their own land. Darius, however, when the Phoenicians brought Metiochus son of Miltiades up to him, did Metiochus no harm, but on the contrary very much good: he gave him a house and possessions and a Persian wife, by whom he had children born who have been ranked as Persians. Miltiades meanwhile came from Imbros to Athens.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 42
paragraphs: In the course of this year nothing further was done by the Persians that tended to strife with the Ionians; but the following things were done in this year very much to their advantage. Artaphrenes the governor of Sardis sent for envoys from all the cities and compelled the Ionians to make agreements among themselves, so that they would give satisfaction for wrongs and not plunder one another's land. This he compelled them to do; he also measured their territories in parasangs—this is the name the Persians give to thirty furlongs—and, measuring by these, he appointed a certain amount of tribute for each people, which continues unaltered even to my own day, just as Artaphrenes appointed it; the tribute was set at nearly the same amount for each as it had been before.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 43
paragraphs: These things tended toward peace for the Ionians. But at the beginning of spring, when the other commanders had all been removed by the king, Mardonius son of Gobryas came down to the coast, bringing with him a very large land-army and a very large naval force. He was a young man, and had lately married Artozostra daughter of King Darius. When Mardonius, leading this army, came to Cilicia, he himself embarked on a ship and proceeded with the other ships, while other leaders led the land-army to the Hellespont. Mardonius, sailing along the coast of Asia, came to Ionia; and here I shall relate something that will be a great marvel to those Hellenes who do not believe that Otanes declared, among the seven men of the Persians, that the Persians ought to have popular rule. For Mardonius deposed all the tyrants of the Ionians and established popular governments in the cities. Having done so, he hurried on to the Hellespont; and when a vast number of ships and a large land-army had been gathered, they crossed the Hellespont in the ships and began to make their way through Europe—and their way was directed against Eretria and Athens.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 44
paragraphs: These cities, I say, furnished them with a pretext for the expedition; but they had it in mind to subdue as many of the Hellenic cities as they could. First they subdued with their ships the Thasians, who did not even raise a hand to defend themselves; then with the land-army they added the Macedonians to the peoples already serving them—for all the nations east of the Macedonians had already before this become subject to them. Crossing over then from Thasos to the opposite coast, they continued their way close to land as far as Acanthus, and then, starting from Acanthus, they attempted to round Mount Athos. But as they sailed round, there fell upon them a violent north wind against which they could do nothing; it handled them very roughly, dashing very many of their ships onto Mount Athos. It is said in fact that the number of ships destroyed was three hundred, and more than twenty thousand men; for since the sea around Athos is very full of sea monsters, some of the men were seized by these and so perished, while others were dashed against the rocks; some of them did not know how to swim and perished for that reason, others again from cold.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 45
paragraphs: Thus the fleet fared. Meanwhile Mardonius and the land-army, while encamped in Macedonia, were attacked in the night by the Brygian Thracians, and many of them were killed by the Brygi, and Mardonius himself was wounded. However, not even these escaped being enslaved by the Persians, for Mardonius did not depart from that region until he had made them subject. After subduing them, he proceeded to lead his army back, since he had suffered heavy losses with his land-army in fighting against the Brygi and with his fleet in going round Athos. So this expedition returned to Asia having gained no honor by its contests.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 46
paragraphs: In the next year after this, Darius first sent a messenger to the men of Thasos, who had been accused by their neighbors of planning revolt, and ordered them to take down the wall around their town and bring their ships to Abdera. The Thasians in fact, having been besieged by Histiaeus the Milesian and at the same time having large revenues coming in, had been using their money to build warships and to surround their city with a stronger wall. Now the revenues came to them from the mainland and from the mines: from the gold mines in Scapte Hyle there came in usually eighty talents a year, and from those on Thasos itself a smaller amount than this—but so much that, in general, the Thasians, without any tax on the produce of their soil, had a revenue from the mainland and from the mines amounting yearly to two hundred talents, and when the amount was at its highest, to three hundred.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 47
paragraphs: I myself saw these mines, and by far the most marvelous of them were those the Phoenicians discovered, who made the first settlement on this island with Thasus; and the island took the name it now has from this Thasus the Phoenician. These Phoenician mines are in the part of Thasos between the places called Aenyra and Coenyra, and opposite Samothrace, where there is a great mountain that has been entirely turned up in the search for metal. So much for that matter; and the Thasians, at the king's command, both razed their walls and brought all their ships to Abdera.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 48
paragraphs: After this, Darius began to test the Hellenes—what they intended, whether to go to war with him or surrender. He sent out heralds, therefore, and appointed them to go, some to one place and some to another, throughout Hellas, ordering them to demand earth and water for the king. These, I say, he sent to Hellas; and meanwhile he was sending other heralds to his own tributary cities along the seacoast, and bidding them have warships built, and vessels to transport horses as well.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 49
paragraphs: These cities, then, were preparing these things; and meanwhile, when the heralds had come to Hellas, many of those who lived on the mainland gave what the Persian demanded, and all those who lived on the islands did so, whomever the heralds came to with their demand. The islanders, I say, gave earth and water to Darius, and among them also those of Aegina. When these had done so, the Athenians at once went urgently against them, supposing that the Aeginetans had given in with hostile intent against themselves, so as to make an expedition against them together with the Persians; and they were also glad to get hold of a pretext against them. So they went back and forth to Sparta and accused the Aeginetans of what they had done, as having proved themselves traitors to Hellas.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 50
paragraphs: In consequence of this accusation, Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides, king of the Spartans, crossed over to Aegina intending to seize the Aeginetans most guilty in the matter. But as he was trying to seize them, certain of the Aeginetans opposed him, and among them especially Crius son of Polycritus, who said that Cleomenes should not carry off a single Aeginetan with impunity, for he was doing this (he said) without the authority of the Spartan state, having been persuaded to it by the Athenians with money; otherwise he would have come and seized them in company with the other king. He said this because of a message received from Demaratus. Then Cleomenes, as he was leaving Aegina, asked Crius what his name was, and he told him the truth; and Cleomenes said to him: “Now then, Ram, bind your horns with bronze, for you will have a great trouble to contend with shortly.” (The Greek word krios also means “ram.”)

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 51
paragraphs: Meanwhile Demaratus son of Ariston had stayed behind in Sparta and was bringing charges against Cleomenes. He too was king of the Spartans, but of the inferior house—which, however, is inferior in no other way, since it is descended from the same ancestor; the house of Eurysthenes has always been honored more, apparently because he was the elder brother.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 52
paragraphs: For the Lacedaemonians, who on this matter agree with none of the poets, say that Aristodemus son of Aristomachus, son of Cleodaeus, son of Hyllus, being their king, himself led them (and not the sons of Aristodemus) to this land which they now possess. Then, not long afterward, the wife of Aristodemus, whose name was Argeia—she was the daughter, they say, of Autesion son of Tisamenus son of Thersander son of Polyneices—is said to have borne twins; and Aristodemus lived only long enough to see his children, and then ended his life by sickness. The Lacedaemonians of that time resolved, according to established custom, to make the elder of the children their king; but they did not know which of them they should take, because they were alike and of equal size. When they were unable to find out, or even before this, they inquired of their mother; but she said that even she herself did not know one from the other. This she said, although she actually knew quite well, because she desired that somehow both might be made kings. The Lacedaemonians were therefore in a difficulty; and being in a difficulty, they sent to Delphi to ask what they should do in the matter. The Pythian priestess bade them regard both children as their kings, but honor most the first in age. So, they say, did the priestess give them her answer; and when the Lacedaemonians were no less at a loss how to find out the elder of them, a Messenian named Panites made a suggestion to them. This Panites, I say, suggested to the Lacedaemonians that they watch the mother and see which of the children she washed and fed first of the two; and if she was seen to do this always in the same order, they would have all they were seeking and wished to discover; but if she too was uncertain and did it in a different order at different times, it would be plain to them that she had no more knowledge than anyone else, and they must turn to some other way. The Spartans, following the Messenian's suggestion, watched the mother of the sons of Aristodemus and found that she gave preference thus to the firstborn, both in feeding and in washing, not knowing she was being watched. They therefore took the child honored by its mother and brought it up in the public hall as the firstborn, and named it Eurysthenes; and the other was called Procles. When they had grown up, both of them, they say, were at variance with one another throughout their whole lives, although they were brothers, and their descendants continued in the same way.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 53
paragraphs: This is the account given by the Lacedaemonians alone of all the Hellenes; but what follows I write in accordance with the general report of the Hellenes: namely, that the names of these kings of the Dorians are correctly enumerated by the Hellenes back to Perseus son of Danaë (leaving out the god), and are shown to be of Hellenic stock—for from that point they were already reckoned as Hellenes. I said “up to Perseus,” and did not trace the descent from a yet higher point, because no name of a mortal father is given for Perseus, as Amphitryon is for Heracles. With good reason, then, I have said “rightly up to Perseus”; but if one enumerates their ancestors in succession going back from Danaë daughter of Acrisius, the rulers of the Dorians will prove to be Egyptians by direct descent.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 54
paragraphs: Thus I have traced the descent according to the account given by the Hellenes; but according to the story as told by the Persians, Perseus himself was an Assyrian and became a Hellene, whereas the ancestors of Perseus were not Hellenes. As for the ancestors of Acrisius—who according to this account were not related to Perseus at all—they say that these were, as the Hellenes also report, Egyptians.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 55
paragraphs: Let it suffice to have said so much about these matters; and as to the question how and by what exploits they, being Egyptians, received the sceptres of royalty over the Dorians, we shall omit these things, since others have told them. But the matters with which other narrators have not dealt—of these I will make mention.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 56
paragraphs: These are the royal rights that the Spartans have given their kings: two priesthoods, of Zeus Lacedaemon and Zeus Uranios; the right to make war against whatever land they choose, and that no Spartan shall hinder this right—or, if he does, he shall be subject to the curse; that on campaigns the kings shall go out first and return last; that a hundred picked men shall be their guard on expeditions; and that they shall use in their marches to war as many cattle as they wish, and take both the hides and the chine-portions of all that are sacrificed.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 57
paragraphs: These are their privileges in war; and in peacetime things have been assigned to them as follows. If any sacrifice is performed at public expense, it is the kings' privilege to sit down to the feast before all others, and for the attendants to begin with them first, and to serve each of them a portion double that given to the other guests; they shall have the first pouring of libations and the hides of the animals slain in sacrifice. On every new moon and seventh day of the month, each of them shall be delivered at public expense a full-grown victim at the temple of Apollo, a measure of barley-groats, and a Laconian quarter of wine; at all the games they shall have seats of honor specially set aside for them. Moreover, it is their privilege to appoint as protectors of strangers (proxenoi) whomever they wish of the citizens, and each to choose two “Pythians” (now the Pythians are men sent to consult the god at Delphi, and they eat with the kings at public expense). If the kings do not come to the public dinner, the rule is that there shall be sent out to their houses two quarts of barley-groats for each and half a pint of wine; but if they are present, they shall be given double shares of everything. They shall be honored in the same way when they have been invited to dinner by private persons. The kings, it is ordained, shall also have charge of the oracles given, but the Pythians too shall have knowledge of them. The rule is moreover that the kings alone give decision on the following cases only: about the maiden who inherits her father's property, namely who ought to have her if her father has not betrothed her to anyone, and about public ways; and if any man wishes to adopt a son, it must be done in the presence of the kings. It is ordained that they shall sit in council with the Senators, who are twenty-eight in number; and if they do not come, those of the Senators most closely related to them shall have the kings' privileges, and give two votes besides their own, making three in all.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 58
paragraphs: These rights have been assigned by the Spartan state to the kings during their lifetime; and after they are dead, these which follow. Horsemen ride around and announce what has happened throughout the whole of the Laconian land, and in the city women go about and strike on a copper kettle. Whenever this happens, two free persons from each household must go into mourning, a man and a woman, and heavy penalties are appointed for those who fail to do this. Now the custom of the Lacedaemonians concerning the deaths of their kings is the same as that of the barbarians who dwell in Asia, for most of the barbarians practice the same customs regarding the death of their kings. Whenever a king of the Lacedaemonians dies, from the whole territory of Lacedaemon, not counting the Spartans, a certain fixed number of the “dwellers round” (the perioeci) are compelled to go to the funeral ceremony.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 59
paragraphs: When many thousands of these and of the Helots and of the Spartans themselves have been gathered together in the same place, with their women intermingled, they beat their foreheads with a will and make lamentation without stint, saying that the one who has died last of their kings was the best of all. Whenever any of their kings has been killed in war, they prepare an image to represent him, laid on a couch with fine coverings, and carry it out to be buried. After the burial, no assembly is held among them for ten days, nor any meeting for the choice of magistrates; but they keep mourning during these days. In another respect too they resemble the Persians: when the king is dead and another is appointed king, this newly incoming king releases any Spartan who was a debtor to the king or to the state—just as among the Persians the new king who comes to the throne remits to all the cities the arrears of tribute due.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 60
paragraphs: In the following respect too the Lacedaemonians resemble the Egyptians: their heralds, flute-players, and cooks inherit the crafts of their fathers, and a flute-player is the son of a flute-player, a cook of a cook, and a herald of a herald. Other men do not lay hands on the office because they have loud and clear voices and so shut them out of it; they practice their craft by inheritance from their fathers.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 61
paragraphs: Thus are these things done; and at the time of which we speak, while Cleomenes was in Aegina doing deeds which were for the common service of Hellas, Demaratus was bringing charges against him—not so much because he cared about the Aeginetans as because he felt envy and jealousy of him. So Cleomenes, after he returned from Aegina, planned to depose Demaratus from the kingship, making an attempt upon him on the following grounds. Ariston, being king in Sparta and having married two wives, yet had no children born to him; and since he did not acknowledge that he himself was the cause of this, he married a third wife, and married her in this way. He had a friend, a man of the Spartans, to whom of all the citizens Ariston was most attached; and this man happened to have a wife who was by far the fairest of all the women in Sparta, one who had become the fairest after having been the foulest. For since she was ugly in appearance, her nurse, considering that she was the daughter of wealthy parents and was ill-favored in looks, and seeing moreover that her parents were distressed by it, devised the following plan. Every day she would carry her to the temple of Helen, which is at the place called Therapne, lying above the temple of Phoebus; and whenever the nurse carried her there, she would place her before the image and pray to the goddess to deliver the child from her ugliness. Once, as the nurse was leaving the temple, it is said that a woman appeared to her, and having appeared, asked what she was carrying in her arms; and she told her she was carrying a child. At this the other bade her show the child to her, but she refused, for she had been forbidden by the parents to show it to anyone; but the woman kept pressing her to show it. So, perceiving that the woman really wanted to see it, the nurse showed her the child. Then the woman stroked the child's head and said that she would be the fairest of all the women in Sparta; and from that day her appearance was changed. Afterwards, when she came of age, she was married to Agetus son of Alcides, this friend of Ariston of whom we spoke.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 62
paragraphs: Now Ariston, it seems, was continually stung by desire for this woman, and so contrived as follows. He made an agreement with his comrade, whose wife this woman was, that he would give him as a gift any one thing he chose from his own possessions; and he asked his comrade to make him a like return. The comrade, fearing nothing for his wife, since he saw that Ariston too had a wife, agreed; and on these terms they imposed oaths on one another. After this, Ariston on his side gave that which Agetus had chosen from Ariston's treasures, whatever the thing was; then he himself, seeking to obtain the like return, tried to take away his comrade's wife. The comrade said that he consented to give anything else except this one thing only; but at last, compelled by the oath and by the treacherous deception, he allowed her to be taken from him.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 63
paragraphs: Thus Ariston had brought into his house the third wife, having dismissed the second; and this wife, not having fulfilled the ten months but in a shorter period of time, bore him the Demaratus of whom we were speaking. One of his servants reported to him, as he was sitting in council with the Ephors, that a son had been born to him. He then, knowing the time when he had taken the wife, and reckoning the months on his fingers, said, denying with an oath: “The child would not be mine.” The Ephors heard this but thought it a matter of no importance at the time; and the child grew up, and Ariston repented of what he had said, for he thought Demaratus was certainly his own son. He gave him the name “Demaratus” for this reason: because before these events the Spartan people as a whole had made a vow, praying that a son might be born to Ariston as one who was preeminent in renown above all the kings who had ever arisen in Sparta.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 64
paragraphs: For this reason the name Demaratus (“prayer of the people”) was given to him. As time went on, Ariston died, and Demaratus obtained the kingdom; but it was fated, apparently, that these things should become known and cause Demaratus to be deposed from his kingdom. That is why Demaratus came to be greatly at variance with Cleomenes, both on that earlier occasion when he withdrew the army from Eleusis, and especially now, when Cleomenes had crossed over to seize those Aeginetans who had gone over to the Medes.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 65
paragraphs: Cleomenes, eager to take revenge on Demaratus, arranged matters with Leotychides, son of Menares, son of Agis — a man of the same royal house as Demaratus. The condition was this: if Leotychides were installed as king in Demaratus's place, he would join Cleomenes on the campaign against the Aeginetans. Leotychides already had reason enough to hate Demaratus, and the cause was as follows. Leotychides had been betrothed to Percalos, the daughter of Chilon son of Demarmenos. But Demaratus plotted against him and deprived him of the marriage, seizing Percalos himself beforehand and taking her for his own wife. This was the origin of the feud between Leotychides and Demaratus. And now, at Cleomenes's prompting, Leotychides stood up and swore an accusation against Demaratus, claiming that he had no right to the throne of Sparta because he was not truly the son of Ariston. After this formal charge he pressed his suit, recalling the old remark that Ariston had made when his servant came to announce that a son had been born to him: Ariston, counting up the months, had denied with an oath that the child was his. Leotychides seized on this utterance and argued that Demaratus was not Ariston's son and therefore had no right to rule Sparta. As witnesses he produced those Ephors who happened to have been sitting in council with Ariston at the time and had heard him say it.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 66
paragraphs: At last, since the dispute went on without resolution, the Spartans decided to send to Delphi and ask the oracle whether Demaratus was indeed the son of Ariston. The question was referred to the Pythian prophetess through Cleomenes's arrangement, and Cleomenes won over to his side Cobon son of Aristophantus, the most powerful man in Delphi. Cobon then persuaded Perialla, the prophetess of the oracle, to give the answer that Cleomenes wanted. So when the envoys arrived and put their question to the god, the Pythia declared that Demaratus was not the son of Ariston. Later, however, the whole business came to light: Cobon was driven into exile from Delphi, and Perialla was removed from her office as prophetess.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 67
paragraphs: That is how the deposing of Demaratus from the kingship came about. As for his flight as an exile from Sparta to the Medes, it happened on account of an insult, as I shall now relate. After he had been stripped of the crown, Demaratus was serving in a public office to which he had been elected. It was the time of the festival of the Gymnopaediae, and Demaratus was among the spectators. Leotychides, who had now become king in his place, sent his servant to ask Demaratus mockingly and insultingly what sort of thing it was to hold a magistracy after having been king. Stung by the question, Demaratus replied that he himself had now had experience of both, whereas Leotychides had not — and that this question would prove the beginning of either endless misfortune or endless good fortune for the Lacedaemonians. With these words he veiled his head, left the theater, and went home. There he at once made ready and sacrificed an ox to Zeus, and after the sacrifice he summoned his mother.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 68
paragraphs: When his mother came, he placed some of the inner parts of the sacrificed animal in her hands and entreated her, saying: “Mother, I beg you, in the name of the other gods and above all of this Zeus, guardian of our household, to tell me the truth — who is really and truly my father? For Leotychides, in his quarrel with me, claimed that you came to Ariston already pregnant by your former husband. Others, repeating what is surely an empty tale, say that you went in to one of the servants, the keeper of the asses, and that I am his son. I therefore beseech you by the gods to tell me the truth. For if you did any of the things that are said of you, you did not do them alone — many other women have done the same. And the common report in Sparta is that there was no seed in Ariston capable of begetting children; for if there had been, his earlier wives would also have borne him children.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 69
paragraphs: Thus he spoke, and she answered him as follows: “My son, since you entreat me so earnestly to tell you the truth, the whole truth shall be told. When Ariston had brought me into his house, on the third night an apparition came to me in the likeness of Ariston; and after lying with me it placed upon me the garlands it was wearing and then went away. Soon afterward Ariston himself came. When he saw me wearing the garlands, he asked who had given them to me, and I said that he had. He denied it, but I began to swear to it, saying that he did wrong to deny it, for he had come only a short while before, lain with me, and given me the garlands. Then Ariston, seeing that I was taking an oath, realized that the matter was of the gods. And so indeed it was: the garlands were found to come from the hero-shrine that stands beside the outer door of our house — the shrine they call the temple of Astrabacus — and the diviners likewise answered that it was this very hero. So, my son, you now have the whole truth, as much as you wished to learn. You are begotten either of this hero — and Astrabacus is your father — or else of Ariston himself, for it was on that night that I conceived you. As for the point on which your enemies most eagerly seize — that Ariston, when your birth was announced, declared in the hearing of many that you were not his son, because the ten months had not yet been completed — he spoke that word out of ignorance of such matters. Women bring forth children at the ninth month as well, and even at the seventh, and not all after the full ten. I bore you, my son, at the seventh month; and Ariston himself before long recognized that he had uttered that saying in folly. Accept then no other reports about your birth; you have heard the entire truth. And as for Leotychides and all who spread such tales — may their own wives bear them children by keepers of asses!”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 70
paragraphs: Having heard what he wished to learn, Demaratus took provisions for the road and set out, pretending that he was going to Delphi to consult the oracle — but his destination was Elis. The Lacedaemonians, suspecting he was trying to escape, set off in pursuit; but before they caught him Demaratus had already crossed from Elis to Zacynthus. The Spartans crossed after him and seized his attendants, though the Zacynthians refused to give up the man himself. From there Demaratus crossed over into Asia, to the court of King Darius, who received him with great honor as a guest and granted him land and cities. That is how Demaratus came to Asia — a man who had distinguished himself among the Lacedaemonians in many ways, by both deeds and counsels, and who, above all, had won them an Olympic victory in the four-horse chariot race, the only king of Sparta ever to do so.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 71
paragraphs: With Demaratus deposed, Leotychides son of Menares succeeded to the kingship. A son was born to him named Zeuxidemus, whom some of the Spartans called Cyniscus. Zeuxidemus, however, never became king of Sparta, for he died before Leotychides, leaving behind a son, Archidamus. After losing Zeuxidemus, Leotychides took a second wife, Eurydame, the sister of Menios and daughter of Diactorides. By her he had no male issue but a daughter, Lampito, whom Archidamus son of Zeuxidemus married, Leotychides himself giving her in marriage.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 72
paragraphs: Leotychides, however, did not himself live out his old age in Sparta; he paid a penalty for what had been done to Demaratus, and this is how. He went as commander of the Lacedaemonians on a campaign into Thessaly, and although he could have reduced the whole country to subjection, he accepted a large bribe instead. He was caught in the act right there in camp, sitting on a glove stuffed full of money. Brought to trial, he was exiled from Sparta and his house was razed to the ground. He went into exile at Tegea and ended his life there.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 73
paragraphs: All of that happened later. At the time of which I am speaking, Cleomenes — having brought the affair of Demaratus to a successful end — at once took Leotychides with him and marched against the Aeginetans, furious at the insults they had offered him. The Aeginetans, now that both kings had come against them, decided that further resistance was pointless. The Spartans picked out ten of the most prominent men of Aegina, ranked by wealth and by birth, and took them off as prisoners — among them Crios son of Polycritus and Casambus son of Aristocrates, who held the greatest power on the island. Having carried them to Attica, they handed them over for safekeeping to the Athenians, who were Aegina's bitterest enemies.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 74
paragraphs: After this, when it came to light that he had engineered the plot against Demaratus, Cleomenes grew frightened of the Spartans and withdrew to Thessaly. From there he went to Arcadia and began to stir up trouble, binding the Arcadians together against Sparta. Among other oaths by which he made them swear that they would follow him wherever he led, he was especially eager to bring the Arcadian leaders to the city of Nonacris and have them swear by the water of the Styx. For near this city, according to the Arcadians, is the water of the Styx, and there is in fact something of the kind: a thin trickle of water drips from a rock into a hollow gully, and a wall of rough stones runs around the gully. Nonacris, where this spring is located, is an Arcadian town near Pheneos.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 75
paragraphs: When the Lacedaemonians learned what Cleomenes was up to, they grew afraid and proceeded to bring him back to Sparta to rule on the same terms as before. But no sooner had he returned than a madness seized him — he had never been entirely of sound mind — and whenever he met one of the Spartans on the street he would strike him in the face with his staff. As he kept doing this and had plainly lost his reason, his kinsmen bound him in stocks. While he was so bound, he noticed that his guard had been left alone by the others, and he asked him for a knife. At first the guard, a Helot, would not give it, but Cleomenes threatened him with what he would do afterwards if he refused, and at last the man was intimidated into handing it over. Then Cleomenes, once he had the blade, began to mutilate himself from the legs upward, slicing his flesh lengthways up from the legs to the thighs, from the thighs to the loins and flanks, until at last he reached his belly; cutting this into strips he died. Most of the Greeks say that this happened to him because he bribed the Pythian prophetess to give the answer she did about Demaratus. The Athenians alone say it was because, when he invaded Eleusis, he laid waste the sacred precinct of the Two Goddesses. The Argives say it was because he dragged out from their sanctuary of Argos those of their people who had fled there for refuge after the battle, slew them, and even set fire to the grove itself, thinking it of no account.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 76
paragraphs: For when Cleomenes was consulting the oracle at Delphi, he was told that he would conquer Argos. So he led the Spartans out and came to the river Erasinos, which is said to flow from the Stymphalian lake — that lake, they say, empties into an unseen chasm, then reappears above ground in the territory of Argos, and from that point onward the Argives call the water Erasinos. When he reached the river, Cleomenes offered sacrifice to it. The omens were entirely unfavorable for crossing, so he declared that he admired the Erasinos for not betraying the men of its own country — but that the Argives would not escape him even so. After this he withdrew and marched his army down to Thyrea. There, sacrificing a bull to the Sea, he shipped them across to the territory of Tiryns and Nauplia.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 77
paragraphs: Learning of this, the Argives hurried to the coast to meet them. Near Tiryns, at the place called Hesipeia, they camped opposite the Lacedaemonians, leaving only a narrow strip of ground between the two armies. The Argives were not afraid of a straight fight, but only of being undone by some trick — for it was to this, they thought, that the oracle given by the Pythia jointly to them and to the Milesians applied. It ran as follows:

“But when the female at length shall conquer the male in the battle, — conquer and drive him forth, and glory shall gain among Argives — then many wives of the Argives shall tear both cheeks in their mourning; so that a man shall say some time, of the men that came after, ‘Quelled by the spear it perished, the three-coiled terrible serpent.’”

All of this together frightened the Argives, and with this in mind they decided to make use of the enemy's herald. Having decided, they acted on it: whenever the Spartan herald announced some order to the Lacedaemonians, the Argives did the same thing.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 78
paragraphs: When Cleomenes realized that the Argives were doing whatever the Lacedaemonian herald announced, he passed the word among his men that when the herald proclaimed breakfast they should instead take up their arms and attack the Argives. This was done: while the Argives, acting on the herald's call, were eating their morning meal, the Lacedaemonians fell upon them. Many were killed, and many more took refuge in the sacred grove of Argos. The Lacedaemonians set up a watch and sat around the grove. Then Cleomenes did the following.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 79
paragraphs: He had some deserters with him, and by questioning them he got the names he needed. He then sent a herald to summon out the Argives shut up in the sanctuary, calling each one by name and saying that their ransom had already been paid. (Among the Peloponnesians the standard ransom is fixed at two minae of silver per prisoner.) One by one Cleomenes called about fifty Argives out and put them to death. For some time those still inside the enclosure did not notice what was happening — the grove was dense, and those inside could not see what was going on outside — until one of them climbed a tree and saw from above what was being done. After that, they would not come out when they were called.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 80
paragraphs: Cleomenes then ordered all the Helots to pile up brushwood around the sacred grove, and when they had done so, he set it on fire. As it was burning, he asked one of the deserters to which god the grove was sacred, and the man answered that it was sacred to Argos. When he heard this, Cleomenes groaned aloud and said, “Apollo, god of oracles, you have surely deceived me badly, saying that I should conquer Argos. I now suspect that the oracle has already been fulfilled for me.”

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 81
paragraphs: After this Cleomenes sent the greater part of his army back to Sparta, but he himself took a thousand of the best men and went to the temple of Hera to sacrifice. When he wanted to offer the sacrifice upon the altar, the priest forbade him, saying that it was not lawful by sacred custom for a foreigner to sacrifice there. Cleomenes, however, ordered the Helots to drag the priest away from the altar and scourge him, and he himself performed the sacrifice. After that he returned to Sparta.

chapters.title: Book VI — Erato, Chapter 82
