paragraphs: So Xerxes spoke to him, and Artabanus was unwilling at first to obey the command, since he did not consider himself worthy to sit on the royal throne; but at last, pressed further, he did as he was bidden, having first spoken these words: “It is equally good, in my judgment, O king, whether a man has wisdom of his own or is willing to follow the counsel of someone who speaks well; and you, who have both of these goods, are being led astray by the communications of bad men. It is as they say of the sea, which of all things is the most useful to men, yet is prevented by the blasts of winds falling upon it from behaving according to its own nature. As for me, it was not that I was so pained by being spoken to harshly by you, as that, when two opinions were laid before the Persians — one tending to increase wanton arrogance, the other tending to check it and to say that it was a bad thing to teach the soul to keep striving for more than it already has — when such opinions were set before us, you chose the one more dangerous both for yourself and for the Persians. And now that you have turned to the better counsel, you tell me that when you were disposed to let go the expedition against the Greeks, a dream came haunting you, sent by some god, forbidding you to abandon the enterprise. But here too, my son, you err: this is not of the Divinity. The dreams of sleep that come wandering to men are, as I — older by many years than you — will tell you, of this nature: the visions of dreams usually hover above us in the shape of the things we were thinking about during the day, and we in the days before had been very much taken up with this campaign. If, after all, this is not what I take it to be but is something divine, you have summed the matter up in what you said. Let it appear, as you say, to me as well, and give its commands. But if it wants to appear to me at all, it is under no more obligation to appear because I am wearing your clothes than it would be if I had my own, nor any more if I sleep in your bed than if I sleep in my own. For whatever this thing is that appears to you in your sleep, surely it is not so foolish as to see me and think that I am you just because the clothing is yours. What we must now find out is this: whether it will ignore me, not thinking fit to appear to me whether I am in my own clothes or in yours, and will continue to haunt you instead. For if it indeed haunts you continually, I too shall be disposed to say that it is of the Divine. But if you have resolved that this is how it must be, and there is no turning your resolve aside, and I must sleep in your bed, then, when I do these things, let it appear to me as well; until then, I shall hold to the opinion I now have.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 17
paragraphs: Having said this, Artabanus — expecting that he would prove Xerxes's words to be folly — did as he was bidden, and having put on Xerxes's robes and seated himself on the royal throne, afterwards lay down in the royal bed. When he had fallen asleep, the same dream that used to come to Xerxes came to him too, and standing over Artabanus it spoke these words: “So you are the man, are you, who is trying to turn Xerxes aside from marching against Greece, pretending to care for him? Neither in the future nor now in the present shall you go unpunished for trying to divert what is destined to happen; and as for Xerxes, what he must suffer if he disobeys has already been made clear to the man himself.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 18
paragraphs: It seemed to Artabanus that the dream uttered these threats and was just about to burn out his eyes with hot irons, when with a loud cry he sprang up from the bed. He sat down beside Xerxes and related the whole vision from beginning to end, and then said: “O king, I, as a man who has seen many great things in my time brought to ruin by lesser ones, urged you not to yield in everything to the impulses of your youth, knowing that it is an evil thing to desire many things at once — remembering the campaign of Cyrus against the Massagetae and what came of it, and the campaign of Cambyses against the Ethiopians, and being myself one who took part with Darius in the Scythian expedition. Knowing these things, I was of the opinion that you were to be envied of all men so long as you kept still. Since, however, there comes a divine impulse, and, it seems, a heaven-sent destruction is taking hold of the Greeks, I for my part both change my mind and reverse my opinions. Make known to the Persians the message that has been sent to you from God: bid them follow the commands you first gave about the preparations. Try, for your own part, that nothing be lacking, since God is putting the matter into your hands.” When these things had been said, both were inspired with confidence by the vision, and as soon as day came Xerxes communicated the matter to the Persians, and Artabanus, who before had been the only one stepping forward to dissuade him, now stepped forward to urge on the plan.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 19
paragraphs: Xerxes, now eager to undertake the expedition, afterwards saw a third vision in his sleep, which, when the Magi heard it, they interpreted as a sign that he would rule the whole earth and that all men would be subject to him. The vision was this: Xerxes dreamed that he had been crowned with a wreath of olive-branch, and that the shoots growing from the olive tree covered the whole earth; and after that the wreath, placed as it was on his head, disappeared. When the Magi had thus interpreted the dream, every one of the Persians who had been assembled there went back to his own province and set to the task of carrying out the commands with all zeal, each one eager to win for himself the gifts that had been offered. So Xerxes was gathering his army together, combing every region of the continent.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 20
paragraphs: For four full years after the conquest of Egypt he was preparing the army and the material needed for it, and in the course of the fifth year he set out on his campaign with a host of enormous size. For of all the armies of which we have any knowledge, this proved by far the greatest — so that the one Darius led against the Scythians seems nothing by comparison; nor the Scythian host, when the Scythians in pursuit of the Cimmerians invaded Media and subdued and occupied nearly the whole of upper Asia (the invasion Darius later tried to avenge); nor the force the sons of Atreus led against Ilium, to judge by the reports of their expedition; nor that of the Mysians and Teucrians, before the Trojan war, who crossed into Europe by the Bosphorus and not only subdued all the Thracians but came down as far as the Ionian Sea and marched south to the river Peneios.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 21
paragraphs: All these expeditions put together, with others added to them if any there be, do not equal this one alone. For what nation did Xerxes not lead out of Asia against Greece? What water, apart from the greatest rivers, was not drunk dry by his army? Some peoples supplied ships; others were assigned to serve in the land army; some were appointed to provide cavalry, others horse-transport vessels while themselves also serving on the expedition; some were ordered to furnish warships for the bridges, others ships for carrying provisions.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 22
paragraphs: In the first place, since the earlier fleet had been ruined in sailing round Athos, preparations had been going on for about three years with regard to Athos: triremes lay at anchor at Elaius in the Chersonese, and using that as a base men of all the nations in the army worked at the digging under the lash, relieving one another in shifts. Those who lived around Athos joined in the digging too. Bubares son of Megabazus and Artachaees son of Artaeus, both Persians, were put in charge of the work. Athos is a great and famous mountain running down to the sea and inhabited by people; where the mountain ends on the mainland side, the ground resembles a peninsula with an isthmus about twelve stades across. Here it is flat or low-hilled country, stretching from the sea off Acanthus to the one off Torone. On this isthmus, where Athos ends, stands a Greek city called Sane; beyond Sane and within the Athos peninsula are others — Dion, Olophyxus, Acrothoön, Thyssus, Cleonae — all of which the Persian had resolved to turn into cities of an island rather than of the mainland.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 23
paragraphs: These are the cities that lie on Athos. They dug in this manner, the country having been divided among the barbarian nations for the job. Starting at the city of Sane, they drew a straight line across the isthmus. When the channel grew deep, those who were standing at the bottom dug, while others passed the earth upward to men above them, who in turn passed it on as if up a flight of steps, until it reached the men at the top, who carried it away and dumped it. All the nations except the Phoenicians had double labor, because the steep sides of their trench kept caving in — which was only to be expected, since they tried to make the opening at the top the same width as the one at the bottom. But the Phoenicians, who generally show cleverness in their work, showed it here as well: once their assigned portion had been allotted to them, they began digging by making the opening at the top twice as wide as the channel itself was to be, and then as the work advanced they kept narrowing it, so that at the bottom their trench came out the same width as the others'. A meadow lay nearby, and in it a market and trading-place was set up for the workmen, and great quantities of grain were brought to them regularly from Asia, already ground.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 24
paragraphs: As I form my own judgment of this project, it seems to me that when Xerxes ordered the digging he was moved by a love of magnificence and by a wish to make a display of his power and leave a memorial behind. They could have dragged the ships across the isthmus with no great trouble, yet he had them dig a channel for the sea wide enough for two triremes to sail through side by side under oar. The same men to whom the digging had been assigned were also charged with throwing a bridge across the river Strymon, yoking its banks together.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 25
paragraphs: While Xerxes was doing these things, he had ropes prepared for the bridges as well, made of papyrus and of white flax, assigning this job to the Phoenicians and Egyptians. He was also making preparations to lay up provisions for his army along the march, so that neither the troops themselves nor the baggage animals would suffer shortage as they advanced into Greece. Having ascertained by inquiry which spots were most convenient, he ordered them to build the depots there, with supplies brought to various points by merchant ships and ferry-boats from all parts of Asia. They conveyed the greater part of the grain to the place in Thrace called Leuke Akte, others to Tyrodiza in the Perinthian territory, others to Doriscus, others to Eion on the Strymon, and others to Macedonia — the work divided among them.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 26
paragraphs: While these men were at their appointed tasks, the whole land army had been brought together and was marching with Xerxes to Sardis, setting out from Critalla in Cappadocia — for it had been ordered that the entire army which was to go with Xerxes himself by land should assemble there. Which of the provincial governors brought the best-equipped force and received the gifts from the king I am unable to say, for I do not know that they even came to such a competition. After they had crossed the river Halys and entered Phrygia, they marched through that country to Celaenae, where the springs of the Maeander rise, and also those of another river no smaller than the Maeander, whose name is Catarractes; this one rises in the very marketplace of Celaenae and flows into the Maeander. Here too is hung up in the city the skin of the Silenus Marsyas, which the Phrygians say was flayed off and hung there by Apollo.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 27
paragraphs: In this city Pythius son of Atys, a Lydian, was waiting for the king, and he entertained Xerxes and his whole army with the most magnificent hospitality; he also declared himself ready to supply funds for the war. When Pythius made this offer of money, Xerxes asked the Persians who were with him who Pythius was and how much money he possessed that he could make such an offer. They answered: “O king, this is the man who presented your father Darius with the golden plane-tree and the golden vine; and he is even now, in wealth, the first of all men we know of, excepting you alone.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 28
paragraphs: Astonished at this last statement, Xerxes himself then asked Pythius how much money he had. Pythius answered: “O king, I will not hide the truth from you, nor will I excuse myself by saying that I do not know my own wealth, but I will tell it to you precisely, since I know. As soon as I heard that you were coming down to the Sea of Greece, wishing to give you money for the war, I ascertained the true figures, and reckoning I found that I had two thousand talents of silver, and in gold four million darics less seven thousand. This money I now present to you. For myself, I have enough to live on from my slaves and my estates.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 29
paragraphs: So he spoke, and Xerxes, pleased by what he said, answered: “Lydian host, ever since I set out from the Persian land I have met no man up to this point who wished to entertain my army, or who came before me and of his own free will offered to contribute money for the war, except you alone. You not only entertained my army magnificently but now also offer me great sums of money. To you, therefore, I give these rewards in return: I make you my guest-friend, and I will complete for you the four million staters out of my own purse by adding the seven thousand, so that your four million may not fall short by seven thousand, but you may have a round sum by my contribution. Keep what you have made for yourself, and continue always to act in this manner, for if you do, you will never have cause for regret, either now or afterwards.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 30
paragraphs: Having said this and kept his word, Xerxes continued his march. Passing by a Phrygian city called Anaua and a lake from which salt is produced, he came to Colossae, a great city of Phrygia, where the river Lycus falls into a chasm in the earth and disappears from sight, and then, after about five stades, reappears above ground; this river too empties into the Maeander. Setting out from Colossae in the direction of the Phrygian-Lydian frontier, the army arrived at the city of Cydrara, where a pillar set up by Croesus bears an inscription declaring that this is the border.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 31
paragraphs: From Phrygia he entered Lydia, and here the road forks: the one going left leads to Caria, the one going right to Sardis. Taking this latter road, one must cross the Maeander and pass the city of Callatebus, where men make their living by producing a honey from tamarisk and wheat flour. Xerxes went by this road and found a plane-tree, to which, for its beauty, he gave an adornment of gold and appointed a keeper for it in perpetual succession. On the next day he came to the city of the Lydians.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 32
paragraphs: On reaching Sardis, he first sent heralds to Greece to demand earth and water and to give notice in advance that meals should be prepared for the king. However, he sent no envoys to Athens or Lacedaemon to ask for earth, but only to the other states. The reason for sending a second time to ask for earth and water was this: those who had not given them to Darius when he asked before, these, Xerxes thought, would certainly give them now out of fear. This was the matter about which he wished to have reliable information, and so he sent the envoys.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 33
paragraphs: After this he made preparations for marching to Abydos; and in the meantime the Hellespont was being bridged from Asia to Europe. Now in the Chersonese of the Hellespont, between the city of Sestos and Madytus, there is a broad headland running down into the sea directly opposite Abydos. This is the place where, not long afterwards, the Athenians under the command of Xanthippus son of Ariphron, having captured a Persian named Artayctes, the governor of Sestos, nailed him alive to a plank with hands and feet outstretched. He was the man who used to take women with him into the temple of Protesilaus at Elaeus and do unlawful things there.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 34
paragraphs: To this headland the men assigned to the job were now building their bridges, starting from Abydos — the Phoenicians constructing one with ropes of white flax, the Egyptians the other with papyrus rope. From Abydos to the opposite shore is a distance of seven stades. When the strait had been bridged, a great storm came on and shattered the whole work, breaking it up. When Xerxes heard of it, he was beside himself with rage, and ordered the Hellespont scourged with three hundred lashes and a pair of fetters lowered into the sea. I have heard, moreover, that he sent branding-irons too, to brand the Hellespont. However that may be, he commanded his men, as they were lashing, to utter these barbarous and presumptuous words: “Bitter water, your master lays this penalty upon you, because you wronged him, having suffered no wrong from him. And Xerxes the king will cross you, whether you like it or not; it is with right, it seems, that no man sacrifices to you, since you are a treacherous and briny stream.” So he ordered the sea to be punished, and he also ordered the heads cut off of those in charge of bridging the Hellespont.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 36
paragraphs: So the men charged with this distasteful work carried out their orders. Meanwhile other master-builders were busy making the bridges, in this way. They laid fifty-oared galleys and triremes together side by side, three hundred and sixty of them to form the bridge on the Black Sea side, and three hundred and fourteen on the other, the vessels lying at an angle to the current of the Hellespont (but crosswise to the Pontus), so as to take the strain of the cables. Having arranged them thus, they dropped very large anchors — those on the Pontus side to hold against the winds blowing out from within, those on the western and Aegean side against the south-east and south winds. They also left an opening as a channel, so that any ship that wished might sail in or out of the Pontus in small vessels. This done, they proceeded to tighten the cables, straining them with wooden windlasses — no longer using the two kinds of rope separately, but assigning to each bridge two ropes of white flax and four of papyrus. The thickness and the quality of workmanship were the same for both; but the flax ropes were heavier in proportion, and of this rope one cubit weighed a talent. With the strait now bridged, they sawed logs into sections equal to the width of the bridge, laid them atop the tensioned cables, and, having set them in order, fastened them together. Once that was done, they carried on brushwood, and having set the brushwood in place, they heaped earth on top of it and tamped it down firmly. Finally they built a barrier along each side, so that the pack animals and horses would not be frightened by looking out over the sea.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 37
paragraphs: When the building of the bridges had been finished, and the works about Athos — both the embankments built around the mouths of the channel (so that the surf beating on the beach would not silt them up) and the channel itself — were reported to be fully completed, then, after wintering at Sardis, the army set forth from there fully equipped at the beginning of spring, to march to Abydos. As it was just setting out, the sun left its place in the sky and was invisible, though there was no gathering of clouds and the sky was perfectly clear; and instead of day it became night. When Xerxes saw and took notice of this, it became a matter of concern to him, and he asked the Magi what the appearance portended. They answered that the god was foreshowing to the Greeks the abandoning of their cities, for the sun, they said, was the foreshower of events for the Greeks, but the moon for the Persians. Thus informed, Xerxes proceeded on the march in very great good cheer.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 38
paragraphs: Then as he was leading his army out on its march, Pythius the Lydian, alarmed by the heavenly sign and emboldened by the gifts he had received, came to Xerxes and said: “Master, I would like to ask you for a certain thing, which as it happens is an easy thing for you to grant but a great thing for me if I obtain it.” Xerxes, thinking that the request would be for anything rather than what it actually was, said he would grant it, and bade him speak out and say what he wanted. Pythius, encouraged by this, said: “Master, I have, as it happens, five sons, and it is their lot to be going with you on the march against Greece — all of them. Have pity on me, O king, seeing that I have come to so great an age, and release one of my sons from serving on the campaign, the eldest, so that he may take care of me and of my wealth. The other four take with you, and after you have accomplished what you have in mind, may you have a safe return home.”

Xerxes was furiously angry and answered: “Wretched man, do you dare — when I myself am marching against Greece, taking my sons and brothers and kinsmen and friends — do you dare mention so much as a son of your own, seeing that you are my slave, who ought to be following me in person with your whole household and your wife as well? Know then this: the passionate spirit of a man dwells within his ears; when it has heard good things, it fills the body with delight; when it has heard the opposite, it swells up with rage. Just as you cannot boast of having outdone the king in benefits before, when you did us good deeds and offered to do still more of the same kind, so now, since you have turned to shamelessness, you shall receive not what you deserve but less than you deserve. Your gifts of hospitality shall save from death yourself and four of your sons; but you shall pay the penalty with the life of the one to whom you cling most.” Having so answered, he at once ordered those whose task it was to find the eldest of Pythius's sons and cut him in two in the middle; and when they had cut him, to place the halves one on the right of the road and the other on the left, so that the army should pass between them on its way.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 40
paragraphs: When they had done this, the army proceeded to pass between the halves. First the baggage-carriers and their horses led the way, and after them came the host of every kind of nation mixed together without distinction. When more than half had gone by, a gap was left to separate these from the king. Before Xerxes himself went first a thousand horsemen, picked out of all the Persians; and after them a thousand spearmen likewise picked from all the Persians, with the points of their spears turned down toward the ground. Then came ten sacred horses, called “Nesaean,” in the most splendid trappings. These horses are called Nesaean for this reason: there is a broad plain in Media called the Nesaean plain, and this plain produces the great horses of which I speak. Behind these ten came the sacred chariot of Zeus, drawn by eight white horses; and behind the horses came, on foot, a charioteer holding the reins — for no mortal ever mounts the seat of that chariot. Then, behind this, came Xerxes himself in a chariot drawn by Nesaean horses; beside him rode a charioteer named Patiramphes son of Otanes, a Persian.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 41
paragraphs: Thus did Xerxes march out of Sardis, and he would change, whenever it suited him, from his chariot to a traveling carriage. Behind him went a thousand spearmen — the best and most noble of the Persians — holding their spears in the usual manner. After them came another thousand cavalry picked from the Persians; and after those horsemen, ten thousand men selected from the rest of the Persians. These went on foot, and of them a thousand had golden pomegranates on their spears instead of butt-spikes, and these enclosed the remaining nine thousand on all sides, who had silver pomegranates. Those who had their spear-points turned toward the earth also had golden pomegranates; those who followed immediately after Xerxes had golden apples. Behind the ten thousand was stationed a force of ten thousand Persian cavalry; and after the cavalry there was a gap of some two stades. Then the rest of the army came on, marching all mixed together.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 42
paragraphs: So the army proceeded on its march from Lydia to the river Caïcus and the land of Mysia; and setting out from the Caïcus and keeping Mount Cane on its left, it marched through the territory of Atarneus to the city of Carene. From there it went through the plain of Thebe, passing the cities of Adramyttium and the Pelasgian Antandrus; and keeping Mount Ida on its left, it came on into the land of Ilium. When it first halted for the night close under Mount Ida, thunder and bolts of lightning fell upon it and destroyed a very great many men in that place.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 43
paragraphs: When the army had come to the river Scamander — the first of all the rivers they had reached since setting out from Sardis, whose stream failed and was not sufficient for the drinking of the army and its animals — when, I say, Xerxes came to this river, he went up to the Citadel of Priam, wishing to see it. Having viewed it and learned all its details by inquiry, he sacrificed a thousand heifers to Athena of Ilium, and the Magi poured libations in honor of the heroes. After they had done this, a panic fell upon the army in the night. At daybreak Xerxes set out from there, keeping on his left the cities of Rhoeteum, Ophryneum, and Dardanus (which borders Abydos), and on his right the Gergith Teucrians.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 44
paragraphs: When Xerxes had come to the middle of Abydos, he desired to review the whole army. A raised seat of white stone had been prepared for him beforehand on a hill at this place, built by the people of Abydos on the king's previous command. There he took his seat, and looking down upon the shore he surveyed both the land army and the ships. As he gazed at them, the wish came over him to see a regatta held among the ships. When it took place and the Sidonian Phoenicians were victorious, he was delighted both with the race and with the whole armament.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 45
paragraphs: Seeing all the Hellespont covered over with his ships, and all the shores and plains of Abydos filled with men, Xerxes declared himself a happy man, and then fell to weeping.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 46
paragraphs: His uncle Artabanus — the same man who had at first boldly given his opinion advising Xerxes not to march against Greece — noticing that Xerxes was in tears, asked him: “O king, how different are the things you are doing now from those of a moment ago! Having just declared yourself a happy man, you are now shedding tears.” Xerxes answered: “Yes — for when I reckoned the matter over, pity stole over me at the thought how brief is the whole life of man, seeing that of all these multitudes not one will be alive a hundred years from now.” Artabanus replied: “In the course of our life we are subject to a thing more pitiable still: though life is so short, no one, of these men or of others, is by nature so happy that there will not come upon him many times — not just once — the wish to be dead rather than alive; for misfortunes falling upon us, and diseases disturbing our happiness, make the span of life, short as it is, seem long. Thus, since life is full of trouble, death has become the most welcome refuge for man; and God, having given him a taste of the sweetness of life, is shown in this matter to be full of envy.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 47
paragraphs: Xerxes answered: “Artabanus, of human life, which is as you define it, let us stop speaking — and let us not remember evils when we have good things in hand. But tell me this: if the vision of the dream had not appeared to you with such clarity, would you still be holding to your former opinion and trying to stop me from marching against Greece, or would you have changed? Come, tell me exactly.” He replied: “O king, may the vision of the dream that appeared have the fulfillment that we both desire! But I am still to this moment full of dread and cannot contain myself, when I consider many things, and especially when I see that two things, which are the greatest of all, are utterly hostile to you.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 48
paragraphs: To this Xerxes answered: “You strangest of men, what is the nature of these two things which you say are utterly hostile to me? Is it that our land army is to be faulted in point of numbers, and that the Greek army seems to you likely to be many times larger than ours? Or do you think that our fleet will fall short of theirs? Or even that both will prove true? For if you think our power falls short in these respects, we could gather a still larger force at once.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 49
paragraphs: Artabanus answered: “O king, no one with sense could fault this army, nor the number of the ships; and indeed, if you assemble more, the two things I am speaking of will become only more hostile. These two things are the land and the sea. Nowhere in the sea, I suppose, is there a harbor large enough to receive this fleet of yours and keep the ships safe if a storm should arise — and it is not one such harbor that is needed, but harbors of that size along the whole of the coastline past which you are sailing. If there are no harbors to receive your ships, know that circumstance will master men, not men circumstance. Having told you of one of the two things, I come now to the other. The land, I say, becomes hostile to you in this way: even if nothing rises up to oppose you, the land becomes more hostile the further you advance, as you steal on still further and further; for men never know satiety of good fortune. And this I tell you: with no one standing against you, the country you traverse, growing larger as time goes on, will produce famine for you. The best condition for a man is this: when taking counsel, to feel fear, and to reckon on suffering everything that might come; but in doing the deed, to be bold.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 50
paragraphs: Xerxes answered: “Artabanus, you reason these matters out reasonably; but do not fear everything, nor weigh each possibility equally. If you set yourself to reckon everything that may happen, weighing it all equally, you would never perform any deed at all. It is better to be of good courage about everything and suffer half the evils that threaten, than to fear everything in advance and suffer nothing at all. If, always arguing against everything that is said, you fail to show the safe course, you earn the same reproach of failure as the man who says the opposite. This, then, is evenly balanced. But how should a mere man know the safe course? I think, in no way. To those who choose to act, gain most often comes; to those who reckon up everything and shrink back, it rarely comes. You see to what great might the power of the Persians has advanced. If the kings who came before me had held opinions like yours, or, without holding them themselves, had had counsellors like you, you would never have seen that power brought forward to this point. As it is, by running risks they brought it here, for great power is generally won by running great risks. We, following their example, are marching now in the finest season of the year; and when we have subdued all Europe, we shall return home, without having met with famine anywhere, or suffering any other unpleasant thing. For we march with great stores of food of our own, and beyond that, we shall have the grain harvests of all the peoples whose lands we come to; and we are marching against men who plow the soil, not against nomad tribes.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 51
paragraphs: After this Artabanus said: “O king, since you urge us to fear nothing, let me ask you to accept one more piece of counsel from me — for when so many things are in question, the discussion must necessarily be longer. Cyrus son of Cambyses subdued all Ionia except the Athenians and made it tributary to the Persians. These men, I counsel you, you should by no means lead against their parent stock, seeing that even without them we are able to get the better of our enemies. For if they go with us, either they must prove themselves great wrongdoers by joining in the enslavement of their mother city, or great righteous men by joining in freeing her. If they show themselves great wrongdoers, they bring us no great advantage besides; but if they show themselves great righteous men, they are capable of doing much harm to your army. Take to heart, then, the ancient saying, how well it was said, that at the very beginning of things the end does not fully appear.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 52
paragraphs: To this Xerxes replied: “Artabanus, of all the opinions you have uttered, in this one you are most mistaken — in fearing that the Ionians might change sides. Of them we have a most certain proof, of which you yourself are witness, and the others too who went with Darius on his march against the Scythians — namely this, that the whole Persian army came to depend upon these men, whether to destroy it or save it, and they showed themselves just and faithful, and did nothing at all unfriendly. Besides this, they have left their children, wives, and possessions in our land, so we must not even imagine that they will rebel. Do not fear this thing either, but be of good heart and keep safe my house and my government; for to you of all men I entrust my sceptre of rule.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 53
paragraphs: Having spoken thus and having sent Artabanus back to Susa, Xerxes next summoned before him the most distinguished men of the Persians, and when they had come, he said: “Persians, I have assembled you because I want you to show yourselves good men and not to disgrace what was done in former times by the Persians, which is great and glorious. Let each of us individually, and all of us together, be zealous in our enterprise — for what we are laboring for is a common good for all. I urge you, moreover, to press on in the war without slackening your efforts, for as I am told we are marching against brave men, and if we defeat them there will be no other army of men that will ever stand against us. So now let us begin the crossing, having first prayed to those gods who have the Persians for their allotted care.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 54
paragraphs: During that day they made preparations to cross over; and on the next day they waited for the sun, wishing to see him rise, and meanwhile they burned every kind of incense upon the bridges and strewed the way with branches of myrtle. As the sun was rising, Xerxes poured a libation from a golden cup into the sea and prayed to the Sun that no accident might befall him such as would make him stop subduing Europe before he had come to its furthest limits. After praying, he threw the cup into the Hellespont, and with it a golden mixing-bowl and a Persian sword, which they call an akinakes. Whether he cast these into the sea as an offering dedicated to the Sun, or whether he had repented of having lashed the Hellespont and wished to make amends by a gift, I cannot say for certain.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 55
paragraphs: When Xerxes had done this, they began to cross. The whole army, both foot and horse, went by one bridge — the one on the Pontus side — while the pack animals and servants went by the other, which was on the Aegean side. First the ten thousand Persians led the way, all wearing wreaths, and after them came the mixed contingents of the army made up of all kinds of nations — these crossed that day. On the next day, first the cavalry and those who carried their spears point-downward, also wearing wreaths; after them the sacred horses and the sacred chariot; and then Xerxes himself, with his spear-bearers and the thousand horsemen; and after them the rest of the army. Meanwhile the ships too put out from shore and crossed to the other side. I have heard, however, another account, that the king crossed very last of all.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 56
paragraphs: When Xerxes had crossed over into Europe, he watched the army crossing under the whip; his army crossed in seven days and seven nights of unbroken passage. Then, it is said, after Xerxes had crossed the Hellespont, a man of that coast exclaimed: “Why, O Zeus, in the likeness of a Persian man and taking for yourself the name Xerxes instead of Zeus, are you proposing to ravage Greece, taking all the nations of men with you? You could have done this without their help.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 57
paragraphs: When all had crossed and had set out on their way, a great portent appeared to them, to which Xerxes paid no attention, though its meaning was easy to guess: a mare gave birth to a hare. The meaning was easy to guess: Xerxes was about to march an army against Greece most proudly and magnificently, but would come running back for his life to the place from which he had started. There had been another portent earlier, while he was still at Sardis: a mule brought forth young, and the offspring was a mule with both male and female genitals, the male above the female. But Xerxes took no notice of either of these portents and went on his way, and the land army with him.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Meanwhile the fleet was sailing out of the Hellespont and coasting along in the opposite direction from the land army, for the fleet was making west toward the promontory of Sarpedon, to which it had been previously ordered to go and wait for the army. The land army meanwhile was marching east, toward the sunrise, through the Chersonese, keeping on its right the tomb of Helle the daughter of Athamas, and on its left the city of Cardia, passing through the middle of a town called Agora. From there, bending around the Gulf of Melas and crossing the river Melas (whose stream did not suffice for the army at that time and ran dry), the army — having crossed this river, from which the gulf also takes its name — went westward, passing the Aeolian city of Aenus and the lake Stentoris, until at last it arrived at Doriscus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 59
paragraphs: Doriscus is a seashore and a plain of great size in Thrace, through which the great river Hebrus flows. Here a royal fortress had been built — the one now called Doriscus — and a Persian garrison had been stationed in it by Darius, ever since the time when he went on his march against the Scythians. The place seemed to Xerxes convenient for marshaling and counting his army, and he proceeded to do so. The commanders of the ships, at Xerxes's bidding, had brought all the vessels, when they reached Doriscus, up to the shore adjoining it, on which stand the Samothracian city of Sale and also Zone, whose furthest point is the promontory of Serreion, a well-known landmark. This region in ancient times had belonged to the Cicones. The ships were beached there, and while they lay drawn up and drying out, he was numbering the army at Doriscus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 60
paragraphs: As for the number each separate nation supplied, I cannot give exact information, since none of my sources give it; but the total of the whole land army proved to be one million seven hundred thousand. They counted them as follows. They gathered together in one place a body of ten thousand men and packed them as tightly as they could, then drew a circle around them on the outside. Having drawn the circle and let the ten thousand go, they built a wall of loose stones around the circumference, rising to a man's navel. Having done this, they made others enter the walled space, until in this way they had counted them all. After counting them, they organized them by nations.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 61
paragraphs: Those who served were these. The Persians, with this equipment: upon their heads they wore soft felt caps called tiaras, and on their bodies colorful sleeved tunics that looked like iron scales such as a fish's; around their legs, trousers. Instead of the ordinary shields they carried wicker shields, beneath which hung their quivers; and they carried short spears, large bows, reed arrows, and daggers hanging from the belt by the right thigh. Their commander, whom they acknowledged as such, was Otanes, the father of Xerxes's wife Amestris. These people were called Cephenes by the Greeks of old, but by themselves and by their neighbors they were called Artaeans. When Perseus son of Danaë and Zeus came to Cepheus son of Belus and married his daughter Andromeda, a son was born to them whom he named Perses, and this son he left behind there — for it happened that Cepheus had no male offspring. It is from him that the race was named.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 62
paragraphs: The Medes served in the expedition equipped in precisely the same way, for this is in fact Median gear, not Persian; the Medes acknowledged as their commander Tigranes, an Achaemenid. In ancient times these people were generally called Arians, but when Medea the Colchian came from Athens to these Arians, they too changed their name. So the Medes themselves say of themselves. The Cissians served with equipment otherwise like that of the Persians, but instead of felt caps they wore turbans; their commander was Anaphes son of Otanes. The Hyrcanians were armed like the Persians, acknowledging as their leader Megapanus, the same man who after these events became governor of Babylon.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 63
paragraphs: The Assyrians served with bronze helmets on their heads, or with helmets plaited in a barbarian style not easily described; they carried shields and spears, and daggers like the Egyptian knives, and also wooden clubs studded with iron knobs, and linen corselets. These are called Syrians by the Greeks, but by the barbarians they have always been called Assyrians; among them were also the Chaldeans. Their commander was Otaspes son of Artachaees.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 64
paragraphs: The Bactrians wore on their heads nearly the same covering as the Medes, and they had native bows of reed and short spears. The Sacae — who are Scythians — wore on their heads caps rising to a point and standing stiff and upright; they wore trousers and carried native bows and daggers, and also axes of the kind called sagaris. These were called the Amyrgian Sacae, though they were in fact Scythians, for the Persians call all Scythians Sacae. The commander of the Bactrians and the Sacae was Hystaspes, son of Darius and of Atossa daughter of Cyrus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 65
paragraphs: The Indians wore garments made of tree-wool (cotton), and they had bows of reed and reed arrows tipped with iron. Such was the equipment of the Indians; they served under the command of Pharnazathres son of Artabates.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 66
paragraphs: The Arians were equipped with Median bows, and in other respects like the Bactrians; their commander was Sisamnes son of Hydarnes. The Parthians, Chorasmians, Sogdians, Gandarians, and Dadicae served with the same equipment as the Bactrians. Their commanders were Artabazus son of Pharnaces over the Parthians and Chorasmians; Azanes son of Artaeus over the Sogdians; and Artyphius son of Artabanus over the Gandarians and Dadicae. The Caspians served wearing skin coats and carrying native reed bows and short swords; such was their equipment, and they acknowledged as their leader Ariomardus, the brother of Artyphius. The Sarangae were conspicuous among the rest for their brightly dyed garments; they wore boots reaching to the knee and carried Median bows and spears. Their commander was Pherendates son of Megabazus. The Pactyes wore skin coats and carried native bows and daggers; they acknowledged as their commander Artayntes son of Ithamitres.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 68
paragraphs: The Utii, Myci, and Paricanii were equipped like the Pactyes; their commanders were Arsamenes son of Darius over the Utii and Myci, and Siromitres son of Oeobazus over the Paricanii.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 69
paragraphs: The Arabians wore loose cloaks belted up, and they carried on their right side long bows that bent backward. The Ethiopians wore leopard-skins and lion-skins tied upon them, and they had bows made of a strip of palm-wood, of great length, no less than four cubits, and for them small reed arrows with a sharpened stone tip instead of iron — the same stone they use for engraving seals. In addition they had spears tipped with a sharpened gazelle horn in place of a spear-head, and knob-studded clubs. Before going into battle they used to smear half their bodies with white and the other half with red. The commander of both the Arabians and of the Ethiopians who lived above Egypt was Arsames, son of Darius and of Artystone, the daughter of Cyrus whom Darius loved most of all his wives and of whom he had an image made in beaten gold.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 70
paragraphs: Such, then, was the commander of the Ethiopians above Egypt and of the Arabians — namely Arsames. But the Ethiopians from the direction of the sunrise (for the Ethiopians were in two contingents) had been assigned to serve with the Indians, differing from the other Ethiopians in no way except in their language and in the nature of their hair: the eastern Ethiopians have straight hair, while those of Libya have hair more thickly curled than any other men's. These Asian Ethiopians were armed for the most part like the Indians, but on their heads they wore the skin of a horse's forehead, flayed off together with the ears and mane, the mane serving as a crest, while the ears were set up straight and stiff. In place of shields they used protections of crane-skin held in front of them.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 71
paragraphs: The Libyans marched in leather gear and carried javelins hardened in fire at the point. They acknowledged as their commander Massages son of Oarizus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 72
paragraphs: The Paphlagonians served with plaited helmets on their heads, small shields, spears of no great size, and also javelins and daggers; on their feet they wore native boots reaching halfway up the shin. The Ligyes, Matieni, Mariandyni, and Syrians served with the same equipment as the Paphlagonians; these Syrians are called Cappadocians by the Persians. The commanders were Dotus son of Megasidrus over the Paphlagonians and Matieni, and Gobryas son of Darius and Artystone over the Mariandyni, Ligyes, and Syrians.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 73
paragraphs: The Phrygians had equipment very much like that of the Paphlagonians, with slight differences. The Phrygians, according to the Macedonians, used to be called Briges during the time when they were natives of Europe and lived among the Macedonians; but after they had migrated to Asia, together with their country they changed their name and came to be called Phrygians. The Armenians were armed just like the Phrygians, being settlers from them. The commander of both together was Artochmes, who was married to a daughter of Darius.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 74
paragraphs: The Lydians had arms very closely resembling those of the Greeks. The Lydians were in older times called Maeonians, and they were renamed after Lydus son of Atys, exchanging their earlier name. The Mysians wore native helmets on their heads, carried small shields, and used javelins hardened at the tip by fire. They are settlers from the Lydians, and from Mount Olympus they take the name Olympieni. The commander of the Lydians and Mysians was Artaphernes son of Artaphernes, the same man who invaded Marathon together with Datis.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 75
paragraphs: The Thracians served wearing fox-skins on their heads and tunics over their bodies, with multicolored cloaks thrown loosely over them; on their feet and lower legs they wore fawn-skin boots. In addition they had javelins, small round shields, and short daggers. After they had crossed over into Asia, these men came to be called Bithynians; but formerly, as they themselves say, they were called Strymonians, since they had lived by the river Strymon; they say they were driven out of their old homes by the Teucrians and Mysians. The commander of the Thracians who lived in Asia was Bassakes son of Artabanus.

They carried small shields of raw oxhide, and each man carried two hunting-spears of Lycian make. On their heads they wore bronze helmets to which the ears and horns of an ox were attached, also in bronze, with crests on top; and their lower legs were wrapped with strips of red cloth. Among these men there is an oracle of Ares.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 77
paragraphs: The Maeonian Cabalians, who are called Lasonians, had the same equipment as the Cilicians — what that was I shall explain when in the course of my catalogue I come to the Cilician contingent. The Milyans carried short spears, and their garments were fastened with brooches; some of them had Lycian bows, and on their heads they wore leather caps. The commander of all these was Badres son of Hystanes.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 78
paragraphs: The Moschi wore wooden caps on their heads and carried shields and small spears with long points set on them. The Tibareni, Macrones, and Mossynoeci served with equipment like the Moschi's, and they were arrayed together under the following commanders: the Moschi and Tibareni under Ariomardus, son of Darius and Parmys, daughter of Smerdis son of Cyrus; the Macrones and Mossynoeci under Artayctes son of Cherasmis, the governor of Sestos on the Hellespont.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 79
paragraphs: The Mares wore on their heads native plaited helmets and carried small hide shields and javelins. The Colchians wore wooden helmets, carried small shields of raw oxhide, short spears, and also knives. The commander of the Mares and Colchians was Pharandates son of Teaspis. The Alarodians and Saspires served armed like the Colchians; their commander was Masistius son of Siromitres.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 80
paragraphs: The island tribes who marched with the army from the Erythraean Sea — those who inhabited the islands where the king settles the people called the “Removed” — had clothing and arms very similar to those of the Medes. Their commander was Mardontes son of Bagaeus, who the year after these events was commander of the army at Mycale and lost his life in the battle.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 81
paragraphs: These were the nations that served in the land campaign and had been assigned to the infantry. Of this army the men mentioned above were the commanders; they were the ones who drew it up in divisions, counted it, and appointed commanders of thousands and commanders of ten thousands. The commanders of hundreds and of tens were appointed by the commanders of ten thousands; and there were others who led divisions and nations.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 82
paragraphs: These, I say, who have been mentioned, were the commanders of the army. But over them, and over the whole infantry together, the commanders were Mardonius son of Gobryas, Tritantaechmes son of that Artabanus who had given the opinion that they should not make the march against Greece, Smerdomenes son of Otanes (both of them sons of Darius's brothers, and thus cousins of Xerxes), Masistes son of Darius and Atossa, Gergis son of Ariazus, and Megabyzus son of Zopyrus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 83
paragraphs: These were the generals of the whole infantry apart from the ten thousand; and of these ten thousand picked Persians the general was Hydarnes son of Hydarnes. These Persians were called the “Immortals,” because whenever any one of them made the number incomplete, whether by death or disease, another was chosen in his place, and they were never either more or fewer than ten thousand. Of all the nations, the Persians showed the greatest splendor of ornament and were themselves the best men. Their equipment was as described above, and besides this they were conspicuous among the rest for the lavish amount of gold they wore. They brought with them carriages, and in them concubines and a multitude of well-appointed attendants; and provisions for them, apart from those of the other soldiers, were carried on camels and pack animals.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 84
paragraphs: The nations that served as cavalry are the following — though not all the nations supplied cavalry, only those listed here. The Persians were equipped in the same way as their infantry, except that on their heads some of them wore beaten metalwork, whether of bronze or iron.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 85
paragraphs: There are also certain nomads called Sagartians, Persian in race and in language, whose dress is a blend of the Persian and the Pactyan. These furnished eight thousand cavalry, and they are not accustomed to carry weapons of either bronze or iron except daggers; instead they rely on ropes twisted of leather, and they trust to these when they go into war. Their way of fighting is this: when they come to grips with the enemy, they throw the ropes with nooses on the end, and whatever the man catches by the throw — horse or rider — he drags it to himself, and thus, entangled in the toils, the victims are destroyed.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 86
paragraphs: Such is the manner of fighting of these men, and they were arrayed next to the Persians. The Medes had the same equipment as their infantry, and the Cissians likewise. The Indians were armed in the same way as their foot soldiers, and they both rode horses and drove chariots drawn by horses or wild asses. The Bactrians were equipped as their infantry were, and the Caspians likewise. The Libyans too were equipped as their infantry, and all of them drove chariots. So too the Caspians and the Paricanians had equipment like their infantry, and they all rode on camels, which were no slower than horses.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 87
paragraphs: These were the only nations that served as cavalry, and their total number proved to be eighty thousand, apart from camels and chariots. The rest of the cavalry was arrayed in squadrons, but the Arabians were placed last of all, since the horses could not bear the camels, and so they were stationed last to keep the horses from being frightened.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 88
paragraphs: The cavalry commanders were Harmamithras and Tithaeus, both sons of Datis. But the third, Pharnouches, who had shared command of the cavalry with them, had been left behind at Sardis sick. For as they were setting out from Sardis, an unwelcome accident happened to him: as he was riding along, a dog darted under his horse's feet, and the horse, not having seen it beforehand, took fright, reared up, and threw Pharnouches off its back. Falling, he vomited blood, and his illness turned into consumption. As for the horse, his servants at once did as he had ordered: they led it away to the spot where it had thrown its master and cut off its legs at the knees. That is how Pharnouches was removed from his command.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 89
paragraphs: The number of the triremes proved to be twelve hundred and seven, and these were the peoples who supplied them. The Phoenicians, together with the Syrians who live in Palestine, furnished three hundred; they were equipped thus: on their heads they wore leather caps very like the Greek kind, and they wore linen corselets and carried rimless shields and javelins. The Phoenicians, according to their own account, lived in ancient times by the Erythraean Sea, and from there passed over and now inhabit the coast of Syria. This part of Syria, all the way to Egypt, is called Palestine. The Egyptians furnished two hundred ships. On their heads they wore plaited helmets; they had hollow shields with wide rims and spears for sea-fighting, and great battle-axes. Most of them wore corselets and carried large knives.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 90
paragraphs: Such was the equipment of the Egyptians. The Cyprians furnished a hundred and fifty ships and were themselves equipped as follows: their kings had their heads wound with turbans, while the rest wore tunics; in other respects they were like the Greeks. Among these there are various races: some come from Salamis and Athens, others from Arcadia, others from Cythnus, others from Phoenicia, and still others from Ethiopia, as the Cyprians themselves report.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 91
paragraphs: The Cilicians furnished a hundred ships; these men too wore native helmets on their heads, and for shields they carried round targets of raw oxhide. They wore woolen tunics, and each man carried two javelins and a sword, the sword very like the Egyptian knife. These people used to be called Hypachaeans in old times, and they took their later name from Cilix son of Agenor, a Phoenician. The Pamphylians furnished thirty ships and were equipped in Greek style. These Pamphylians are descended from those who were scattered from Troy together with Amphilochus and Calchas.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 92
paragraphs: The Lycians furnished fifty ships. They wore corselets and greaves, and carried bows of cornel-wood, featherless reed arrows, javelins, and a goat-skin slung over the shoulder; on their heads they wore feather-wreathed felt caps, and they carried daggers and falchions as well. The Lycians were formerly called Termilae, being originally from Crete, and they took their later name from Lycus son of Pandion, an Athenian.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 93
paragraphs: The Asian Dorians furnished thirty ships; they carried Greek arms and were originally from the Peloponnese. The Carians supplied seventy ships; they were equipped mostly like Greeks but also had falchions and daggers. What their former name was has been told in the first part of the history.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 94
paragraphs: The Ionians furnished a hundred ships and were equipped like Greeks. The Ionians, during the long time they lived in the Peloponnese, in the country now called Achaea, and before Danaus and Xuthus came to the Peloponnese, were called, as the Greeks report, Pelasgians of the Coast, and then were called Ionians after Ion son of Xuthus.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 95
paragraphs: The islanders furnished seventeen ships and were armed like Greeks; these too are a Pelasgian race, though they came later to be called Ionian by the same principle as the Ionians of the Twelve Cities, who came from Athens. The Aeolians supplied sixty ships; they were equipped like Greeks and used in old times to be called Pelasgians, as the Greeks report. The people of the Hellespont — except those of Abydus (for the men of Abydus had been appointed by the king to stay in place and guard the bridges) — the rest of those who served in the expedition from the Pontic region furnished a hundred ships and were equipped like Greeks. These are colonists of the Ionians and Dorians.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 96
paragraphs: On all the ships there served as fighting men Persians, Medes, or Sacae. Of the ships, those that sailed best were supplied by the Phoenicians, and among the Phoenicians the best were those of Sidon. Over all these men, and over those of them who were assigned to the land army as well, there were native chieftains for each people; but since the inquiry does not oblige me, I make no mention of them in passing — first because the chieftains of each nation were not persons worthy of mention, and second because within each nation there were as many chieftains as there were cities. These men went with the expedition not as commanders but like the rest, serving as slaves; for the generals who held absolute power and commanded the various nations — that is, those who were Persians — have already been named by me.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 97
paragraphs: The commanders of the naval force were these: Ariabignes son of Darius, Prexaspes son of Aspathines, Megabazus son of Megabates, and Achaemenes son of Darius. That is, the Ionian and Carian contingent was commanded by Ariabignes, son of Darius and of the daughter of Gobryas; the Egyptians by Achaemenes, full brother of Xerxes; and the rest of the armament by the other two. In all, the thirty-oared and fifty-oared galleys, the light craft, and the long horse-transport vessels had been gathered together, as it turned out, to a total of three thousand.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 98
paragraphs: Of those who sailed in the ships, the men of most note after the commanders were these: from Sidon, Tetramnestus son of Anysus; from Tyre, Matten son of Siromus; from Aradus, Merbalus son of Agbalus; from Cilicia, Syennesis son of Oromedon; from Lycia, Cyberniscus son of Sicas; from Cyprus, Gorgus son of Chersis and Timonax son of Timagoras; from Caria, Histiaeus son of Tymnes, Pigres son of Hysseldomus, and Damasithymus son of Candaules.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 99
paragraphs: Of the rest of the officers I make no mention in passing (since I am not obliged to), but only of Artemisia, who astonishes me most of all that she should have joined the expedition against Greece, being a woman. After her husband died, she held the power herself; and though she had a son who was a grown young man, she went on the expedition driven by her own high spirit and manly courage, under no compulsion. Her name, as I said, was Artemisia; she was the daughter of Lygdamis, and by descent she was on her father's side of Halicarnassus and on her mother's of Crete. She ruled over the people of Halicarnassus, Cos, Nisyrus, and Calydna, and supplied five ships. Her ships were reputed the best in the whole fleet after those of Sidon, and of all his allies she gave the king the best counsel. The states I say she led, I declare to be all of Dorian race: the people of Halicarnassus are Troezenians, and the rest are Epidaurians. So much, then, for the naval force.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 100
paragraphs: When Xerxes had had the army numbered and arranged in its divisions, he resolved to drive through it himself and review it, and he then proceeded to do so. Driving past each nation in turn in a chariot, he inquired about them, and his scribes wrote down the names, until he had gone from end to end both of the cavalry and of the infantry. When he had done this, the ships were drawn down into the sea, and Xerxes, changing from his chariot to a Sidonian ship, sat down under a golden canopy and sailed along past the prows, questioning each contingent as he had done with the land army and having the answers written down. The captains had taken their ships out to about four plethra from the beach and were holding them there, all with the prows turned in an even line toward the shore and the fighting men fully armed for war; Xerxes inspected them sailing in the channel between the prows and the beach.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 101
paragraphs: When he had sailed through the fleet and had disembarked from his ship, he sent for Demaratus son of Ariston, who was marching with him against Greece. When Demaratus was brought, Xerxes asked him this: “Demaratus, it now pleases me to ask you something I wish to know. You are not only a Greek, but also, as I have been told both by you and by the other Greeks who speak with me, of a city that is neither the smallest nor the weakest in Greece. Tell me, therefore, whether the Greeks will bring themselves to raise a hand against me. In my own view, even if all the Greeks and the other peoples of the west were gathered together, they would not be strong enough in battle to withstand my attack, if they should be my enemies. Still, I would like to hear your own opinion, whatever you have to say about these matters.” So he asked, and the other replied: “O king, shall I speak the truth to you, or that which will please?” Xerxes bade him speak the truth, saying that he would suffer nothing unpleasant in consequence, any more than he had before.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 102
paragraphs: When Demaratus heard this, he spoke as follows: “O king, since you bid me by all means to speak the truth, and so to speak as one who shall not afterwards be convicted by you of having lied, I say this: with Greece, poverty is always a native growth, but valor is one that has been brought in, gained by intelligence and the force of law. By means of this valor Greece defends herself continually, both against poverty and against a master's rule. Now, I have words of praise for all the Greeks settled in the Dorian lands, but what I am about to say concerns not all of them, only the Lacedaemonians. Of them I say, first, that there is no possibility they will ever accept your terms, which bring slavery to Greece; and second, that they will stand against you in battle even if all the other Greeks are on your side. As for numbers, do not ask how many they must be to do this. If a thousand of them have taken the field, they will fight with you — or if it is fewer than that, or more.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 103
paragraphs: Xerxes, hearing this, laughed and said: “Demaratus, what a thing is this you have said — that a thousand men will fight with so vast an army! Come, tell me: you say that you yourself were once king of these men. Will you, then, be willing right now to fight with ten men? And yet, if your state is such throughout as you describe, you, their king, ought by your own laws to stand in battle against twice as many as another man — that is, if each one of them is a match for ten of my army, I expect you to be a match for twenty. Thus the report you give of them would be borne out. But if you, who make so great a boast, are men of the same size and quality as the Greeks I commonly deal with, yourself included, then take care that what has been said does not turn out to be an empty boast. For come, let me examine the matter by every probability. How could a thousand men, or ten thousand, or even fifty thousand, all equally free and not ruled by one man, stand against so great an army? Since, as you know, there will be more than a thousand of us for each one of them, supposing them to be five thousand in number. Now if they were ruled by one man after our fashion, they might, out of fear of him, become braver than is their nature, or they might be driven by the lash to fight with greater numbers while being fewer themselves. But left to their own freedom, they would do neither. For my part I suppose that even if they were matched equally in numbers, the Greeks would hardly dare fight the Persians alone. With us, the thing you speak of is to be found in single men — not often, but rarely; for there are some Persian spearmen of mine who will consent to fight three Greeks at a time. You have had no experience of such men, and so you speak very much at random.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 104
paragraphs: To this Demaratus replied: “O king, from the first I was sure that if I told the truth, I would not be speaking anything pleasing to you. But since you compelled me to speak the very truth, I told you about the affairs of the Spartans. Yet you know better than anyone how I am at this present time affectionately disposed toward them — seeing that they first stripped me of the rank and privileges inherited from my fathers, and then made me a stateless exile. Your father took me in, gave me a livelihood and a house to live in. It is surely not reasonable to suppose that a prudent man would push aside the friendliness offered to him; rather he would accept it gratefully. I do not profess that I can fight ten men, or even two; if I had my choice, I would not even fight one. But if there were necessity, or some great cause pressing me into combat, I would most willingly fight one of those men who claim each to be a match for three Greeks. So too the Lacedaemonians, one against one, are inferior to no men, and in a body they are the best of all. For though they are free, they are not free in all things: over them is set Law as their master, whom they fear far more than your people fear you. At any rate, whatever their master commands, they do; and he commands always the same thing — he forbids them to flee out of battle before any multitude of men, but orders them to stay at their post and either win the victory or lose their life. If I seem to you to be speaking foolishly in saying these things, I prefer from now on to be silent about the rest; I spoke now only because I was forced. May it nevertheless turn out as you wish, O king.”

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 105
paragraphs: Such was his reply, and Xerxes turned the matter into laughter and felt no anger, but dismissed him kindly. After their conversation, having appointed Mascames son of Megadostes to be governor at Doriscus, removing the one whom Darius had appointed, Xerxes marched his army on through Thrace to invade Greece.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 106
paragraphs: Mascames, whom he left behind here, proved to be a man of such qualities that to him alone Xerxes used to send gifts, reckoning him the best of all the men whom he or Darius had appointed as governors. He used to send him gifts every year, and so did Artaxerxes son of Xerxes afterwards to Mascames's descendants. For even before this campaign, governors had been appointed throughout Thrace and everywhere around the Hellespont; but all of these — both in Thrace and on the Hellespont — were conquered by the Greeks after this expedition, except only the one at Doriscus. Many tried to take Mascames at Doriscus, but none ever succeeded. For this reason the gifts are sent continually for him from whatever Persian king reigns at the time.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 107
paragraphs: Of those who were conquered by the Greeks, Xerxes reckoned no one a man of worth except Boges, who was at Eion; him he never ceased praising, and he paid very high honor to his children who survived him in Persia. Boges indeed proved worthy of great praise. When he was being besieged by the Athenians under Cimon son of Miltiades, and could have come out under a truce and returned home to Asia, he chose not to do so, for fear the king might think he had survived through cowardice; instead, he held out to the last. When there were no longer any provisions within the wall, he heaped up a great pyre, cut the throats of his children, his wife, his concubines and his servants, and threw them into the fire; after that he scattered all the gold and silver of the city from the wall into the river Strymon, and having done so, he threw himself into the fire. For this reason he is justly praised by the Persians to this day.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 108
paragraphs: From Doriscus Xerxes was pushing on to invade Greece, and as he went he compelled those he came across to join his march. For the whole country as far as Thessaly had, as I have set out before, been reduced to subjection and was tributary to the king, having been conquered by Megabazus and afterwards by Mardonius. Marching out of Doriscus, he passed first by the Samothracian strongholds, the westernmost of which is a city called Mesambria. Next comes Stryme, a city of the Thasians; between them flows the river Lisus, which at that time did not suffice to supply water for Xerxes's army but ran dry. This country was once called Gallaice, but is now called Briantice; strictly, however, it too belongs to the Cicones.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 109
paragraphs: Having crossed the dry bed of the river Lisus, he passed the Greek cities of Maroneia, Dicaea, and Abdera. These he passed by, along with the following notable lakes lying near them: the Ismarian lake, between Maroneia and Stryme; the Bistonian lake near Dicaea, into which two rivers, the Travus and the Compsatus, pour their waters. At Abdera he passed no noteworthy lake, but did pass the river Nestus, which there flows into the sea. Then, beyond these places, he went past cities of the mainland; near one of them happens to lie a lake about thirty stades in circumference, full of fish and very brackish, which the baggage animals alone drank dry by watering there. The name of this city is Pistyros.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 110
paragraphs: These coastal Greek cities, then, he passed, leaving them on his left. The Thracian tribes whose territory he marched through were the following: the Paeti, Cicones, Bistones, Sapaeans, Dersaeans, Edonians, and Satrae. Of these, those who lived along the coast accompanied him with their ships, while those of them who lived inland — the ones I have just listed — were compelled to accompany him on land, except the Satrae.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 111
paragraphs: The Satrae, so far as we know, have never yet submitted to any man; they remain to my own day still free, alone of all the Thracians. For they live in high mountains, covered with forests of every kind and with snow, and they are also highly skilled in war. These are the people who possess the oracle of Dionysus; that oracle is in their highest mountains. Of the Satrae, those who act as the interpreters of the shrine are the Bessi; a prophetess utters the oracles, as at Delphi; and beyond this there is nothing of a notable character.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 112
paragraphs: Having passed through the country just described, Xerxes next went by the strongholds of the Pierians, one of which is called Phagres and the other Pergamos. This way he made his march, passing close under the walls of these places and keeping Mount Pangaeum on his right, which is both great and lofty and has mines of gold and silver held by the Pierians and the Odomantians, and especially by the Satrae.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 113
paragraphs: Thus passing by the Paeonians, Doberes, and Paeoples, who live beyond Pangaeum toward the north, he went on westward until at last he came to the river Strymon and the city of Eion, of which Boges — the man I was speaking of a little earlier — was commander as long as he lived. The country about Mount Pangaeum is called Phyllis; it stretches westward as far as the river Angites, which flows into the Strymon, and southward as far as the Strymon itself. At this river the Magi offered sacrifices for good omens, slaughtering white horses.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 114
paragraphs: After these rites and many other charms for the river, at the Nine Ways in the land of the Edonians they crossed by the bridges, for they had found the Strymon already bridged. On being told that the place was called the Nine Ways, they buried alive there that number of boys and girls, children of the local inhabitants. Burying alive is a Persian custom: I am told that Amestris, the wife of Xerxes, when she had grown old, repaid her own life to the god who is said to dwell beneath the earth by burying twice seven children of Persian men of note.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 115
paragraphs: As the army marched on from the Strymon, it found a shore running toward the setting sun, and it passed by the Greek city of Argilus, which is situated there. This region, and the country lying above it, is called Bisaltia. Then, keeping on his left the gulf off Posideion, he went through the plain called the plain of Syleus, passing the Greek city of Stageirus, and so came to Acanthus, taking along with him as he went every one of these tribes and of those who dwell around Pangaeum, just as he had done with those I listed before — those by the coast serving in the fleet, those inland accompanying him on foot. This road along which Xerxes the king led his army, the Thracians neither disturb nor sow over, but hold it in the greatest reverence to this day.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 116
paragraphs: When he reached Acanthus, Xerxes proclaimed a formal guest-friendship with its people, presented them with Median dress, and praised them, seeing their zeal in his service and hearing of the work they had done on the digging.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 117
paragraphs: While Xerxes was at Acanthus, it happened that the man who had been in charge of the making of the channel, Artachaees by name, died of sickness. He was held in high regard by Xerxes, belonged to the Achaemenid family, was in stature the tallest of all the Persians — falling short by only four fingers of being five royal cubits in height — and he had the loudest voice of any man. Xerxes was deeply grieved at the loss of him, and carried him out and buried him with great honor, and the whole army joined in heaping up a mound for him. The people of Acanthus, on the instruction of an oracle, sacrifice to this Artachaees as a hero, invoking his name in their worship.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 118
paragraphs: Xerxes, then, was deeply grieved at the loss of Artachaees. Meanwhile the Greeks who were entertaining his army and providing Xerxes with his dinners had been brought to utter ruin, to the point that they were being driven from house and home. For instance, when the Thasians entertained Xerxes's army and provided him with dinner on behalf of their towns on the mainland, Antipater son of Orgeus, a man of standing among the citizens equal to the best and appointed to this business, reported that four hundred talents of silver had been spent on that single meal.

chapters.title: Book VII — Polymnia, Chapter 119
