On being told that they had resolved to take the ships out to the Isthmus and fight a sea-battle in defense of the Peloponnese, he said: “Then if they set sail with the ships from Salamis, you will fight no more sea-battles at all for your fatherland — for they will each make off to their own cities, and neither Eurybiades nor anyone else will be able to hold them or prevent the fleet from being scattered; and Greece will perish through bad counsel. But if there is any means by which you can do it, go and try to upset what has been decided, in the hope of persuading Eurybiades to change his plans and stay here.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 58
paragraphs: This advice strongly commended itself to Themistocles; and without making any reply he went to Eurybiades's ship. Arriving there, he said he wished to communicate a matter that concerned the common good; Eurybiades told him to come on board and speak, if he had anything to say. So Themistocles, sitting down beside him, repeated everything Mnesiphilos had said, as if the ideas were his own, adding many more besides; until at last, by urgent request, he persuaded Eurybiades to come out of his ship and summon the commanders to a council.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 59
paragraphs: When they were gathered, and before Eurybiades had proposed the matters for which he had called the commanders together, Themistocles spoke with great vehemence, being very eager to gain his point. As he was speaking, the Corinthian commander, Adeimantos son of Okytos, said: “Themistocles, at the games those who step up for the contest before their time are beaten with rods.” Justifying himself, Themistocles replied: “Yes, but those who remain behind are not crowned.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 60
paragraphs: At that moment he answered the Corinthian mildly; and to Eurybiades he now said none of the things he had said before — about how, if they set sail from Salamis, the fleet would scatter in different directions — for it was unseemly to make accusations against the allies in their presence. Instead he held to another line of argument, saying: “Now it is in your power to save Greece, if you will follow my advice, which is to stay here and fight a sea-battle, and not follow the counsel of those among these men who urge you to move the ships to the Isthmus. Hear both options and compare them. If you engage battle at the Isthmus, you will fight in an open sea — into which it is in no way convenient for us to go, since our ships are heavier and fewer in number than the enemy's. Secondly, you will hand over Salamis, Megara, and Aegina to destruction, even if we succeed in everything else; for with their fleet will come their land-army too, and so you yourself will lead them to the Peloponnese and will put the safety of all Greece at risk. If, however, you do as I say, you will find in it all the advantages I shall describe: first, by engaging in a narrow space with few ships against many, if the fighting turns out as it is reasonable to expect, we shall have a great advantage — for fighting a sea-battle in a narrow space is to our advantage, while fighting in a wide open space is to theirs. Next, Salamis will be preserved, where our children and wives have been taken for safety; and there is this further point, which you value most of all: by remaining here you will fight in defense of the Peloponnese just as much as if the battle were at the Isthmus, and you will not lead the enemy to the Peloponnese, if you are wise. Then, if what I expect comes to pass and we win a victory with our ships, the barbarians will not come against you at the Isthmus nor advance beyond Attica, but will retreat in disorder; and we shall gain by the preservation of Megara, Aegina, and Salamis — the place where an oracle also tells us we shall overcome our enemies. When men take reasonable counsel for themselves, reasonable outcomes tend to follow; but if they do not take reasonable counsel, God is not usually inclined to attach himself to human judgment.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 61
paragraphs: When Themistocles spoke thus, the Corinthian Adeimantos attacked him a second time, telling him to be silent because he had no native land, and urging Eurybiades not to put to the vote the proposal of a man who was citizen of no city; he said that Themistocles might bring opinions before the council only if he could point to a city of his own, otherwise not. He made this objection because Athens had been taken and was held by the enemy. At this Themistocles said many harsh things of him and of the Corinthians both, and declared that he and his countrymen did in truth have a city and a land larger than the Corinthians', so long as they had two hundred ships fully manned — for none of the Greeks would be able to repel the Athenians if they came to fight against them.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 62
paragraphs: After this hint he turned to Eurybiades and spoke yet more urgently: “If you stay here and, staying, prove yourself a good man, well and good. But if not, you will bring about the ruin of Greece, for on the ships depends all our strength in the war. No — do as I advise. If, however, you will not do this, then we will at once take up our households and sail to Siris in Italy, which has long been ours, and which the oracles say is destined to be colonized by us. And you, left alone and deprived of such allies as we are, will remember my words.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 63
paragraphs: When Themistocles spoke thus, Eurybiades was persuaded to change his mind; and, I think, he changed his mind chiefly from fear that the Athenians might depart and abandon them if he moved the ships to the Isthmus — for if the Athenians left them and went, the rest would no longer be able to fight the enemy. So he chose this course: to remain where they were and decide matters there in a sea-battle.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 64
paragraphs: So those at Salamis, after their skirmishing with one another in speech, were now preparing for a sea-battle there, since Eurybiades had so decided. As day was dawning, just when the sun rose, an earthquake was felt both on land and on sea; and they decided to pray to the gods and call on the sons of Aiacos to be their helpers. As they decided, so they did: having prayed to all the gods, they called on Ajax and Telamon to come to their aid from Salamis, where the fleet was, and sent a ship to Aegina to bring back Aiacos himself and the rest of his sons.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 65
paragraphs: Dicaios son of Theokydes, an Athenian who was in exile and had become of great repute among the Medes at this time, declared that while Xerxes's land-army was ravaging Attica — deserted by the Athenians — he happened to be with Demaratos the Lacedaemonian in the Thriasian plain, and he saw a cloud of dust going up from Eleusis as though raised by a company of about thirty thousand men, and they wondered what men had caused the cloud. Then at once they heard a sound of voices, and Dicaios recognized the sound as the mystic cry “Iacchos!”; but Demaratos, having no knowledge of the sacred rites performed at Eleusis, asked him what was making the sound. He said: “Demaratos, it cannot be otherwise than that some great destruction is about to come upon the king's army. For it is plainly evident, since Attica is deserted, that what utters this sound is of the gods, and is going from Eleusis to help the Athenians and their allies. If it comes down into the Peloponnese, there is danger for the king himself and for the army on the mainland; but if it makes its way toward the ships at Salamis, the king will be in danger of losing his fleet. This feast the Athenians celebrate every year to the Mother and the Daughter; and anyone who wishes, both of them and of the other Greeks, is initiated into the mysteries. The sound of voices you hear is the cry ‘Iacchos!' which they utter at this feast.” To this Demaratos replied: “Keep silent and tell no one else this tale; for if these words of yours are reported to the king, you will surely lose your head, and neither I nor anyone else on earth will be able to save you. Stay quiet; the gods will provide concerning this expedition.” So he advised. After the cloud of dust and the sound of voices, there came a mist which rose aloft and was carried toward Salamis to the camp of the Greeks; and thus (said he) they learned that Xerxes's fleet was destined to be destroyed. Such was the report given by Dicaios son of Theokydes, appealing to Demaratos and others as witnesses.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 66
paragraphs: Meanwhile those appointed to serve in Xerxes's fleet, having observed from Trachis the disaster of the Lacedaemonians and crossed over from there to Histiaia, after staying three days sailed through the Euripos, and in another three days reached Phaleron. As I suppose, they made their attack on Athens with forces, both by land and sea, no fewer than when they had arrived at Sepias and Thermopylae. Against those who perished in the storm and those who fell at Thermopylae and in the sea-fights at Artemisium, I would set those who at that time had not yet been accompanying the king: the Malians, Dorians, Locrians, and Boeotians (who accompanied him as a body, except the Thespians and Plataeans), and moreover the men of Carystos, Andros, and Tenos, with all the other islanders except the five cities I named before. For the further the Persian advanced toward the center of Greece, the more nations joined him.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 67
paragraphs: So when all these had come to Athens, except the Parians (for the Parians had remained behind at Kythnos, waiting to see how the war would turn out) — when all the rest, I say, had arrived at Phaleron, Xerxes himself then came down to the ships, wishing to visit them and hear the opinions of those who sailed in them. When he had come and taken a conspicuous seat, the tyrants of their own nations and the divisional commanders, being summoned, came before him from their ships and took their seats in the rank the king had assigned each — first the king of Sidon, then of Tyre, and after them the rest. When they were seated in order, Xerxes sent Mardonius around, making trial of each, to ask whether he should fight a sea-battle.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 68
paragraphs: So as Mardonius went round questioning them, beginning with the king of Sidon, the others all gave the same opinion, advising him to fight at sea — but Artemisia spoke these words: “Tell the king, I pray you, Mardonius, that I — who have proven myself not the worst in the sea-fights near Euboea, having performed deeds not inferior to those of others — speak to him thus: ‘Master, it is right that I set forth the opinion I really hold, and say what I happen to think best for your cause: and this I say — spare your ships, and do not make a sea-fight. For the men are stronger than your men at sea by as much as men are stronger than women. And why must you run the risk of a sea-battle? Do you not have Athens in your possession — for which you marched out — and the rest of Greece as well? No one stands in your way to resist; those who did stand against you have come off as they deserved. Now I will declare how I think your adversaries' affairs will turn out. If you do not hurry to make a sea-fight, but keep your ships here by the land — either remaining here yourself or even advancing toward the Peloponnese — what you have come to do, O master, will easily be accomplished. For the Greeks cannot hold out against you for long; you will soon scatter them, and they will flee to their various cities, since (as I am told) they have no provisions with them on this island, nor is it likely that, if you march your land-army against the Peloponnese, those of them who came from there will remain still — for they will have no concern to fight a battle in defense of Athens. But if you hurry to fight at once, I fear that damage to the fleet may ruin the land-army as well. Moreover, O king, consider this too: servants of good men tend to become bad, while those of bad men become good. You, the best of all men, have bad servants — those reckoned among your allies: Egyptians, Cyprians, Cilicians, Pamphylians, who are of no use to you.'”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 69
paragraphs: When she spoke this way to Mardonius, those friendly to Artemisia were distressed by her words, supposing she would suffer some harm from the king for urging him not to fight at sea, while those who envied and resented her — because she had been honored above all the allies — rejoiced at the contradiction, supposing she was now ruined. When, however, the various opinions were reported to Xerxes, he was greatly pleased with Artemisia's; and whereas he had already thought her excellent, he commended her now even more. Nevertheless he gave orders to follow the advice of the majority, believing that when they had fought at Euboea they had been deliberately slack because he was not present, whereas now he had made himself ready to watch while they fought the battle.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 70
paragraphs: So when the word was passed to put to sea, they brought their ships out toward Salamis and quietly arranged themselves along the shore in their various positions. Daylight was no longer sufficient at that hour for them to engage, night having come on; but they made their preparations to fight the next day. Meanwhile the Greeks were seized with fear and dismay, especially those from the Peloponnese. They were dismayed because, remaining at Salamis, they were to fight a battle on behalf of the Athenians' land, and if defeated they would be cut off from escape and blockaded on an island, while leaving their own country undefended. And indeed the barbarians' land-army was marching forward that very night toward the Peloponnese.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 71
paragraphs: Yet every means had been taken to prevent the barbarians from entering the Peloponnese by land. As soon as the Peloponnesians heard that Leonidas and his company had perished at Thermopylae, they quickly gathered from their cities and took up position at the Isthmus, and over them was set as commander Cleombrotos, son of Anaxandrides and brother of Leonidas. Posted at the Isthmus, they had destroyed the Skironian way, and after this (having so decided in council) they began building a wall across the Isthmus. Being many tens of thousands, with every man joining in the work, it proceeded fast: stones, bricks, timbers, and baskets of sand were brought to it continually, and those who had come to help never paused in their labor either by night or by day.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 72
paragraphs: Those of the Greeks who came in full force to the Isthmus to help their country were these: the Lacedaemonians, Arcadians of every division, Eleians, Corinthians, Sikyonians, Epidaurians, Phliasians, Troizenians, and Hermionians. These were the ones who came to Greece's aid in her danger and felt alarm for her, while the rest of the Peloponnesians showed no concern — and by this time the Olympic and Carnean festivals had passed.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 73
paragraphs: The Peloponnese is inhabited by seven races. Of these, two are native to the soil and are settled in the place they dwelt in of old — the Arcadians and the Kynurians. One race, that of the Achaians, though it did not move out of the Peloponnese, did shift in former times from its own land and now lives in a land that was not originally its own. The remaining four races have come in from outside: the Dorians, Aitolians, Dryopians, and Lemnians. Of the Dorians there are many cities of great renown; of the Aitolians, Elis alone; of the Dryopians, Hermion and Asine (the latter opposite Cardamyle in Laconian territory); and of the Lemnians, all the Paroreatai. The Kynurians, though native to the soil, seem alone to be Ionians, but they have become thoroughly Dorian because they are subject to the Argives and by lapse of time, being originally citizens of Orneai or dwellers in the country around it. Of these seven nations, the remaining cities, apart from those I have just listed, stood aside and did nothing; and if one may speak freely, by standing aside they were in fact taking the side of the Medes.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 74
paragraphs: Those at the Isthmus were struggling with the labor I have described, since now they were running a race in which their very existence was at stake, and they did not expect any brilliant success from their ships. Those at Salamis, though informed of this work, were still dismayed, fearing not so much for themselves as for the Peloponnese. For a while they spoke of it in private, one man beside another, marveling at Eurybiades's bad counsel; but at last it broke out in public. A meeting was held, and much was said on the same points as before: some argued that they should sail away to the Peloponnese and take the risk in defense of that country, not stay and fight for a land that had already been taken by the enemy, while the Athenians, Aeginetans, and Megarians urged that they remain and defend themselves there.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 75
paragraphs: Then Themistocles, when his opinion was about to be defeated by the Peloponnesians, slipped secretly out of the assembly, and once outside sent a man in a boat to the Median camp, charging him with what to say. This man's name was Sikinnos; he was a servant of Themistocles and tutor to his children. After these events Themistocles enrolled him as a Thespian citizen, when the Thespians were admitting new citizens, and made him a wealthy man. At this time he came in a boat and said to the barbarian commanders these words: “The commander of the Athenians has sent me privately, without the knowledge of the other Greeks (for, as it happens, he is disposed to the king's cause and prefers that your side should win rather than the Greeks'), to inform you that the Greeks are planning to take flight, struck with dismay. Now you can accomplish a most noble deed, if you do not let them escape — for they are not of one mind with one another and will not stand against you in battle, but you will see them fighting a sea-battle among themselves, those who favor your side against those who do not.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 76
paragraphs: Having delivered this message, he slipped away. The Persians, thinking the report deserved credit, first landed a large contingent of their own men on the small island of Psyttaleia, which lies between Salamis and the mainland; and then, as midnight approached, they put the western wing of their fleet to sea, circling around toward Salamis. Those stationed about Keos and Kynosura also launched their ships, and they occupied the whole strait with their vessels as far as Munychia. The reason they put their ships out was so that the Greeks would not even be allowed to escape, but, cut off at Salamis, would pay the price for the battles at Artemisium. They landed Persian troops on the little island of Psyttaleia for this reason: that when the fight took place, these men might save their own side's survivors and kill those of the other, since that island especially was where men and wreckage were likely to be cast up on shore, lying as it did in the path of the coming sea-battle. All this they did in silence, so that the enemy should not have word of it.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 77
paragraphs: They, then, were making these preparations in the night without having taken any sleep at all. As for oracles, I am not able to raise objections that they are untrue; I do not wish to try to overthrow their credit when they speak clearly, in view of such things as these which follow:

“But when with ships they shall reach the sacred strand of the goddess — Artemis of the golden sword, and you, wave-washed Kynosura — driven by a maddening hope, having given rich Athens to plunder, then shall divine Justice subdue Riot, first-born son of Insolence, who longs to overturn everything and pants terribly for blood. Bronze shall meet bronze, and Ares shall dye the sea, tinting its waves with blood. Then shall come a day of freedom for Greece from far-seeing Zeus and from Victory, lady and mother.”
Looking at such things, and when Bakis speaks so clearly, I do not myself venture to raise any objections about oracles, nor can I accept them from others.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 78
paragraphs: Among the commanders at Salamis a great contention of speech had arisen, and they did not yet know that the barbarians were surrounding them with their ships; they thought that they were still in the positions they had seen them in during the day.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 79
paragraphs: While the commanders were quarreling, Aristides son of Lysimachos came across from Aegina — an Athenian who had been ostracized by the people, a man whom I hold (based on what I hear of his character) to have been the best and most upright of all Athenians. He came into the council and called out Themistocles, who was no friend but an enemy of the deepest kind; yet because of the magnitude of the present troubles he let those matters be forgotten and summoned him, wishing to speak with him. He had heard beforehand that the Peloponnesians were pressing to take the ships off to the Isthmus. So when Themistocles came out to him, Aristides said: “Both at other times when occasion arises, and especially now, we ought to compete as to which of us will do more service to our country. Now, I tell you that it is indifferent whether the Peloponnesians say many words or few about sailing away from here; for I have been an eye-witness, and I tell you that now, even if the Corinthians and Eurybiades himself wish to sail out, they will not be able to — for we are surrounded by the enemy. Go inside, then, and inform them of this.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 80
paragraphs: He answered as follows: “You advise very well, and the news you bring is good, since you have come having witnessed with your own eyes what I wished would come to pass. For you should know that what the Medes are doing was prompted by me, because when the Greeks would not come to battle of their own will, it was necessary to bring them to it against their will. But since you have come bearing good news, report it to them yourself. For if I speak of these things, I shall be thought to have invented them, and I shall not convince them, but they will believe that the barbarians are doing no such thing. Come forward yourself and tell them how matters stand; and when you have declared it, if they are persuaded, that will be best; but if they do not find it credible, it will make no difference as far as we are concerned, for they will no longer be able to flee — if, as you say, we are surrounded on all sides.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 81
paragraphs: Accordingly Aristides came forward and told them this, saying that he had come from Aegina and had barely escaped detection by those who were blockading them, for the whole Greek encampment was encircled by the ships of Xerxes, and he urged them to prepare to defend themselves. Having said this, he withdrew, and among them dispute broke out again, for most of the commanders did not believe what they had been told.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 82
paragraphs: While they were still in doubt, a trireme manned by Tenians arrived, deserting from the enemy, commanded by Panaitios son of Sosimenes, which brought them the whole truth. For this deed the Tenians were inscribed at Delphi on the tripod among those who had conquered the barbarians. With this ship deserting at Salamis, and the Lemnian ship that had deserted earlier and come to Artemisium, the Greek naval force reached the complete number of 380 ships — for before this two were still lacking to fill that total.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 83
paragraphs: The Greeks, since they now believed what the Tenians reported, were preparing for battle. And as dawn appeared, they held an assembly of those who fought on board the ships and addressed them, Themistocles making a speech that was eloquent beyond the rest. The substance of it was to set forth all that is better as opposed to all that is worse of the various elements that arise in human nature and constitution; and having exhorted them to choose the better, and so bringing his speech to a close, he bade them embark in their ships. These accordingly began to board; and meanwhile the trireme arrived from Aegina that had gone to bring the sons of Aiacos.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 84
paragraphs: Then the Greeks launched all their ships, and while they were still putting out from shore, the barbarians attacked them at once. The rest of the Greeks began to back water and were on the point of running their ships aground, but Ameinias of Pallene, an Athenian, drove his ship forward and rammed one of the enemy; and when his ship became entangled in combat and the crew could not get free, the others joined in the fight to assist him. The Athenians say this was how the battle began; but the Aeginetans say it was the ship that had gone to Aegina to bring back the sons of Aiacos that started the fight. It is also reported that an apparition of a woman appeared to them, and having appeared she urged them on to the fight so loudly that the entire Greek army heard her, first reproaching them with these words: “Madmen! How much further will you keep backing your ships?”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 85
paragraphs: Opposite the Athenians had been stationed the Phoenicians, for these held the wing toward Eleusis and the west; and opposite the Lacedaemonians were the Ionians, who held the wing extending eastward toward the Piraeus. A few of the latter were deliberately slack in the fight, as Themistocles had urged, but most were not. I could mention the names of many captains who destroyed Greek ships, but I will use no names except those of Theomestor son of Androdamas and Phylacos son of Histiaios, both of Samos — and I mention these and not the rest for this reason: Theomestor was for this deed made tyrant of Samos by the Persians, and Phylacos was recorded as a benefactor of the king and received much land as a reward. The benefactors of the king are called, in the Persian tongue, orosangai.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 86
paragraphs: So it was with these. But the greater part of their ships were disabled at Salamis, destroyed some by the Athenians and others by the Aeginetans. For since the Greeks fought in good order and in their assigned places, while the barbarians were no longer in order and did nothing by design, it was likely that such a result would follow. Yet on this day they surpassed themselves far more than when they had fought at Euboea, every man being eager and fearing Xerxes, each thinking that the king's eye was particularly on him.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 87
paragraphs: As for the rest, I cannot speak of them individually or say precisely how the barbarians or Greeks fought each on their own. But with regard to Artemisia, this is what happened, by which she gained even more esteem from the king than before. When the king's affairs had fallen into great confusion, at that crisis a ship of Artemisia was being pursued by an Athenian ship; unable to escape (since ahead of her lay other ships of her own side, while her own ship happened to be the most advanced toward the enemy), she decided what to do, and it proved greatly to her advantage that she did. Being pursued by the Athenian ship, she charged at full speed into a ship of her own side manned by Calyndians, with the king of the Calyndians, Damasithymos, aboard. Now even if it be true that she had had some quarrel with him earlier, while still at the Hellespont, I cannot say whether she did this by design, or whether the Calyndian ship happened by chance to fall in her way. Having rammed it and sunk it, she enjoyed good fortune and gained benefit two ways over. First, the Athenian captain, when he saw her ram a ship manned by barbarians, turned away and went after others, supposing Artemisia's ship was either a Greek vessel, or a deserter from the barbarians fighting for the Greeks.

First, I say, it was her good fortune to escape and not be destroyed. Secondly, though she had done harm, she yet gained great reputation by this act with Xerxes. For it is said that the king, looking on at the battle, noticed that her ship had rammed the other; and someone present said: “Master, do you see Artemisia, how well she is fighting, and how she has just now sunk an enemy ship?” He asked whether this was truly Artemisia's deed, and they said it was — they declared they knew her ship's device very well — and that what had been destroyed must surely be one of the enemy. For besides the other things that turned out fortunately for her, as I have said, there was this too: not one of the Calyndian ship's crew survived to become her accuser. And Xerxes, in reply to what was said to him, is reported to have uttered these words: “My men have become women, and my women, men.” So, it is said, Xerxes spoke.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 89
paragraphs: In this struggle was slain the commander Ariabignes, son of Darius and brother of Xerxes, and many other notables of the Persians, Medes, and their allies were killed as well. Of the Greeks, on the other hand, only a few fell, for knowing how to swim, those whose ships were destroyed and who were not killed in hand-to-hand combat swam over to Salamis. But of the barbarians, most perished in the sea, not being able to swim. When the first ships turned to flight, then the largest numbers perished — for those stationed behind, trying to push their ships forward to the front so that they too might display some deed of valor for the king to see, crashed into ships of their own side that were fleeing.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 90
paragraphs: In the confusion it also happened that some of the Phoenicians whose ships had been destroyed came to the king and accused the Ionians, saying that their ships had been lost through the Ionians' fault, and that the Ionians had been traitors to the cause. Now it turned out that not only did the Ionian commanders not lose their lives, but the Phoenicians who accused them received the reward I shall describe. While the Phoenicians were still speaking, a Samothracian ship rammed an Athenian ship. As the Athenian was being sunk, an Aeginetan vessel came up against the Samothracian and ran it down. Then the Samothracians, skilled javelin-throwers, with their javelins cleared the marines off the ship that had wrecked theirs and then boarded it and took possession. This event saved the Ionians from punishment; for when Xerxes saw they had performed a great exploit, he turned on the Phoenicians (he was exceedingly vexed and disposed to find fault with everyone) and ordered their heads cut off, so that they, having been cowards themselves, should not accuse others who were better men than they. For whenever Xerxes (seated just below the mountain opposite Salamis, called Aigaleos) saw anyone on his side perform a deed of valor in the sea-fight, he would inquire who had done it, and his scribes recorded the ship captain's name with his father's name and his city. Moreover, Ariaramnes, a Persian who was present, shared the fate of the Phoenicians, being their friend. So they proceeded to deal with the Phoenicians.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 91
paragraphs: Meanwhile, as the barbarians turned to flight and were sailing out toward Phaleron, the Aeginetans waited for them in the strait and performed memorable deeds. While the Athenians, in the confused tumult, were disabling both the ships that resisted and those that were fleeing, the Aeginetans were destroying those that attempted to sail away; and whenever any escaped the Athenians, they ran at full course into the Aeginetans.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 92
paragraphs: Then the ship of Themistocles, in pursuit of an enemy, met that of Polycritos son of Crios the Aeginetan. Polycritos had rammed a Sidonian vessel, the same one that had taken the Aeginetan ship on advance watch at Skiathos, on which had been Pytheas son of Ischenoös — whom the Persians kept aboard, hacked to pieces as he was, in admiration of his valor. The Sidonian ship, then, was captured carrying this man along with the Persians I mentioned, so Pytheas came safely to Aegina. When Polycritos looked at the Athenian ship and saw the sign of the admiral's vessel, he shouted out, addressing Themistocles mockingly about the charge that had been brought against the Aeginetans of siding with the Medes, and so reproached him. This taunt Polycritos threw at Themistocles after ramming the Sidonian ship. Meanwhile, those barbarians whose ships had escaped destruction fled and came to Phaleron for shelter under the land-army.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 93
paragraphs: In this sea-battle, the Aeginetans were reported as the best of the Greeks, and next to them the Athenians. Of individuals, the most distinguished were Polycritos the Aeginetan, and the Athenians Eumenes of Anagyrus and Ameinias of Pallene — the one who had pursued Artemisia. Had he known she was aboard that ship, he would not have given up until he had either captured her or been captured himself; for orders had been issued to the Athenian captains, and a prize of ten thousand drachmas had been offered for whoever should take her alive, since they thought it intolerable that a woman should march an expedition against Athens. She, however, as I have said, escaped; and the others whose ships had survived were at Phaleron.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 94
paragraphs: As for Adeimantos, the Corinthian commander, the Athenians say that at the very start, when the ships were just engaging, struck by panic and terror he hoisted his sails and fled; and the Corinthians, seeing their flagship in flight, departed as well. The story goes on that when in their flight they came opposite the temple of Athena Skiras in the land of Salamis, a light vessel fell in with them by divine guidance — no one was ever found who had sent it — and it approached the Corinthians at a time when they knew nothing of what was happening with the fleet. From this it was inferred that the affair was of the Deity. When it drew near the ships, the men in the light vessel said: “Adeimantos, you have turned your ships away and set out in flight, deserting the Greek cause, while they are in fact winning a victory and getting the better of their foes just as they desired.” Since Adeimantos doubted them, they spoke a second time, offering themselves as hostages to be killed if the Greeks should prove not to be winning. Then he turned his ship back, he and the others with him, and they reached camp when the work was done. Such is the report the Athenians spread against them; but the Corinthians do not allow this, and maintain they were among the first in the sea-fight — and the rest of Greece also bears witness on their side.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 95
paragraphs: Aristides son of Lysimachos, the Athenian, of whom I made mention shortly before as a very good man, did this in the tumult around Salamis: taking with him a number of Athenian hoplites who had been stationed along the shore of Salamis, he landed with them on the island of Psyttaleia; and they killed every Persian who was on that little island.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 96
paragraphs: When the sea-fight had broken off, the Greeks towed to Salamis as many of the wrecks as happened still to be about there, and held themselves ready for another sea-battle, expecting the king would still use the ships left intact. But many of the wrecks were caught by the west wind and carried to that part of the Attic coast called Colias — so as to fulfil, besides that other oracle spoken about this sea-battle by Bakis and Musaios, especially, with regard to the wreckage cast up here, what had been uttered in an oracle many years before these events by Lysistratos, an Athenian oracle-monger, which none of the Greeks had noticed:
“Then shall the Colian women roast barley with oars for firewood.”
This was destined to come to pass after the king had marched away.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 97
paragraphs: When Xerxes realized the disaster that had befallen him, he feared that one of the Ionians might suggest to the Greeks, or they might themselves conceive the idea, of sailing to the Hellespont and breaking up the bridges; and so he might be cut off in Europe and run the risk of utter destruction. Therefore he began to think about taking flight. But he wished his intention not to be perceived either by the Greeks or by his own side; so he undertook to build a mole across to Salamis, lashing Phoenician merchant ships together to serve him both as a bridge and a wall, and made preparations for fighting as though he intended to have another sea-battle. Seeing this, all the rest assumed he had made himself ready in earnest and meant to stay and fight; but Mardonius did not fail to perceive the true meaning of all this, being very well versed by experience in the king's way of thinking.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 98
paragraphs: While Xerxes was doing this, he sent a messenger to the Persians to announce the calamity that had befallen them. Now there is nothing mortal that completes a journey with more speed than these messengers — so ingeniously has this been devised by the Persians. They say that for as many days as the entire journey takes, that many horses and men are stationed at intervals along the route, each man and horse assigned for a day's ride. Neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor darkness of night prevents each one from completing his assigned task with the utmost speed. The first rider delivers the message entrusted to him to the second, and the second to the third, and so on it goes, passed from hand to hand, like the torch-race among the Greeks which they hold for Hephaistos. This kind of horse-relay the Persians call the angareion.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 99
paragraphs: The first message, then, to come to Susa — announcing that Xerxes had Athens in his possession — so greatly delighted the Persians who had been left behind that they strewed all the roads with myrtle boughs and burned incense continually, and kept up sacrifices and feasting themselves. But the second message that arrived afterwards so disturbed them that they all tore their garments and gave themselves over to crying and lamentation without restraint, laying the blame on Mardonius. This the Persians did not so much because they were grieved about the ships as because they feared for Xerxes himself.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 100
paragraphs: As for the Persians, this went on for the whole intervening period until the coming of Xerxes himself made them cease. Mardonius, seeing that Xerxes was greatly troubled by the sea-fight and suspecting that he meant to flee from Athens, considered, for himself, that he would have to pay the penalty for having persuaded the king to march against Greece, and that it was better for him to take the risk of either subduing Greece or ending his own life honorably, staking his safety on a great end — though his own opinion was rather that he would subdue Greece. Weighing all this, he addressed the king as follows: “Master, do not grieve, nor feel great distress over what has happened. For the outcome of all our fortunes does not depend on a contest of timbers, but of men and horses. None of those who now think they have achieved everything will try to disembark from their ships and stand against you, nor will anyone here on the mainland do so; those who did stand against us paid the penalty. If, then, you think it good to do so, let us at once attempt the Peloponnese; or if you think it better to hold back, we can do that. Do not despair: there is no escape for the Greeks but to become your slaves, after they have first given an account of what they did to you both now and before. That is the best course. But if you have indeed decided to withdraw yourself and take your army away, I have another counsel to offer in that case too. Do not, O king, let the Persians be an object of mockery to the Greeks; for nothing of yours has suffered through the Persians, nor can you name any place where we showed ourselves cowards. If Phoenicians, Egyptians, Cyprians, or Cilicians proved cowards, the calamity that followed has nothing to do with the Persians. Now, therefore, since the Persians are not guilty towards you, follow my counsel. If you have determined not to remain here, withdraw to your own home, taking with you the main body of the army, and it will then be for me to deliver over to you Greece subdued — choosing for this purpose three hundred thousand from the army.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 101
paragraphs: On hearing this, Xerxes was as rejoiced and delighted as he could be after his misfortunes, and he told Mardonius that when he had taken counsel he would reply and say which of these two courses he would follow. So when he was taking counsel with those Persians summoned to advise him, it seemed good to him to send for Artemisia too, because she alone on the former occasion had shown perception of what ought to be done. When Artemisia arrived, Xerxes removed everyone else — both the Persian councillors and the spearmen of the guard — and spoke to her thus: “Mardonius bids me stay here and make an attempt on the Peloponnese, saying that the Persians and the land-army are in no way to blame for my calamity, and that they would gladly give me proof of this. He urges me either to do this, or else he himself offers to choose three hundred thousand from the army and deliver over to me Greece reduced to subjection, while I withdraw with the rest of the army to my own home. Since you counseled well about the sea-battle that was fought — urging that we should not bring it on — advise me now too which of these things I should do, so that I may succeed in deciding well.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 102
paragraphs: He thus consulted her, and she spoke these words: “O king, it is hard for me to succeed in saying the best thing when I am asked for counsel; yet, in the present situation, it seems best to me that you should withdraw and leave Mardonius here, if he wishes and undertakes this task, together with those whom he wishes to have. For on the one hand, if he subdues those whom he says he desires to subdue, and if the matters he has in mind when he speaks this way succeed well, the deed will after all be yours, master, since your slaves accomplished it. And on the other hand, if the opposite happens of what Mardonius intends, it will be no great misfortune, since you yourself will remain safe, and the power concerning your house in those parts will remain safe too: for if you remain safe with your house, the Greeks will have many contests, many times over, to pass through for their own existence. As for Mardonius, if he suffers any disaster, no account will be made of it; and even if the Greeks conquer, they gain a victory that is no victory, having destroyed only a slave of yours. You, meanwhile, will withdraw having done what you set out to do — that is, having delivered Athens to the fire.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 103
paragraphs: Xerxes was greatly pleased with this advice, since she had succeeded in saying the very thing he himself was meaning to do — for not even if all the men and women in the world had counseled him to remain would he have done so, I think, so thoroughly had he been struck with terror. He commended Artemisia, then, and sent her away to escort his sons to Ephesus, since certain illegitimate sons of his were traveling with him.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 104
paragraphs: With these sons he sent Hermotimos to take charge of them, a man of the Pedasan race who, in the king's estimation, was second to none of the eunuchs. (The Pedasians dwell above Halicarnassus, and at this Pedasa a thing happens as follows: whenever some trouble is about to come upon the whole number of those who dwell around the city within a certain time, then the priestess of Athena there grows a long beard. This has happened to them twice before now.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 105
paragraphs: Of these Pedasians was Hermotimos.) This man, of all persons whom we know up to this time, obtained the greatest revenge for a wrong done to him. He had been captured by enemies and was being sold, and Panionios, a man of Chios, bought him — a man who had made a livelihood by the most impious practices: whenever he obtained boys who possessed some beauty, he would castrate them and then, taking them to Sardis or Ephesus, sell them for large sums of money, since among the barbarians eunuchs are held to be of more value for all matters of trust than men who are not eunuchs. Panionios, then, castrated many others, since that was how he made his living, and also this man of whom I speak. Yet Hermotimos, not in every respect unfortunate, was sent from Sardis to the king among other gifts, and as time went on, he came to be more honored than all the other eunuchs in the sight of Xerxes.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 106
paragraphs: When the king, being at that time in Sardis, was setting the Persian army in motion to march against Athens, Hermotimos, having gone down on some business to that part of Mysia occupied by the Chians and called Atarneus, found Panionios there. Recognizing him, he spoke to him with many friendly words — first recounting all the good things he now had through him, and next making promises in return, saying how many benefits he would do for him if he would bring his household and settle in that land; so that Panionios gladly accepting the offer, brought his children and his wife. Then, when Hermotimos had him in his grasp together with his whole household, he spoke as follows: “You — who of all men who ever lived until now, gained your substance by the most impious deeds — what evil did I myself or any of my forefathers ever do to you or yours, that you made me a nothing instead of a man? Did you suppose you would escape the notice of the gods for the things you devised? They, following the rule of justice, delivered you into my hands for your impious deeds, so that you shall have no cause to complain of the penalty I shall inflict upon you.” Having reproached him thus, he had the man's sons brought into his presence, and Panionios was compelled to castrate his own sons, four in number; and once compelled, he did so. Then, when he had done this, the sons were compelled to do the same thing to him. Thus did vengeance at the hands of Hermotimos overtake Panionios.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 107
paragraphs: When Xerxes had entrusted his sons to Artemisia to take back to Ephesus, he called Mardonius and bade him choose from the army whom he wanted, and make his deeds, if possible, correspond to his words. So matters went that day. In the night, on the king's command, the commanders of the fleet began to withdraw their ships from Phaleron to the Hellespont, each as quickly as he could, to guard the bridges for the king to cross. As the barbarians sailed near Zoster, seeing the small points of rock that stretch out to sea from this part of the mainland, they took these for ships and fled for some distance. At length, perceiving that they were not ships but rocky points, they regrouped and continued their voyage.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 108
paragraphs: When day dawned, the Greeks, seeing that the land-army was still in place, supposed the fleet was still at Phaleron as well; and thinking they would fight another sea-battle, they prepared to repel it. But when they learned that the ships had departed, they at once decided to pursue them. They pursued as far as Andros, but caught no sight of Xerxes's fleet; and when they reached Andros, they deliberated what to do. Themistocles expressed the opinion that they should take their course through the islands and pursue the ships, afterwards sailing straight to the Hellespont to break up the bridges. But Eurybiades expressed the opposite view, saying that if they broke up the floating bridges, they would do Greece the greatest possible harm. For if the Persian were cut off and compelled to remain in Europe, he would try not to remain still, since if he stayed still, none of his affairs could advance, no way back to his country would appear, and his army would perish of hunger. Whereas if he pressed on, all Europe might go over to him city by city, nation by nation — the inhabitants either conquered or surrendering on terms before they were conquered; and he would have for food the Greeks' crops growing year by year. On the other hand (Eurybiades thought), a Persian defeated in the sea-fight would not stay in Europe, and so he should be allowed to flee until in his flight he reached his own land. Then afterwards they could begin the contest for the land that belonged to the Persian. The other Peloponnesian commanders adhered to this opinion as well.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 109
paragraphs: When Themistocles perceived that he would not be able to persuade them — or at least the majority — to sail to the Hellespont, he changed tack and turned to the Athenians (for these were the most grieved at the enemy's escape and were eager to sail to the Hellespont even on their own if the others were unwilling). He spoke to them as follows: “I myself have been present on many occasions before now, and have heard of many more, when something of this sort has happened: men forced into great extremity, after being defeated, fought again and made good their earlier disaster. As for us, since we have won from fortune the continued existence of ourselves and of Greece by repelling so great a cloud of men from our land, let us not pursue enemies who are fleeing from us. For it was not we who accomplished these things, but the gods and heroes, who grudged that one man should be king of both Asia and Europe — a man unholy and presumptuous, who made no distinction between things sacred and things profane, burning and casting down the images of the gods, and who even scourged the sea and let fetters down into it. As things stand, it is good that we now remain in Greece and look to ourselves and our households. Let each man repair his house and attend to the sowing of his land, once we have completely driven away the barbarian; and then, at the beginning of spring, let us sail down toward the Hellespont and Ionia.” He spoke thus intending to lay up a store of gratitude with the Persian, so that if he should meet with any evil at the hands of the Athenians he might have a place of refuge. And that is in fact what came to pass.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 110
paragraphs: Themistocles, then, by speaking thus was trying to deceive them, and the Athenians followed his advice. For he had had the reputation even in former times of being an able man, and he had now proved himself truly both capable and of good judgment; so they were ready in every way to follow his counsel when he spoke. So, once these had been persuaded by him, Themistocles at once sent men in a boat — whom he trusted to keep silence no matter what test they might be put to — with what he charged them to tell the king; and among them was again Sikinnos his servant. When they came to Attica, the rest stayed behind in the ship while Sikinnos went up to Xerxes and spoke these words: “Themistocles son of Neocles has sent me — Themistocles who is commander of the Athenians and the best and ablest man of all the allies — to tell you that Themistocles the Athenian, wishing to do you a service, held back the Greeks when they wanted to pursue your ships and destroy the bridges on the Hellespont. You may, therefore, make your way home quite undisturbed.” Having delivered this, they sailed back.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 111
paragraphs: The Greeks, meanwhile, having resolved not to pursue the barbarians' ships further, nor to sail to the Hellespont to break up the crossing, were besieging Andros, intending to take it. For the Andrians were the first of the islanders who, when asked by Themistocles for money, refused to give it. When Themistocles made his demand and said that the Athenians had come bringing with them two great deities, Persuasion and Compulsion, and that they must therefore by all means give money, they replied that, not without reason, as it now appeared, was Athens great and prosperous, since the Athenians were well supplied with serviceable gods; but as for the Andrians, they were poor, having attained the greatest heights in that regard, and there were two unprofitable gods who never left their island but always remained attached to the place — namely Poverty and Helplessness — and the Andrians, possessed of these deities, would not give money, for the power of the Athenians could never overcome their inability.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 112
paragraphs: These, I say, having answered thus and refused to give the money, were being besieged. Themistocles, not ceasing in his desire for gain, sent threatening messages to the other islands and demanded money from them through the same envoys — those he had sent earlier to the king — saying that if they did not hand over what was demanded, he would bring the Greek fleet against them to besiege and capture them. By saying this he collected great sums from the Carystians and the Parians, who, hearing that Andros was being besieged for siding with the Medes, and that Themistocles was held in more regard than any other commander, sent money out of fear. Whether any other islanders gave money I cannot say, but I think some did — not only these. Yet the Carystians got no respite from trouble on that account; the Parians, however, escaped attack by appeasing Themistocles with money. So Themistocles, taking Andros as his starting-point, was acquiring sums of money for himself from the islanders without the knowledge of the other commanders.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 113
paragraphs: Meanwhile Xerxes with his army remained for a few days after the sea-fight, and then they all began to march off toward Boeotia by the same route they had come. Mardonius thought it was good both to escort the king on his way and also that it was now too late in the year to carry on the war; it was better, he reasoned, to winter in Thessaly and then at the beginning of spring to attempt the Peloponnese. When he reached Thessaly, Mardonius first chose for himself all those Persians called the “Immortals,” except their commander Hydarnes (for Hydarnes said he would not be left behind by the king); then, from the other Persians, those who wore cuirasses and the body of a thousand horse; and also the Medes, Sacans, Bactrians, and Indians, both foot and horse. These nations he took en masse, but from the other allies he picked out only a few at a time, choosing those of fine appearance and those whom he knew had rendered good service. From the Persians he took more than from any other single nation, and these wore collars of twisted metal and bracelets; after them came the Medes, who were not inferior in number to the Persians, only in bodily strength. The result was a force of three hundred thousand in all, including cavalry.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 114
paragraphs: During this period, while Mardonius was selecting his army and Xerxes was in Thessaly, an oracle had come from Delphi to the Lacedaemonians, bidding them demand satisfaction from Xerxes for the murder of Leonidas and accept whatever he should give. The Spartans therefore sent a herald as quickly as possible, who, finding the whole army still in Thessaly, came before Xerxes and spoke these words: “O king of the Medes, the Lacedaemonians and the Heraclid sons of Sparta demand satisfaction of you for murder, because you killed their king, who was fighting in defense of Greece.” Xerxes laughed and was silent for some time; then, pointing to Mardonius, who happened to be standing beside him, he said: “Then Mardonius here shall give them satisfaction, such as is fitting for them to have.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 115
paragraphs: The herald accepted the utterance and departed. Xerxes, leaving Mardonius in Thessaly, hurried on himself to the Hellespont, and reached the crossing in thirty-five days, bringing back next to nothing, one might say, of his army. Wherever they came on their march, to whatever nation, they seized the crops of that people and used them for provisions; and if they found no crops, then they took the grass growing from the earth, stripped the bark from the trees, plucked down the leaves, and devoured them — both of cultivated trees and of those growing wild — leaving nothing behind them, such was their famine. Then plague also struck the army and dysentery, which destroyed them as they went; some of the sick the king left behind, charging the cities where at the time he happened to be on his march with their care and support. He left some in Thessaly, some at Siris in Paionia, and some in Macedonia. In those parts he had also left behind the sacred chariot of Zeus when he was marching against Greece, but on his return he did not get it back: the Paionians had given it to the Thracians, and when Xerxes asked for it, they said the mares had been carried off while pasturing by the upland Thracians who dwelt around the source of the Strymon.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 116
paragraphs: Here too a Thracian, king of the Bisaltians and of the Crestonian land, did a deed of surpassing horror. He had said that he would not be subject to Xerxes of his own will, and had withdrawn up to Mount Rhodope; he had also forbidden his sons to march against Greece. They, however — either because they did not care for his command, or because a desire came upon them to see the war — went on the march with the Persian; and when they returned all unhurt, being six in number, their father for this cause plucked out their eyes.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 117
paragraphs: Such was the reward they received. As for the Persians, passing on from Thrace they came to the crossing, where they crossed the Hellespont in haste to Abydos by means of the ships — for they did not find the floating bridges still stretched across, but broken up by a storm. While staying there for a time they were given more abundant rations than they had received on the way, and from sating their hunger without restraint and from the changes of water, many of those in the army who had survived until then died. The rest arrived with Xerxes at Sardis.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 118
paragraphs: There is also another story reported, namely that when Xerxes, marching away from Athens, came to Eïon on the Strymon, from that point he did not continue by road but handed his army over to Hydarnes to lead back to the Hellespont, while he himself embarked on a Phoenician ship and set out for Asia. As he sailed, he was caught by a wind from the Strymon, violent and raising great waves; and since he was tossed by the storm worse and worse, the ship being heavily laden (for great numbers of Persians — those who traveled with Xerxes — were on deck), the king, falling into fear, shouted out to ask the pilot whether there was any means of safety for them. The pilot said: “Master, there is none, unless some way can be found to rid ourselves of the excessive number of passengers.” Then it is said that Xerxes, on hearing this, spoke thus: “Persians, now let each one of you show that he has concern for the king; for my safety, it seems, depends on you.” So he spoke, they say, and the Persians made obeisance to him and leapt into the sea; and so the ship, lightened, came safely to Asia. As soon as they had landed Xerxes, it is said, he first presented the pilot with a wreath of gold for having saved the king's life, and then cut off his head, because he had caused the death of many Persians.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 119
paragraphs: This other story, I say, is reported about Xerxes's return, but I myself can in no way believe it — neither in other respects, nor concerning what is said to have happened to the Persians. For if what I have related had truly been said by the pilot to Xerxes, not one person's opinion in ten thousand would differ from mine that the king would have done something like this: he would have made those on deck go down below into the hold, since they were Persians of the highest rank; and of the rowers, who were Phoenicians, he would have thrown into the sea a number equal to the Persians on deck. In fact, however, as I have said before, he returned to Asia together with the rest of the army by road.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 120
paragraphs: This is also strong evidence that it was so: Xerxes is known to have come to Abdera on his way back, and to have made a guest-friendship with them, presenting them with a Persian gold sword and a gold-spangled tiara. And as the men of Abdera themselves say (though I myself can by no means believe it), he loosed his girdle for the first time during his flight back from Athens, considering himself safe at last. Now Abdera lies farther toward the Hellespont than the river Strymon and Eïon, from which place the story says he embarked on the ship.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 121
paragraphs: Meanwhile the Greeks, when it proved that they were unable to take Andros, turned to Carystos, and having laid waste the land of that people they departed and went to Salamis. First, for the gods they set aside first-fruits of the spoils, including three Persian triremes — one to be dedicated at the Isthmus, which was still there in my time; another at Sunion; and the third to Ajax at Salamis, where they were. After this they divided the rest of the spoils among themselves and sent the first-fruits to Delphi, from which was made a statue holding in its hand the beak of a ship and measuring twelve cubits in height. This statue stood in the same place as the golden statue of Alexander the Macedonian.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 122
paragraphs: When the Greeks had sent their first-fruits to Delphi, they asked the god on behalf of all whether the first-fruits he had received were fully sufficient and acceptable to him. He said that from the Greeks he had received enough, but not from the Aeginetans, and demanded from them the offering of their prize of valor for the sea-fight at Salamis. On hearing this, the Aeginetans dedicated three gold stars on a bronze ship's mast, which are placed in the corner close to the mixing-bowl of Croesus.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 123
paragraphs: After the division of the spoils, the Greeks sailed to the Isthmus to award the prize of valor to the Greek who had proved himself most worthy in this war. When they had come there, and the commanders cast their votes at the altar of Poseidon, choosing from the whole number the first and the second in merit, each man voted for himself, thinking he had been the best; but for the second place the majority of votes agreed, going to Themistocles. So while the others were left alone in their own votes, Themistocles far surpassed them all in the second-place voting.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 124
paragraphs: Although the Greeks, out of envy, would give no decision on this but sailed off each to his own city without reaching a verdict, Themistocles was nevertheless loudly talked about and esteemed throughout Greece as by far the ablest of the Greeks. Since he had received no honor from those who had fought at Salamis, even though he was first in the voting, he at once went on to Lacedaemon, wishing to receive honor there. The Lacedaemonians received him well and gave him great honors. As a prize of valor they gave Eurybiades a wreath of olive; and for ability and skill they gave Themistocles too a wreath of olive, and presented him besides with the chariot judged the best in Sparta. Having praised him highly, they escorted him on his departure with three hundred picked Spartans — those called the “Horsemen” — as far as the borders of Tegea. He is the only man we know of to whom the Spartans ever gave an escort on his way.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 125
paragraphs: However, when he had come to Athens from Lacedaemon, Timodemos of Aphidnai, one of Themistocles's opponents but otherwise not among the men of distinction, maddened with envy, attacked him, bringing up his trip to Lacedaemon and saying that it was because of Athens that he had received those marks of honor from the Lacedaemonians, not on his own account. As Timodemos kept on repeating this, Themistocles said: “I tell you how it is: if I had been a native of Belbina, I would never have been honored this way by the Spartans; but neither would you have been, my friend — for all that you are an Athenian.” So far, then, went these matters.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 126
paragraphs: Artabazos son of Pharnakes, meanwhile — a man already held in esteem among the Persians before this, and still more after the events at Plataea — was escorting the king as far as the crossing with sixty thousand of the army Mardonius had selected for himself. When the king was in Asia and Artabazos on his march back came near Pallene, finding that Mardonius was wintering in Thessaly and Macedonia and was not at present urging him to come and rejoin the rest of the army, he thought it not good to pass by without reducing the Potidaians to slavery, having found them in revolt. For the Potidaians, once the king had marched past and the Persian fleet had fled from Salamis, had openly revolted from the barbarians; and so had the others who occupy Pallene.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 127
paragraphs: So Artabazos began to besiege Potidaia, and suspecting that the men of Olynthos were also intending to revolt from the king, he began to besiege this city too, which was held by Bottiaians who had been driven from the Thermaian gulf by the Macedonians. When he had taken these men by siege, he led them out to a lake and slaughtered them there; he then handed the city over to the charge of Critobulos of Torone and to the native Chalcidians. Thus it was that the Chalcidians came into possession of Olynthos.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 128
paragraphs: Having taken this city, Artabazos set about attacking Potidaia with vigor; and as he was pressing the work hard, Timoxeinos the commander of the troops from Skione arranged with him to hand the town over by treachery. By what means he did this at first, I cannot say, as it is not reported; but at last it came about as follows. Whenever either Timoxeinos wrote a note to send to Artabazos, or Artabazos wished to send one to Timoxeinos, they would wind it around the finger-notches of an arrow, cover the note with feathers, and shoot it to a spot agreed between them. It came to be discovered, however, that Timoxeinos was trying to betray Potidaia: for Artabazos, shooting an arrow at the agreed spot, missed and struck a man of Potidaia in the shoulder; when he was struck, a crowd gathered around him, as tends to happen in fighting, and they at once seized the arrow, discovered the note, and carried it to the commanders. Now an allied force of other men of Pallene was also present. When the commanders had read the note and discovered who was guilty of the treachery, they resolved not to convict Timoxeinos openly of treachery, for the sake of the city of Skione — lest the men of Skione should be regarded as traitors for all time to come.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 129
paragraphs: So he was discovered in this manner. Three months had gone by while Artabazos was besieging the town, when there came a great, long-lasting ebb of the sea; and the barbarians, seeing the shallow water, tried to cross into the peninsula of Pallene. When, however, they had passed through two-fifths of the distance, with three-fifths still remaining before they would be inside Pallene, a great flood-tide came upon them, higher than ever before — as the natives of the place say, though high tides come often. Those who could not swim perished, and those who could were killed by the men of Potidaia, who put out to them in boats. The cause of the high tide and flood and of what befell the Persians was this, as the Potidaians say: these same Persians who perished in the sea had committed impiety against the temple of Poseidon and his image in the suburb of the town. In saying this was the cause, in my opinion they say well. The survivors of his army Artabazos led away to Thessaly to join Mardonius. Thus fared those who escorted the king on his way.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 130
paragraphs: What remained of Xerxes's fleet, once it had reached Asia in its flight from Salamis and had ferried the king and his army from the Chersonese to Abydos, passed the winter at Kyme. At the dawn of spring it assembled early at Samos, where some of the ships had in fact spent the winter. Most of the Persians and Medes still served as fighting men on board. New commanders arrived: Mardontes son of Bagaios and Artaÿntes son of Artachaies, with whom Ithamitres was also in joint command, being a brother's son to Artaÿntes and added by Artaÿntes's own choice. Having taken a heavy blow, they did not advance further to the west, nor did anyone compel them to; but they stayed where they were at Samos, keeping watch over Ionia lest it revolt, with three hundred ships (Ionian ships included). They did not expect that the Greeks would come to Ionia, thinking it would satisfy them to guard their own land — judging from the fact that the Greeks had not pursued them in their flight from Salamis, but were well content to depart for home. At sea, then, their spirit was broken; but on land they thought Mardonius would have much the advantage. So, being at Samos, they were taking counsel to do what damage they could to their enemies, while also listening for news of how Mardonius's affairs would turn out.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 131
paragraphs: The Greeks, for their part, were stirred up both by the coming of spring and by the presence of Mardonius in Thessaly. Their land-army had not yet begun to assemble when the fleet arrived at Aegina, 110 ships strong, and the commander and admiral was Leotychides son of Menares, son of Hegesilaos, son of Hippocratides, son of Leotychides, son of Anaxilaos, son of Archidemos, son of Anaxandridas, son of Theopompos, son of Nicander, son of Charilaos, son of Eunomos, son of Polydectes, son of Prytanis, son of Euryphon, son of Procles, son of Aristodemos, son of Aristomachos, son of Cleodaios, son of Hyllos, son of Heracles — being of the other royal house. All of these, except the two listed first after Leotychides, had been kings of Sparta. And of the Athenians the commander was Xanthippos son of Ariphon.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 132
paragraphs: When all the ships had reached Aegina, Ionian envoys came to the Greek camp who had also come a short time before this to Sparta, asking the Lacedaemonians to set Ionia free; one of them was Herodotos son of Basileides. These men had banded together and plotted to put to death Strattis, tyrant of Chios — they were originally seven in number; but when one of their accomplices informed on them and they were discovered plotting against him, the remaining six escaped from Chios and came both to Sparta and now to Aegina, asking the Greeks to sail over to Ionia. But the Greeks brought them forward only with difficulty as far as Delos, since what lay beyond was all fearful to them, lacking experience of those regions — everything seemed to them to be filled with armed force, and they were convinced that Samos was as long a voyage away as the Pillars of Heracles. So it happened that at the same time, the barbarians dared sail no further west than Samos, being struck with fear, and the Greeks dared sail no further east than Delos, though the Chians pleaded with them. Thus fear guarded the space between them.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 133
paragraphs: The Greeks, then, sailed to Delos; and meanwhile Mardonius had been wintering in Thessaly. From there he sent round a man, a native of Europos named Mys, to the various oracles, charging him to go everywhere to consult them, wherever it was permitted to put the oracles to the test. What he wished to learn from the oracles when he gave this commission, I cannot say, for it is not reported; but I for my part suppose he sent to consult about his present affairs, not about other matters.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 134
paragraphs: This Mys is known to have come to Lebadeia and to have persuaded one of the locals, by a payment of money, to descend to Trophonios; and he also came to the oracle at Abai of the Phokians. Moreover, when he came to Thebes for the first time, he not only consulted the Ismenian Apollo (where consultation is by victims, as at Olympia), but also, by payment, persuaded a stranger who was not a Theban and induced him to sleep in the temple of Amphiaraos. In this temple no Theban is permitted to seek divination, for the following reason: Amphiaraos, speaking through oracles, bade them choose which of two things they wanted — either to have him as a diviner, or as an ally in war — and refrain from the other use. They chose that he should be their ally in war; and for this reason no Theban is permitted to sleep in that temple.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 135
paragraphs: After this, a thing that seems to me a very great marvel is said by the Thebans to have happened. This Mys of Europos, as he journeyed round all the oracles, came also to the sacred precinct of Ptoan Apollo. This temple is called “Ptoon,” belongs to the Thebans, and lies above Lake Copais at the foot of the mountains, close to the town of Acraiphia. When the man called Mys came to this temple with three men chosen from the citizenry, who were sent by public authority to write down whatever the god should utter in his divination, the god's prophet (it is said) at once began to give the oracle in a barbarian tongue; and while the Thebans accompanying him were astonished to hear a foreign language instead of Greek and did not know what to make of the matter, the man of Europos, Mys, snatched the tablet they were carrying and wrote on it what the prophet was saying, saying that the prophet was delivering his answer in the Carian tongue. When he had written it, he went away and returned to Thessaly.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 136
paragraphs: Mardonius, having read whatever the oracles uttered, then sent Alexander son of Amyntas, the Macedonian, as an envoy to Athens — both because the Persians were connected with him by marriage (for Gygaia, Alexander's sister and daughter of Amyntas, had been married to a Persian, Bubares, and from her had been born to him that Amyntas who lived in Asia, bearing the name of his mother's father, to whom the king had given Alabanda, a great city of Phrygia, as his possession) — and also because Mardonius had been informed that Alexander was a public guest-friend and benefactor of the Athenians. By this means he thought he would be most likely to gain the Athenians over to his side — a people he heard was numerous and brave in war, and whom he also knew had done more than any others to bring about the disasters the Persians had suffered at sea. Therefore, if these were added to him, he thought he would easily gain command of the sea (which would indeed have been the case), while on land he supposed himself already much superior in force. So he reckoned that his power would be far greater than that of the Greeks. Perhaps, too, the oracles had told him this beforehand, counseling him to make the Athenian his ally; and so he was sending in obedience to their advice.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 137
paragraphs: Now the seventh ancestor of this Alexander was that Perdiccas who first became tyrant of the Macedonians, in the following manner. From Argos three brothers descended from Temenos fled to the Illyrians — Gauanes, Aëropos, and Perdiccas. Passing from the Illyrians into upper Macedonia, they came to the city of Lebaia, where they became hired farm servants in the king's household — one pasturing horses, the second oxen, and the youngest, Perdiccas, the smaller cattle. For in ancient times even those who ruled over men were poor in money, not only the common people, and the king's wife herself cooked their food. Whenever she baked, the loaf of the boy servant, Perdiccas, would grow to double its natural size. This kept happening in the same way, and she told her husband; when he heard it, he at once conceived it to be a portent pointing to something great. He summoned the farm servants and told them to depart from his land; they replied that it was only right that before leaving they should receive the wages due to them. As it happened, the sun was shining down into the house through the smoke hole, and the king, hearing about the wages, said, struck with divine folly: “I pay you, then, this as your wages — just what you deserve,” pointing to the sunlight. Gauanes and Aëropos, the elder brothers, stood stunned at hearing this, but the boy, who happened to have a knife in his hand, said: “We accept, O king, what you give us.” He traced a line with his knife around the sunlight on the floor of the house, and having drawn the line around, he three times drew the sunlight into his bosom, and then he and his fellows departed.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 138
paragraphs: They then were going away, and one of the king's table-companions told him what the boy had done, and how the youngest of them had received what was given with some purpose. When the king heard this, he was moved with anger and sent horsemen after them to kill them. Now there is a river in that land to which these Argive descendants sacrifice as a savior; for as soon as the sons of Temenos had crossed it, this river began to flow with such great volume of water that the horsemen could not cross. So the brothers, reaching another part of Macedonia, settled near what are called the gardens of Midas son of Gordias, where roses grow wild, each with sixty petals, surpassing all others in fragrance. In these gardens, as the Macedonians tell, Silenos was captured. Above the gardens stands a mountain called Bermion, impassable because of the cold. Having gained that region, they used it as their starting-point and went on to subdue the rest of Macedonia.
