chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 139
paragraphs: From this Perdiccas, Alexander's descent was as follows: Alexander was the son of Amyntas; Amyntas son of Alketes; the father of Alketes was Aëropos; of him Philip; of Philip Argaios; and his father was Perdiccas, who first obtained the kingdom.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 140
paragraphs: Such, then, was Alexander son of Amyntas's ancestry; and when he came to Athens, sent by Mardonius, he spoke as follows: “Athenians, Mardonius speaks these words: ‘A message has come to me from the king, which says: To the Athenians I remit all the offenses they committed against me; and now, Mardonius, do this — first, give them back their own land; then let them choose another in addition to their own, whichever they wish, remaining independent; and set up all their temples again, which I burned, provided that they agree to a treaty with me.' This message having come to me, I must do so unless I am prevented by you. Now I say to you: Why are you so mad as to raise war against the king? You will neither overcome him nor be able to hold out against him forever. You saw Xerxes's host and its deeds, and you know the power now with me, so that even if you defeat us (of which you can have no real hope if you are rightly minded), another army will come many times as large. Do not, then, try to match yourselves against the king and so be both deprived of your land and forever running for your lives; but make peace with him. You have a most honorable occasion for making peace, since the king has himself set out upon this road. Agree to a league with us, then, without fraud or deceit, and remain free. These things Mardonius charged me to say to you, Athenians. For myself, I will say nothing of my goodwill toward you — you are not learning of it now for the first time. But I ask you to do as Mardonius says, since I see that you will not be able to war with Xerxes forever. If I saw that you had the ability to do that, I would never have come to you speaking these words. For the king's power is above mortal measure and his arm is very long. If, therefore, you do not make an agreement at once, when they are offering you great things as terms for a treaty — I fear for you, seeing that you dwell more on the highway than any of your allies, and are forever exposed alone to destruction, the land you hold being cut off from the rest and lying between the armies contending together. Be persuaded — for this is a matter of great consequence to you, that to you alone of the Greeks the great king remits the offenses committed and desires to become a friend.'”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 141
paragraphs: So Alexander spoke. The Lacedaemonians, having been told that Alexander had come to Athens to bring the Athenians to a treaty with the barbarians, and remembering the oracles — which said that it was destined for them, together with the other Dorians, to be driven out of the Peloponnese by the Medes and the Athenians combined — had become very afraid that the Athenians would indeed make a treaty with the Persians, and had resolved at once to send envoys. It so happened that they were introduced at the same time as Alexander; for the Athenians had delayed matters, well aware that the Lacedaemonians would hear that an envoy had come from the barbarians to make a treaty and, hearing this, would send envoys themselves with all speed. So the Athenians acted deliberately to let the Lacedaemonians see their inclination.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 142
paragraphs: So when Alexander had ceased speaking, the envoys from Sparta followed him at once and said: “As for us, the Lacedaemonians sent us to ask of you not to make any change in what concerns Greece, nor to accept proposals from the barbarian — since this is in no way just, nor honorable for any of the Greeks to do, and least of all for you, for many reasons. It was you who stirred up this war, when we by no means wanted it; and the contest came about for your dominion, but now it extends to all of Greece. Besides, it is by no means tolerable that you Athenians, who are the authors of all this, should prove to be the cause of slavery to the Greeks — you who have been known from ancient times as the liberators of many. Still, we feel sympathy for you in your sufferings, because you have been deprived of your crops twice now and have had your substance ruined for a long time. In compensation for this, the Lacedaemonians and their allies offer to support your wives and all members of your households who are unfit for war for as long as this war shall last. But do not let Alexander the Macedonian persuade you by smoothing Mardonius's speech. It is fitting for him to do these things, since being himself a tyrant he is working in league with a tyrant; but for you these things are not fitting, if you are rightly minded. For you know there is neither faith nor truth in barbarians.”
So spoke the envoys.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 143
paragraphs: To Alexander the Athenians answered thus: “We ourselves know well enough that the Mede's power is many times greater than ours — there is no need for you to cast this in our teeth. Nevertheless, because we long for liberty, we shall defend ourselves as we can. Do not try to persuade us to make a treaty with the barbarian, for we on our part will not be persuaded. Now report to Mardonius that the Athenians say this: so long as the sun keeps the same course on which he goes now, we will never make an agreement with Xerxes. We shall go forth to defend ourselves against him, trusting the gods and heroes as our allies — whom he had no respect for when he set fire to their houses and sacred images. And in the future do not appear before the Athenians with any such proposals, nor think you are doing them a service by advising them to do what is not lawful. For we do not wish you to suffer anything unpleasant at the hands of the Athenians, being their public guest and friend.”

chapters.title: Book VIII — Urania, Chapter 144
paragraphs: To the envoys from Sparta they made this answer: “That the Lacedaemonians should be afraid we might make a treaty with the barbarian was natural enough — but it seems an unworthy fear in men who know so well the spirit of the Athenians: that there is neither so much gold anywhere on earth, nor any land so excelling in beauty and worth, that we would accept it and enslave Greece by taking the side of the Medes. For many and great are the reasons that prevent us from doing this, even should we desire it: first and greatest, the images and houses of the gods burnt and reduced to ruin, which we must necessarily avenge to the utmost rather than make an agreement with the one who did these deeds; and secondly, the bond of Greek kinship, by which we are of one blood and one speech, our common temples, our common sacrifices, our ways of life which are the same for all — things the Athenians could not justly betray. Be assured, if you were not assured of it before, that so long as one Athenian remains alive, we will never make an agreement with Xerxes. We admire, however, the forethought you showed on our behalf, in that you took thought for us who have had our property destroyed and are willing to support the members of our households; as far as you are concerned, the kindness has been fully performed. We, however, shall endure as we can and not be any trouble to you. Now, therefore, with full conviction that this is so, send out an army as quickly as you can; for, as we conjecture, the barbarian will be here invading our land at no distant time — as soon as he hears of the message sent, that we will do none of the things he wanted from us. Therefore, before he arrives in Attica, it is fitting that you come quickly to our aid in Boeotia.” So the Athenians answered, and the envoys departed back to Sparta.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 1
paragraphs: Mardonius, when Alexander had returned and reported to him what the Athenians had said, set out from Thessaly and began leading his army with all diligence toward Athens, taking up with him the people of whatever land he passed through. The leaders of Thessaly, meanwhile, were not sorry for anything they had already done, but on the contrary urged the Persian on even more; and Thorax of Larissa, who had joined in escorting Xerxes during his flight, now openly gave Mardonius passage for the invasion of Greece.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 2
paragraphs: When the army on its march came into Boeotia, the Thebans tried to detain Mardonius, counseling him that there was no region more suitable for him to encamp in than that one. They urged him not to advance further but to sit down there and try to subdue the whole of Greece without fighting: to overcome the Greeks by open force when they were united, as they were now in common accord, was (they said) a difficult task even for all the world combined. “But if you follow our advice,” they went on, “you will with little effort have in your power all their plans of resistance. Send money to the men who hold power in the cities; by doing this you will divide Greece into two parties, and after that you will easily subdue, with the help of your party, those who are not inclined to your side.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 3
paragraphs: So they advised, but he did not follow their counsel, for a great desire had taken hold of him to capture Athens a second time — partly from obstinacy and partly because he meant to signal to the king at Sardis, by beacon-fires through the islands, that he held Athens. Even this time, however, he did not find the Athenians there when he came to Attica; he was informed that most of them were either on Salamis or on the ships, and he captured the city finding it deserted. Now the king's capture of the city had taken place ten months before this later expedition of Mardonius against it.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 4
paragraphs: When Mardonius had reached Athens, he sent Morychides, a man of the Hellespont, to Salamis, bearing the same proposals Alexander the Macedonian had brought over to the Athenians. He sent them a second time, being aware beforehand that the Athenians' disposition was not friendly, but hoping they would give way and abandon their obstinacy, since the Attic land had been captured by the enemy and was in his power.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 5
paragraphs: For this reason he sent Morychides to Salamis. He came before the Council and delivered the words of Mardonius. Then one of the Councillors, Lykidas, expressed the opinion that it was better to accept the proposal Morychides had brought and refer it to the assembly of the people. This was the opinion he gave — whether because he had taken money from Mardonius, or because it was his own inclination. However the Athenians, both those of the Council and those outside, when they heard of it, were greatly indignant; they gathered around Lykidas and stoned him to death. The Hellespontian Morychides they dismissed unharmed. When there had arisen much uproar in Salamis about Lykidas, the Athenian women heard what was being done, and one passing the word to another and one bringing another along, they went of their own accord to Lykidas's house and stoned his wife and children to death.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 6
paragraphs: The Athenians had crossed over to Salamis as follows. As long as they were expecting an army to come from the Peloponnese to help them, they remained in Attica; but the Peloponnesians acted very slowly and with great delay, while the invader was said to be already in Boeotia, so they removed everything out of danger and crossed over to Salamis themselves. At the same time they sent envoys to Lacedaemon to reproach the Lacedaemonians for having permitted the barbarian to invade Attica and for having failed to join them in going to Boeotia to meet him, and also to remind them how many things the Persian had promised to give the Athenians if they changed sides — telling the envoys to warn them that, if they did not help the Athenians, the Athenians would find some shelter for themselves.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 7
paragraphs: The Lacedaemonians, in fact, were keeping a festival during this time and celebrating the Hyakinthia; they counted it of the utmost importance to attend to the things concerning the god, while at the same time the wall they had been building at the Isthmus was at this very moment being completed with battlements. And when the envoys from the Athenians came to Lacedaemon — bringing with them also envoys from Megara and Plataea — they came before the Ephors and said as follows: “The Athenians sent us to say that the king of the Medes not only offers to give us back our land, but also wishes to make us his allies on fair and equal terms without deceit or treachery, and is even willing to give us another land in addition to our own, whichever we choose. We, however, out of respect for Zeus of the Greeks and disdaining to be traitors to Greece, did not agree but refused — although we were unjustly treated by the other Greeks and left to destruction, and although we knew it was more profitable to make a treaty with the Persian than to carry on the war. Nor shall we make a treaty at any future time, if we have our way. Thus sincerely is our duty done toward the Greeks. But as for you, after having come into great dread lest we should make a treaty with the Persian, as soon as you learned for certain what our spirit was — that we would never betray Greece — and because your wall across the Isthmus is all but finished, you now make no account of the Athenians; though you agreed with us to come into Boeotia to meet the Persian, you have now deserted us, and you permitted the barbarian to invade Attica. For the present, then, the Athenians are angry with you, for you did not do what was right. They now bid you with all speed to send out an army with us, so that we may receive the barbarian in the land of Attica; for since we have missed Boeotia, the most suitable place to fight in our land is the Thriasian plain.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 8
paragraphs: When the Ephors heard this they deferred their reply to the next day, and then to the day after, and so on for ten days, postponing the matter from day to day while during this time the whole body of Peloponnesians were diligently building the wall across the Isthmus and were just about to complete it. Now I cannot say why, when Alexander the Macedonian came to Athens, they had been so very anxious that the Athenians might side with the Medes, whereas now they showed no concern — unless it was simply that their wall across the Isthmus had now been built, and they thought they no longer had any need of the Athenians. When Alexander came to Attica, the wall had not yet been completed, and they were working on it in great dread of the Persians.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 9
paragraphs: At last, however, the answer was given and the Spartans' departure came about in the following way. On the day before the one appointed for the last hearing of the envoys, Chileos of Tegea — who of all foreigners had the greatest influence in Lacedaemon — heard from the Ephors all that the Athenians were saying; and he, it seems, said to them these words: “This is how matters stand, Ephors: if the Athenians are not friendly to us but become allies of the barbarian, then though a strong wall may have been built across the Isthmus, a wide gate has been opened for the Persian into the Peloponnese. Listen to their request, before the Athenians resolve on something else tending to the fall of Greece.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Thus he advised them, and they at once took his words to heart. Without saying a word to the envoys from the cities, while it was still night they sent out five thousand Spartans, with no fewer than seven Helots to attend each man, appointing Pausanias son of Cleombrotos to lead them. The leadership actually belonged to Pleistarchos son of Leonidas; but he was still a boy, and Pausanias was his guardian and cousin. For Cleombrotos, father of Pausanias and son of Anaxandrides, was no longer alive: not long after he led home from the Isthmus the army that had built the wall, he died. The reason Cleombrotos led the army home from the Isthmus was this: as he was offering sacrifice for fighting against the Persian, the sun was darkened in the sky. Pausanias chose as his fellow commander Euryanax son of Dorieos, a man of the same royal house.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 11
paragraphs: So Pausanias with his army had gone out of Sparta. The envoys, at daybreak, knowing nothing of this departure, came before the Ephors intending to leave themselves, each for his own city; and when they had come before them, they said this: “You, Lacedaemonians, are staying here celebrating the Hyakinthia and amusing yourselves, while you have left your allies to destruction. And the Athenians, being wronged by you and lacking allies, will make peace with the Persians on whatever terms they can. Once they have made peace, we clearly become allies of the king and therefore we shall join him in expeditions against whatever land the Persians lead us; and then you shall learn what the outcome of this matter will be for you.” When the envoys said this, the Ephors replied, swearing it with an oath, that they supposed by now the men were at Orestheion, on their way against the strangers — for they used to call the barbarians “strangers.” So the envoys, knowing nothing of this, asked what the words meant, and asking they learned the whole truth. Struck with amazement, they set out in pursuit as quickly as possible; and along with them five thousand picked Lacedaemonian hoplites of the perioikoi did the same.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 12
paragraphs: They, then, were hurrying toward the Isthmus; and the Argives, as soon as they heard that Pausanias had gone out from Sparta with his army, sent as a herald to Attica the best long-distance runner they could find — because previously, on their own initiative, they had undertaken to Mardonius to stop the Spartans from going forth. When the herald came to Athens, he spoke as follows: “Mardonius, the Argives sent me to tell you that the young men have gone out from Lacedaemon, and the Argives are not able to stop them. With this in mind, may it be your good fortune to take measures well.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 13
paragraphs: Having said this, he departed and went back; and Mardonius was no longer at all eager to remain in Attica when he heard the message. Before he was informed of this, he had been waiting because he wanted the Athenians' news of what they were about to do, and he had not been injuring or laying waste the land of Attica, because he kept hoping they would make a treaty with him. When he failed to persuade them, and was now informed of everything, he began to withdraw from the country before Pausanias's force arrived at the Isthmus — having first set fire to Athens and torn down and destroyed whatever was left standing of the walls, houses, or temples. He marched away for this reason: first, because Attica was not a land where cavalry could operate freely, and also because if he were defeated in battle in Attica, there was no way of retreat except through a narrow pass, so that a few men could block them. He intended, therefore, to retreat to Thebes and fight near a friendly city and in country where cavalry could operate freely.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 14
paragraphs: Mardonius, then, was withdrawing; and when he was already on the road, a message came to him saying that another body of troops, in advance of the rest, had reached Megara — a thousand Lacedaemonians. Being informed of this, he took counsel with himself, wanting if possible to capture these first. So he turned back and began leading his army toward Megara, the cavalry going ahead of the rest and overrunning the Megaran land. This was the furthest point in Europe toward the sunset to which this Persian army came.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 15
paragraphs: After this a message came to Mardonius that the Greeks were assembled at the Isthmus; so he marched back by way of Dekeleia. The chiefs of Boeotia had sent for those of the Asopians who dwelt near the line of march, and these were his guides along the road to Sphendaleis and from there to Tanagra. Having encamped for the night at Tanagra, and the next day having directed his march to Scolos, he was within Theban territory. Then he proceeded to cut down the trees in the lands of the Thebans, though they were on the Median side — moved not by enmity to them, but pressed by urgent necessity to make a defense for his camp, and also a refuge in case, when he engaged battle, things should not turn out as he desired. Now the encampment of his army stretched from Erythrai along Hysiai and reached the river Asopos; but he was not making the wall extend that far, rather about ten furlongs on each side.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 16
paragraphs: While the barbarians were engaged in this work, Attaginos son of Phyrnon, a Theban, having made magnificent preparations, invited Mardonius himself and fifty of the most distinguished Persians to a feast; they came, and the dinner was held at Thebes. What follows I heard from Thersander, an Orchomenian of great reputation in Orchomenos. Thersander said that he too had been invited by Attaginos to this dinner, and fifty Thebans had also been invited; and their host did not place them to recline separately each nation by itself, but a Persian and a Theban on every couch. When dinner was over and they were drinking toasts to each other, the Persian sharing his couch, speaking in Greek, asked him where he was from, and he answered that he was of Orchomenos. The other said: “Since you have become my fellow-diner and sharer of my libation, I wish to leave behind with you a memorial of my opinion, so that you too may know in advance and be able to take such counsels as are profitable for yourself. Do you see these Persians who are feasting here, and the army we left behind encamped on the river? Of all of them, a little time from now you shall see only very few still alive.” While the Persian said this, he shed many tears, as Thersander reported; and Thersander, astonished at his words, said: “Surely, then, you should tell Mardonius and the Persians of standing after him.” He replied: “Friend, that which is destined to come from God, it is impossible for a man to avert; for no one is willing to follow good counsel, even when one speaks reasonably. Many of us Persians know these things well; yet we go with the rest, bound in the chains of necessity. And the most hateful grief of all human griefs is this: to have knowledge of the truth but no power over the outcome.” These things I heard from Thersander of Orchomenos, and in addition this: that he told them to various people at once, before the battle took place at Plataea.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 17
paragraphs: While Mardonius was encamped in Boeotia, the rest of the Greeks who lived in these parts and took the Medes' side were all supplying troops and had joined in the invasion of Attica. Only the Phokians had not joined in the invasion — the Phokians, I say, for they too were now actively taking the side of the Medes, not of their own will but under compulsion. Not many days after Mardonius's arrival at Thebes, a thousand of their hoplites came, led by Harmokydes, the man of greatest repute among their citizens. When these too came to Thebes, Mardonius sent horsemen and bade the Phokians take up position by themselves in the plain. After they had done so, the whole cavalry suddenly appeared, and a rumor spread through the Greek army on the Median side that the cavalry was about to shoot them down with javelins; this same report went through the Phokians themselves. Then their commander Harmokydes exhorted them as follows: “Phokians, it is clear that these men mean to deliver us to an easily foreseen death, because we have been falsely accused by the Thessalians, I conjecture. Now, therefore, it is right that every one of you prove himself a good man, for it is better to end our lives performing deeds of valor and defending ourselves than to be destroyed by a dishonorable death as offered victims. Let each of them learn that they are barbarians, and we — against whom they devised murder — are Greeks.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 18
paragraphs: While he was thus exhorting them, the horsemen, having surrounded them, were riding toward them as if to destroy them, and were already aiming their missiles as if about to discharge them — indeed, some perhaps did discharge them. Meanwhile the Phokians stood facing them, drawn close together with their ranks closed as tightly as possible on every side. Then the horsemen turned and rode back. I cannot say for certain whether they came to destroy the Phokians at the request of the Thessalians, and then, seeing them take up defense, feared they too might suffer loss and so rode away — as Mardonius had commanded them; or whether, on the other hand, he wanted to test them and see whether they had any warlike spirit. Then, when the horsemen had ridden back, Mardonius sent a herald who spoke to them as follows: “Be of good courage, Phokians, for you have proved yourselves good men, and not as I was informed. Now, therefore, carry on with zeal, for you shall not surpass either myself or the king in rewards.” So far went matters with the Phokians.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 19
paragraphs: When the Lacedaemonians reached the Isthmus, they encamped there; and when the rest of the Peloponnesians who favored the better cause heard this — and some, too, because they saw the Spartans going out — they did not think it right to lag behind. So from the Isthmus, when the sacrifices had proved favorable, they all marched together and came to Eleusis; and having performed sacrifices there too, with favorable signs they marched on, and the Athenians went with them, having crossed from Salamis and joined them at Eleusis. When they had come to Erythrai in Boeotia, they learned that the barbarians were encamped on the Asopos, and perceiving this they drew up against them on the lower slopes of Kithairon.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 20
paragraphs: Then Mardonius, since the Greeks did not come down into the plain, sent against them all his cavalry, commanded by Masistios (whom the Greeks called Makistios), a man of reputation among the Persians, who had a Nesaian horse with a golden bridle and was otherwise splendidly caparisoned. When the horsemen had ridden up to the Greeks they attacked them by squadrons, and in attacking they did them much damage, and moreover in contempt they called them women.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 21
paragraphs: It happened by chance that the Megarians were posted in the most assailable part of the whole position, where the cavalry could best approach. So as the cavalry made its attacks, the Megarians, being hard pressed, sent a herald to the Greek commanders, who said: “The Megarians say: ‘We, O allies, are not able by ourselves to withstand the attacks of the Persian cavalry, holding the position we took at first. Even so far, by endurance and valor alone, we have held out against them, hard pressed as we are; and now, unless you send others to take up our position in our place, know that we shall leave the position where we now are.'” The herald reported this to them, and upon hearing it Pausanias tested the Greeks, asking whether any others would volunteer to go to this place and take post there in succession to the Megarians. When the rest did not wish to go, the Athenians undertook the task — specifically those three hundred picked men whose captain was Olympidoros son of Lampon.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 22
paragraphs: These were the ones who undertook the task and were posted at Erythrai in advance of the other Greeks present, having chosen to take the archers with them. For some time, then, they fought, and at last the fighting was ended in the following way. While the cavalry was attacking by squadrons, the horse of Masistios, going in advance of the rest, was struck in the side by an arrow; in pain it reared upright and threw Masistios off. When he had fallen, the Athenians at once pressed upon him; they took his horse, and killed him as he resisted — though at first they could not, for his armor was such: under a crimson tunic he wore a cuirass of golden scales. As they struck the cuirass they could do nothing, until someone, seeing the problem, thrust into his eye. Then at last he fell and died. By chance the rest of the cavalry did not see this happen — they neither saw him fall from his horse nor saw him being killed — and as the retreat and the wheeling about were taking place, they did not perceive what was happening. But when they halted their horses, they immediately missed him, since there was no one to command them; and once they grasped what had happened, they passed the word to one another and all rode back together, so that they might, if possible, recover the body.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 23
paragraphs: The Athenians, seeing the cavalry riding against them no longer by squadrons but all together, shouted to the rest of the army to come help. While the whole body of foot-soldiers was coming to their aid, a sharp fight arose over the body. As long as the three hundred were alone they had much the worse of it and were about to abandon the body; but when the mass of the army came to their aid, then the horsemen could no longer sustain the fight, nor did they succeed in recovering the body; and besides him they lost others of their number too. They then drew off about two furlongs away and deliberated what to do; and it seemed best to them, having no commander, to ride back to Mardonius.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 24
paragraphs: When the cavalry reached the camp, the whole army and Mardonius himself made great mourning for Masistios — cutting off their own hair, their horses' and beasts of burden's, and giving themselves over to unrestrained lamentation. All Boeotia was filled with the sound of it, because the man who had perished was, after Mardonius, of the greatest account with the Persians and the king.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 25
paragraphs: So the barbarians were paying honor in their own fashion to the slain Masistios. The Greeks, however, having sustained the cavalry's attack and, having sustained it, having driven them back, were much more encouraged. First they placed the dead body in a cart and conveyed it along their ranks — and the body was a sight worth seeing for its size and beauty, so that the men even left their places in ranks and went one after another to gaze upon Masistios. After this they resolved to come further down toward Plataea, for the Plataean region was seen to be far more convenient for them to camp in than Erythrai — both for other reasons and because it is better watered. To this region, then, and to the spring Gargaphia which is there, they resolved they must go and encamp in their separate positions. So they took up their arms and went along the lower slopes of Kithairon past Hysiai to the Plataean land; and on arrival they posted themselves by nations near the spring Gargaphia and the sacred precinct of the hero Androcrates, over low hills and level ground.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 26
paragraphs: Then, in the arranging of the various posts, there arose much heated argument between the Tegeans and the Athenians, for each claimed to occupy the other wing of the army themselves, citing deeds both new and old. The Tegeans said: “We have always been judged worthy of this post by the whole body of allies in every joint expedition the Peloponnesians have made, whether long ago or recently, ever since the time when the sons of Heracles tried, after the death of Eurystheus, to return to the Peloponnese. We gained this honor then because of this event: when we, with the Achaians and the Ionians then in the Peloponnese, had come out to the Isthmus to help and were encamped opposite those wishing to return, Hyllos is said to have proposed that it was not right for one army to risk its safety in battle with the other, and urged instead that the man whom the Peloponnesian army judged to be the best of them should fight Hyllos himself in single combat on terms agreed between them. The Peloponnesians resolved that this should be done, and they swore an oath together on this condition: if Hyllos conquered the Peloponnesians' chosen man, then the sons of Heracles should return to their father's inheritance; but if he were conquered, then the sons of Heracles should depart and lead away their army and not try for a hundred years to return to the Peloponnese. Of all the allies there was chosen — he himself making a voluntary offer — Echemos son of Aëropos son of Phegeus, who was our commander and king. He fought a single combat and killed Hyllos. Because of this deed, we obtained among the Peloponnesians of that time — besides many other great privileges we still possess — this one too: always leading the other wing of the army whenever a joint expedition is made. To you Lacedaemonians we offer no opposition, and we give you the choice of whichever wing you wish to command; but of the other, we say, it belongs to us to lead, as in former times. And apart from this deed just related, we are worthier than the Athenians to hold this post, for we have fought many glorious contests against you, Spartans, and many against others too. So it is just that we have the other wing rather than the Athenians, since they have performed no such deeds as ours, old or new.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 27
paragraphs: So they spoke, and the Athenians replied: “Though we know this gathering was assembled for battle with the barbarian and not for speeches, yet since the Tegean has set us the task of speaking of things both old and new — the deeds of merit achieved by each of our two nations through all time — we must point out to you from what source it is that we, who have always been brave men, have the chief place as a heritage rather than the Arcadians. First, as to the sons of Heracles — whose leader they claim to have killed at the Isthmus — in earlier times, when they were being driven away by all the Greeks to whom they had fled to escape slavery under the Myceneans, we alone received them, and joining with them we subdued the insolence of Eurystheus, defeating in battle those who then dwelt in the Peloponnese. Again, when the Argives who marched with Polyneikes against Thebes had been killed and lay unburied, we declare that we marched an army against the Cadmeians and recovered the dead bodies, burying them in our own land at Eleusis. We have another glorious deed performed against the Amazons who once invaded Attica from the river Thermodon. And in the toils of Troy we were inferior to none. But it is no use making mention of these things — for though we were brave men then, we might by now have become worthless; or though we were worthless then, we might be better now. Let what concerns ancient deeds suffice. But even if we had displayed no other deed (though many glorious ones there are, no fewer than any other Greek people's), by reason of the deed accomplished at Marathon alone we are worthy to have this privilege, and others besides — for we alone of all the Greeks fought in single combat with the Persian, and having undertaken so great a task, we overcame and defeated forty-six nations. Are we not worthy, then, to hold this post on that deed alone? However, since at such a time as this it is not fitting to contend for a post, we are ready to follow what you say, Lacedaemonians, as to where you think it most suitable for us to stand and against whom; for wherever we are posted, we shall try to be brave men. Prescribe to us, then, and we shall obey.” Thus they answered; and the whole body of Lacedaemonians shouted aloud that the Athenians were more worthy to hold the wing than the Arcadians. So the Athenians got the wing and overcame the Tegeans.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 28
paragraphs: After this the Greeks were arrayed as follows, including both those who kept arriving and those who had come at first. The right wing was held by ten thousand Lacedaemonians; of these, the five thousand who were Spartans were attended by thirty-five thousand Helots serving as light-armed troops, seven appointed to each man. To stand next to themselves, the Spartans chose the Tegeans — both to do them honor and for their valor — and of these there were fifteen hundred hoplites. After them were posted five thousand Corinthians, who had obtained permission from Pausanias for the three hundred Potidaians of Pallene present to stand beside them. Next to these were six hundred Arcadians of Orchomenos; next, three thousand Sikyonians; after them, eight hundred Epidaurians. Beside these were drawn up a thousand Troizenians; next to the Troizenians, two hundred Lepreates; next, four hundred men of Mykene and Tiryns; then a thousand Phliasians. Beside these stood three hundred Hermionians; next to the Hermionians were posted six hundred Eretrians and Styrians; next to these, four hundred Chalcidians; and then five hundred men of Amprakia. After these stood eight hundred Leucadians and Anactorians; next to them, two hundred from Pale in Cephallenia. After these were arrayed five hundred Aeginetans; beside them, three thousand Megarians; and next to these, six hundred Plataeans. Last — or, if you prefer, first — were arrayed the Athenians, holding the left wing, eight thousand in number, and their commander was Aristides son of Lysimachos.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 29
paragraphs: All these, except those appointed to attend the Spartans at seven per man, were hoplites, totaling 38,700. This was the total number of hoplites assembled against the barbarian. The number of light-armed men was as follows: of the Spartan division, 35,000, at seven per man, all of them equipped for fighting; and the light-armed troops of the rest of the Lacedaemonians and the other Greeks, about one for each man, amounted to 34,500.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 30
paragraphs: Of the light-armed fighting men, then, the total was 69,500. The entire Greek force assembled at Plataea numbered (including both hoplites and light-armed fighters) 110,000 — less by 1,800. With the Thespians present, the full figure of 110,000 was made up; for of the Thespians who survived, about 1,800 were present in the army — also without heavy armor. These, then, having been drawn up in order, were encamped on the river Asopos.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 31
paragraphs: Meanwhile, Mardonius's barbarians, when they had sufficiently mourned for Masistios and were informed that the Greeks were at Plataea, themselves came to that part of the Asopos which flows there. Once arrived, Mardonius ranged them against the enemy as follows: against the Lacedaemonians he stationed the Persians; and since the Persians much outnumbered the Lacedaemonians, he arrayed them in deeper ranks, and even so they extended in front of the Tegeans as well. He arranged them in this way: all the strongest part of that body he picked out from the rest and posted opposite the Lacedaemonians, and the weaker part he ranged beside them, opposite the Tegeans. This he did on the information and suggestion of the Thebans. Next to the Persians he placed the Medes, who extended in front of the Corinthians, Potidaians, Orchomenians, and Sikyonians. Next to the Medes he ranged the Bactrians, who extended in front of the Epidaurians, Troizenians, Lepreates, Tirynthians, Myceneans, and Phliasians. After the Bactrians he posted the Indians, who extended in front of the Hermionians, Eretrians, Styrians, and Chalcidians. Next to the Indians he placed the Sacans, extending in front of the men of Amprakia, Anactorians, Leucadians, Palians, and Aeginetans. Next to the Sacans, and opposite the Athenians, Plataeans, and Megarians, he stationed the Boeotians, Locrians, Malians, Thessalians, and the thousand men of the Phokians: for not all the Phokians had taken the side of the Medes — some were even supporting the Greek cause, being shut up on Parnassos, and setting out from there they plundered from the army of Mardonius and those Greeks with him. He ranged the Macedonians, too, and those dwelling around the borders of Thessaly opposite the Athenians.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 32
paragraphs: These mentioned were the greatest of the nations arrayed by Mardonius — the most renowned and of greatest consideration. But in his army were also men of various other nations mixed in: Phrygians, Thracians, Mysians, Paionians, and the rest, including some Ethiopians, and of the Egyptians those called the Hermotybians and Calasirians, armed with knives, who alone of the Egyptians are warriors. These men, while still at Phaleron, he had caused to disembark from the ships where they had served as marines; for the Egyptians had not been appointed to serve in the land-army that came with Xerxes to Athens. There were 300,000 barbarians, as has been said before; but of the Greeks who were allies of Mardonius, no one knows the number, for they were not counted; by conjecture I judge they were assembled to the number of 50,000. These drawn up side by side were on foot, and the cavalry was stationed apart from them as a separate body.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 33
paragraphs: When all had been drawn up by nations and divisions, on the next day they offered sacrifice on both sides. For the Greeks, Tisamenos son of Antiochos was the one who sacrificed, since he accompanied the army as diviner. This man the Lacedaemonians had made one of their own citizens, being an Eleian of the race of the Iamidai. For when Tisamenos was seeking divination at Delphi concerning issue, the Pythian priestess answered him that he should win five of the greatest contests. Missing the oracle's meaning, he turned to athletic games, supposing he would win athletic contests; he practiced for the pentathlon and came within a single fall of winning an Olympic victory, being matched against Hieronymos of Andros. But the Lacedaemonians perceived that the oracle given to Tisamenos referred not to athletic but to martial contests, and they tried to persuade Tisamenos by payment of money to become a leader in their wars alongside the kings of the house of Heracles. He, seeing that the Spartans set much store on gaining him as a friend, raised his price and made clear that he would do what they wanted only if they made him a citizen of their state with full rights — but for no other payment. At first the Spartans, hearing this, displayed indignation and gave up their request altogether; but at last, when great fear of this Persian armament hung over them, they gave in and agreed. He, perceiving they had changed their minds, then said that even so he could not now be satisfied with these terms alone: it was also necessary that his brother Hegias be made a Spartan citizen on the same terms as himself.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 34
paragraphs: By saying this he followed Melampus's example in his demand, if one may compare royal power with mere citizenship. For Melampus, when the women of Argos were seized by madness and the Argives tried to hire him to come from Pylos and cure their women, demanded as payment for himself half the royal power; and the Argives would not allow this and departed. But afterwards, when more of their women became mad, at last they accepted what Melampus had proposed and went to offer it to him. Then he, seeing they had changed their minds, raised his demand and said he would not do what they wanted unless they also gave his brother Bias a third share in the royal power. Driven into a corner, the Argives consented to this too.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 35
paragraphs: Just so the Spartans too, being in great need of Tisamenos, agreed to whatever terms he demanded. And once the Spartans had agreed to this demand as well, then Tisamenos the Eleian, now a Spartan, shared with them in winning five of the greatest contests as their diviner; and these were the only men ever made fellow citizens of the Spartans. The five contests were these: first, this one at Plataea; after this, the battle at Tegea against the Tegeans and Argives; then the contest at Dipaieis against all the Arcadians except the Mantineians; after that, the contest with the Messenians at Ithome; and last of all, the contest at Tanagra against the Athenians and Argives. This, I say, was accomplished last of the five contests.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 36
paragraphs: This Tisamenos was now acting as diviner for the Greeks in the Plataean land, having been brought by the Spartans. For the Greeks the sacrifices were of good omen only if they defended themselves, but not if they crossed the Asopos and began a battle.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 37
paragraphs: Mardonius too, eager to begin a battle, found the sacrifices unfavorable for that purpose, though they were of good omen for him if he merely defended himself; for he too used the Greek manner of sacrifice, having as diviner Hegesistratos, an Eleian and the most famous of the Telliadai. Before these events the Spartans had captured and bound him, intending to put him to death for the much mischief they had suffered from him. In this evil state, seeing that he was running for his life and was likely to suffer much torment before death, he did a deed that is scarcely credible. Being fastened on a block bound with iron, he obtained an iron tool that had somehow been brought in, and at once devised a feat as courageous as any we know: for having first calculated how the remaining part of his foot might be freed from the block, he cut off the flat of his own foot. After that, since he was still guarded by warders, he broke through the wall and ran off to Tegea, traveling during the nights and in daytime entering a wood and resting there. Although the Lacedaemonians searched for him in full force, he reached Tegea on the third night. The Lacedaemonians were struck with great wonder both at his courage (when they saw the severed piece of foot lying there) and at their inability to find him. So he escaped them then, taking refuge at Tegea, which at that time was not friendly with the Lacedaemonians. Once healed, and having procured a wooden foot for himself, he became an open enemy of the Lacedaemonians. In the end, however, the enmity he had fallen into with the Lacedaemonians was not to his advantage; for he was caught by them while practicing divination in Zakynthos and was put to death.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 38
paragraphs: The death of Hegesistratos, however, occurred later than the events at Plataea; at this time he was at the Asopos, having been hired by Mardonius for no small sum, sacrificing and showing zeal for his cause both because of his enmity toward the Lacedaemonians and because of the money he was earning. But as the sacrifices were not favorable for battle either for the Persians themselves or for those Greeks with them (they too had their own diviner, Hippomachos the Leucadian), and as the Greeks had men constantly streaming in and growing in number, Timagenides son of Herpys, a Theban, counseled Mardonius to set a guard on the pass of Kithairon, saying that the Greeks were pouring in every day and he would thus cut off large numbers.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 39
paragraphs: Eight days had now passed while they sat opposite one another, when Timagenides gave this advice to Mardonius. Mardonius, seeing that the advice was good, sent the cavalry, when night came on, to the pass of Kithairon leading toward Plataea — which the Boeotians call “Three Heads” and the Athenians “Oak Heads.” Sent in this way, the cavalry did not act in vain: they caught five hundred pack-animals coming out into the plain, carrying provisions from the Peloponnese to the army, along with the men accompanying the carts. Having taken this prize, the Persians began slaughtering them without sparing either beast or man; and when they were sated with killing, they surrounded what was left and drove them into the camp to Mardonius.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 40
paragraphs: After this deed they spent two more days, neither side willing to begin a battle; for the barbarians advanced as far as the Asopos to test the Greeks, but neither side would cross the river. However, Mardonius's cavalry made attacks continually and did damage to the Greeks; for the Thebans, strongly on the Medes' side, pressed the war with vigor, and always led the way up to the moment of fighting; and after this, the Persians and Medes took up the work and were the ones who displayed valor in their turn.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 41
paragraphs: For ten days nothing more was done than this; but when the eleventh day came, while they still sat opposite one another at Plataea, the Greeks by now having grown much more numerous and Mardonius being greatly vexed at the delay, Mardonius son of Gobryas and Artabazos son of Pharnakes — a man esteemed by Xerxes above almost all Persians — came to speak with each other. In their discussion, the opinions expressed were these. Artabazos's opinion was that they must set the whole army in motion as soon as possible and move to the walls of the Thebans, where great stores of grain had been brought in for them and fodder for their beasts; there they should settle quietly and get their business done as follows. They had, he said, great quantities of gold (both coined and uncoined) as well as silver and drinking cups, and he advised that these should be sent around without stint to the Greeks, especially to those who were leaders in their various cities; these, he said, would speedily surrender their freedom. He advised that they not risk a battle. His opinion, then, was the same as the Thebans', for he too had some true foresight. But Mardonius's opinion was more vehement and more obstinate, and he was by no means disposed to yield; for he said he thought their army far superior to that of the Greeks, and gave as his opinion that they should engage in battle as quickly as possible and not allow them to assemble in still greater numbers than were already gathered. As for the sacrifices of Hegesistratos, they should leave them alone and not try to force a favorable sign, but follow Persian custom and engage in battle.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 42
paragraphs: When he expressed this judgment, no one opposed him, and so his opinion prevailed; for it was he, and not Artabazos, who had been given command of the army by the king. He therefore summoned the commanders of the divisions and the generals of the Greeks with him, and asked whether they knew of any oracle about the Persians that said they were destined to be destroyed in Greece. Those summoned to council fell silent, some not knowing the oracles and others knowing them but thinking it unsafe to speak; then Mardonius himself said: “Since you either know nothing or do not venture to speak, I will tell you, for I know very well. There is an oracle saying that the Persians are destined, when they come to Greece, to plunder the temple at Delphi, and having plundered it to perish, every one of them. We, therefore, precisely because we know this, will not go to that temple, nor will we attempt to plunder it; and for this reason we shall not perish. So those of you who happen to wish well to the Persians, rejoice so far as this matter is concerned, and be assured that we shall overcome the Greeks.” Having spoken to them thus, he next commanded them to prepare everything and set all in order, since at dawn of the next day a battle would be fought.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 43
paragraphs: Now this oracle, which Mardonius said referred to the Persians, I know for my part was composed with reference to the Illyrians and the army of the Enchelians, not to the Persians at all. However, the oracle composed by Bakis with reference to this battle —

“The gathering of Greeks together and cry of barbarian voices, where the Thermodon flows, by the banks of the grassy Asopos; here very many shall fall before destiny gave them to perish, bow-bearing Medes in fight, when the fatal day approaches them” —
these sayings, and others like them composed by Musaios, I know had reference to the Persians. Now the river Thermodon flows between Tanagra and Glisas.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 44
paragraphs: After the inquiry about the oracles and the exhortation given by Mardonius, night came on and the guards were set. When night was well advanced and it seemed that there was quiet everywhere in the camps, the men being in their deepest sleep, then Alexander son of Amyntas, commander and king of the Macedonians, rode his horse up to the Athenian guard-posts and asked to have speech with their generals. While the greater number of the guards stayed at their posts, some ran to the generals, and when they reached them they said that a man had come riding on a horse out of the Median camp who revealed nothing further, only named the generals and said he wished to have speech with them.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 45
paragraphs: On hearing this, they at once accompanied the men to the guard-posts; and when they had arrived, Alexander said to them: “Athenians, I entrust these words of mine to you as a deposit, charging you to keep them secret and tell them to no one except Pausanias, so that you may not bring me to ruin. For I would not utter them if I did not care greatly for the general safety of Greece, seeing that I am a Greek myself by original descent and would not wish to see Greece enslaved instead of free. I tell you, then, that Mardonius and his army cannot get the sacrifices to turn out as he wishes, otherwise you would long since have fought. Now, however, he has resolved to let the sacrifices alone and to bring on a battle at dawn; for, as I conjecture, he fears you may assemble in greater numbers. Therefore prepare yourselves. If Mardonius should after all put off the battle and not bring it on, stay where you are and hold out patiently, for they have provisions only for a few days remaining. And if this matter turns out according to your wish, each of you ought then to remember me too with regard to liberation, since I have done so hazardous a deed for the Greeks' sake out of zeal for you, wishing to reveal to you Mardonius's design so that the barbarians may not fall upon you unprepared. I am Alexander the Macedonian.” Having spoken, he rode back to the camp and to his own position.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 46
paragraphs: Then the Athenian generals came to the right wing and reported to Pausanias what they had heard from Alexander. At this, he, struck with fear of the Persians, spoke as follows: “Since, then, the battle comes on at dawn, it is right that you Athenians take your stand opposite the Persians, and we opposite the Boeotians and those Greeks now posted against you. The reason is that you are acquainted with the Medes and their manner of fighting, having fought them at Marathon, while we have no experience of these men and are ignorant of them; for not one Spartan has tested himself against the Medes in combat, though we have experience of the Boeotians and the Thessalians. It is right, therefore, that you take up your arms and come to this wing, and we go to the left.” To this the Athenians answered: “To us also, long ago at the very first, when we saw the Persians being drawn up opposite you, it occurred to say these very things, which you now bring forward before we have uttered them; but we feared that these words might not please you. Since, however, you yourselves have mentioned this, know that your words have given us pleasure, and that we are ready to do what you propose.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 47
paragraphs: Both sides, then, were content to do this, and as dawn appeared they began exchanging their positions with one another. But the Boeotians, perceiving what was being done, reported it to Mardonius, who on hearing it at once tried to change positions himself, bringing the Persians across so as to face the Lacedaemonians. When Pausanias learned that this was being done, he perceived that he was not unobserved, and led the Spartans back again to the right wing; and Mardonius likewise returned to his left.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 48
paragraphs: When they had been brought back to their former positions, Mardonius sent a herald to the Spartans who spoke as follows: “Lacedaemonians, you are said by those here to be very good men — they admire you because you do not flee in war nor leave your post, but stay and either destroy your enemies or perish yourselves. In this, however, as it now appears, there is no truth. For before we engaged in battle and came to hand-to-hand combat, we saw you already in flight and leaving your station, desiring to make trial first with the Athenians while you arrayed yourselves opposite our slaves. These are not at all the deeds of good men in war; we were greatly deceived in you. We expected, because of your renown, that you would send a herald to us, challenging us and desiring to fight the Persians alone; we on our part were ready to do this, but found you saying nothing of the kind — rather, you cowered in fear. Now, therefore, since you were not the first to say this, we are. Why do we not fight at once — you on behalf of the Greeks (since you have the reputation of being the best), and we on behalf of the barbarians — with equal numbers on both sides? And if we think it good that the rest should fight too, then let them fight afterward; but if we think it enough that we alone should fight, let us fight it out to the end, and whichever of us are victors, let them be counted victorious with their whole army.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 49
paragraphs: The herald, having spoken thus, waited some time; and then, as no one answered him, he departed and went back. On his return he reported to Mardonius what had happened to him. Mardonius, greatly rejoiced and elated by his empty victory, sent the cavalry to attack the Greeks. And when the horsemen rode up to attack, they damaged the whole Greek army by hurling javelins and shooting arrows, being mounted archers and therefore hard to fight against; they also disturbed and choked up the spring Gargaphia, from which the whole Greek army was drawing its water. Now the Lacedaemonians alone were posted near this spring, and it was at some distance from the rest of the Greeks (each being posted where they happened to be), while the Asopos was close at hand; but when they were kept away from the Asopos, they would go back and forth to this spring — for the horsemen and archers prevented them from fetching water from the river.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 50
paragraphs: Such being the situation, the Greek generals — their army cut off from its water and being harassed by the cavalry — assembled to consult about these and other matters, coming to Pausanias on the right wing. For other things troubled them even more than these I have mentioned, since they had no provisions left, and their attendants who had been sent to the Peloponnese for the purpose of getting them had been cut off by the cavalry and could not reach the camp.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 51
paragraphs: The generals in council with one another resolved that, if the Persians put off the battle for that day, they would go to the Island. This is ten furlongs from the Asopos and the spring Gargaphia where they were then encamped, and lies in front of the Plataeans' city. And if it be asked how there can be an island on the mainland, here is how: the river parts in two upstream, flowing from Kithairon down into the plain, with about three furlongs between its streams, and then joins again into one; its name is Oëroe, said by the natives to be the daughter of Asopos. To this place, I say, they decided to move so that they might have an abundant water supply and not be damaged by the cavalry, as they now were while they stood directly opposite. They proposed to make the move when the second watch of the night had come, so that the Persians might not see them set out and harass them with the cavalry in pursuit. They also planned, after arriving at this place — around which, as I say, Oëroe the daughter of Asopos flows, parting into two streams as she runs down from Kithairon — to send half the army to Kithairon during that same night to pick up the attendants who had gone for provisions, since those were cut off from them in Kithairon.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 52
paragraphs: Having so resolved, during that whole day they had unceasing trouble while the cavalry pressed them. But when the day drew to a close and the cavalry's attacks had ceased, then, as night was coming on and the hour arrived at which they had agreed to retire from their place, most of them set out and began to withdraw — but not keeping it in mind to go to the agreed place. On the contrary, once they had begun to move, they readily took the chance to flee from the cavalry toward the city of the Plataeans; and in their flight they came as far as the temple of Hera, which stands before the Plataean city, twenty furlongs from the spring Gargaphia. Having arrived there, they halted in front of the temple.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 53
paragraphs: These, then, were camping around the temple of Hera. Pausanias, seeing them retiring from the camp, gave the word to the Lacedaemonians also to take up their arms and follow after the others who had gone before, supposing these were going to the agreed place. When all the other commanders were ready to obey Pausanias, Amompharetos son of Poliades, commander of the Pitanate division, said he would not flee from the strangers, nor would he willingly disgrace Sparta; he expressed wonder at what was being done, not having been present at the earlier discussion. Pausanias and Euryanax were greatly disturbed that he did not obey them — and still more that they might be forced to leave the Pitanate division behind, since he refused. They feared that, if they left it in order to carry out what they had agreed with the other Greeks, Amompharetos himself would perish being left behind, along with the men with him. With this in mind they kept the Lacedaemonian force from moving, while they tried to persuade him that it was not right for him to do this.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 54
paragraphs: They, then, were exhorting Amompharetos, the only one of the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans left behind. Meanwhile the Athenians were keeping themselves quietly in the place where they had been posted, knowing the Spartan spirit — that they tend to say one thing and mean another. When the army began to move, the Athenians sent a horseman from their own number to see whether the Spartans were attempting to set out, or whether they really had no intention of retreating, and they told him to ask Pausanias what they ought to do.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 55
paragraphs: When the herald came to the Lacedaemonians, he saw they were still in their place and their leaders had come to strife with one another. For although Euryanax and Pausanias both urged Amompharetos not to risk remaining behind with his men, alone of all the Lacedaemonians, they did not persuade him at all, and at last they had come to outright strife. Meanwhile the Athenian herald had arrived and was standing beside them. Amompharetos, in his disputing, took up a rock in both hands and set it at Pausanias's feet, saying that with this pebble he cast his vote not to flee from the strangers — meaning the barbarians. Pausanias, calling him a madman and out of his senses, bade the Athenian herald — who was asking what he had been charged to ask — be told the state of their affairs; and at the same time he asked the Athenians to come toward the Lacedaemonians and to do the same as they did regarding the retreat.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 56
paragraphs: He, then, went back to the Athenians. As dawn still found them arguing with one another, Pausanias, who had stayed still throughout all this time, gave the signal and led all the rest away over the low hills, supposing that Amompharetos would not stay behind when the other Lacedaemonians departed — in which he was in fact right. With them went the Tegeans too. Meanwhile the Athenians, following the orders given them, were going in the direction opposite to the Lacedaemonians; for these clung to the hills and the lower slope of Kithairon out of fear of the cavalry, while the Athenians marched below in the direction of the plain.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 57
paragraphs: As for Amompharetos, at first he did not believe Pausanias would ever dare to leave him and his men behind, and he insisted they stay there and not abandon their post; but when Pausanias and his troops were well away in front, then he perceived that they had actually left him behind. He made his division take up their arms and led them slowly toward the main body. This main body, having gone about ten furlongs, waited for Amompharetos's division, halting at the river Moloeis and the place called Argiopion, where also stands a temple of Eleusinian Demeter. It stopped there for this reason: so that, if Amompharetos and his division should not leave the place where they had been posted but should remain there, it might be able to come back to their aid. So Amompharetos and his men were coming up to join them, and the barbarians' cavalry was at the same time beginning to attack them in full force. For the horsemen acted on this day as they had been in the habit of doing every day: seeing the place empty where the Greeks had been posted in the previous days, they rode their horses further and further forward, and as soon as they came up with them began to attack.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Then Mardonius, when he learned that the Greeks had departed during the night and saw their place deserted, called Thorax of Larissa and his brothers Eurypylos and Thrasydeios and said: “Sons of Aleuas, will you still say anything now, seeing these places deserted? You who dwell near them used to say that the Lacedaemonians did not flee from battle but were men unsurpassed in war. These men you saw before this changing their post, and now we all see that they have run away during the past night. By this they made plain, when the time came for them to contend in battle with those who were truly the best of all men, that after all they were men of no worth, who had been making a display of valor among the Greeks — a worthless race. As for you, since you had no experience of the Persians, I was very willing to excuse you for praising these men, of whom you did know something good; but much more did I marvel that Artabazos should have been afraid of the Lacedaemonians, and that in his fear he uttered that most cowardly opinion — namely, that we should move our army away and go to the city of the Thebans to be besieged there — an opinion about which the king shall yet be informed by me. But we will speak of these things elsewhere. For now, we must not allow them to act thus, but must pursue them until they are caught and pay the penalty to us for all they did to the Persians in time past.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 59
paragraphs: Having said this, he led the Persians on at a run, after they had crossed the Asopos, on the track of the Greeks, supposing they were running away from him; and he directed his attack against the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans only, not seeing the Athenians, whose march was toward the plain, because of the hills. The rest of the barbarian division commanders, seeing that the Persians had set off in pursuit of the Greeks, all at once raised the signals for battle and began to pursue, each as fast as they could, with no order or sequence of posts.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 60
paragraphs: These, then, came on shouting and in confused numbers, thinking to make short work of the Greeks. Pausanias, when the cavalry began to attack, sent a horseman to the Athenians and said: “Athenians, now that the greatest contest is set before us — one whose outcome is the freedom or slavery of Greece — we, the Lacedaemonians, and you, the Athenians, have been deserted by our allies, who have run away during the past night. Now, therefore, it is determined what we must do about this: we must defend ourselves and protect one another as best we may. If the cavalry had set out to attack you first, we and the Tegeans (who with us refuse to betray the cause of Greece) would have been bound to go to your aid; but as it is, since the whole body has come against us, it is right that you should come to that portion of the army which is hardest pressed, to give aid. However, if something has befallen you that makes it impossible to come help, do us a kindness by sending the archers to us. We know that you have been by far the most zealous in this present war, so we trust you will listen to this request too.”

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 61
paragraphs: When the Athenians heard this they were eager to come to their help and assist them as much as possible; but as they were already on their way, they were attacked by those Greeks on the king's side who had been ranged opposite them, so that they were no longer able to come to the Lacedaemonians' aid — the force attacking them gave them much trouble. Thus the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans were left alone, numbering together with light-armed men fifty thousand of the former and three thousand Tegeans (the Tegeans were not separated at all from the Lacedaemonians). They began to offer sacrifice, meaning to engage in battle with Mardonius and the force that had come against them. Then, since their offerings did not prove favorable and many of them were being killed in the meantime and many more wounded — for the Persians had made a palisade of their wicker shields and were discharging their arrows in vast numbers and without sparing — Pausanias, seeing the Spartans hard pressed and the offerings not favorable, fixed his gaze on the temple of Plataean Hera and called on the goddess to help, praying that they might by no means be cheated of their hope.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 62
paragraphs: While he was still calling on her, the Tegeans sprang forward before the rest and advanced against the barbarians; and immediately after Pausanias's prayer the sacrifices proved favorable for the Lacedaemonians as they offered them. So when at last this came to pass, they too advanced against the Persians; and the Persians put aside their bows and came against them. Then first there was fighting over the wicker shields, and when these had been overturned, the fighting by the temple of Demeter was fierce and went on for a long time, until at last they came to grappling; for the barbarians would seize hold of the spears and break them off. In courage and strength the Persians were not inferior to the others, but they had no defensive armor, and moreover they were unversed in war and unequal to their opponents in skill; they would dart out one at a time or in groups of about ten, some more, some fewer, and fall upon the Spartans and perish.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 63
paragraphs: In the place where Mardonius himself was — riding on a white horse and having around him the thousand best Persians picked from the rest — there they pressed upon their opponents most of all. As long as Mardonius was alive, they held out and in defending themselves cut down many of the Lacedaemonians; but when Mardonius was killed and the men ranged around his person (the strongest portion of the whole army) had fallen, then the others also turned and gave way before the Lacedaemonians. Their manner of dress, without defensive armor, was a very great cause of destruction to them, since in truth they were fighting light-armed against hoplites.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 64
paragraphs: So satisfaction for the murder of Leonidas was paid by Mardonius, according to the oracle given to the Spartans; and the most famous victory known to us was won by Pausanias son of Cleombrotos, son of Anaxandrides, whose earlier ancestors have been named in connection with Leonidas, since as it happens they are the same for both. Now Mardonius was killed by Arimnestos, a man of standing in Sparta, who afterwards, when the Median wars were over, with three hundred men fought a battle against the entire Messenian army then at war with the Lacedaemonians, at Stenycleros; and both he was killed and the three hundred along with him.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 65
paragraphs: When the Persians were put to flight at Plataea by the Lacedaemonians, they fled in disorder to their own camp and to the palisade they had built in Theban territory. It is a marvel to me that, though they fought beside the sacred grove of Demeter, not one of the Persians was found to have entered the enclosure or to have been killed within it — but around the temple, on unconsecrated ground, the greater part of the slain fell. I suppose (if one ought to suppose anything about divine matters) that the goddess herself refused to receive them, because they had set fire to the temple — the so-called “palace” at Eleusis.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 66
paragraphs: Thus far, then, had this battle gone. Artabazos son of Pharnakes, however, had been displeased from the very first that Mardonius remained behind after the king had gone, and afterwards had continually raised objections and done nothing, always urging them not to fight a battle. Since he was not pleased with what Mardonius was doing, for himself he acted as follows. The men under his command — and he had with him no small force, as much as forty thousand — when the fighting began, knowing well what the outcome of the battle would be, he led them carefully, having first given orders that all should go by the way he led them and at the same pace he went. Having given these orders, he led his troops on the pretense of taking them into battle; and when he was well on his way, he saw the Persians already in flight. Then he no longer led his men in the same order as before, but set off at a run, fleeing by the quickest route — not to the palisade or to the wall of the Thebans, but toward Phokis, eager to reach the Hellespont as quickly as possible.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 67
paragraphs: These, I say, were thus directing their march. Meanwhile, while the other Greeks on the king's side were deliberately slack in the fight, the Boeotians fought with the Athenians for a long time. The Thebans who took the Median side had no small zeal for the cause, and they fought and were not slack — so that three hundred of them, the first and best of all, fell there by the hands of the Athenians. When these too turned to flight, they fled to Thebes, not to the same place as the Persians; and the main body of the other allies fled without having fought steadily with anyone or shown any deeds of valor.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 68
paragraphs: This too is additional proof to me that all the fortunes of the barbarians depended on the Persians — namely that at that time these men fled before they had even engaged the enemy, because they saw the Persians doing so. Thus all were in flight except only the cavalry, including that of the Boeotians; and this rendered a service to the fugitives by constantly staying close to the enemy and keeping their own side's fugitives separated from the Greeks.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 69
paragraphs: The victors, then, were pressing after Xerxes's troops, pursuing and slaughtering them. During this panic, news was brought to the other Greeks — those who had taken position around the temple of Hera and had been absent from the battle — that a battle had taken place and Pausanias's troops were winning. On hearing this, without forming any order, the Corinthians and those near them turned to go along the skirts of the mountain and the low hills on the way leading straight up to the temple of Demeter, while the Megarians, Phliasians, and those near them went by the plain along the smoothest route. But when the Megarians and Phliasians drew near the enemy, the Theban cavalry caught sight of them from a distance hurrying along in no order, and rode up to attack — their cavalry commander being Asopodoros son of Timander. Falling upon them, they killed six hundred, and pursued and drove the rest to Kithairon.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 70
paragraphs: These, then, perished thus ingloriously. Meanwhile the Persians and the rest of the throng, having fled for refuge to the palisade, succeeded in getting up onto the towers before the Lacedaemonians came up; and once up, they reinforced the defensive wall as best they could. When the Lacedaemonians came up to attack it, a vigorous fight for the wall began between them. As long as the Athenians were away, they defended themselves and had much the advantage over the Lacedaemonians, who did not understand the art of fighting against walls; but when the Athenians came up to help, then there was a fierce fight for the wall lasting a long time, and at last, by valor and endurance, the Athenians mounted the wall and made a breach, through which the Greeks poured in. The Tegeans were the first to enter the wall, and they plundered Mardonius's tent, taking, besides the other things in it, the manger of his horse, which was all of bronze and a sight worth seeing. This manger of Mardonius was dedicated by the Tegeans as an offering in the temple of Athena Alea; but everything else they took, they brought to the common stock of the Greeks. The barbarians, once the wall was captured, no longer formed themselves into any close body, nor did any of them think of making a stand, but they were utterly at a loss, as you would expect from men in a panic with many tens of thousands shut up in a small space; and the Greeks were able to slaughter them, so that out of an army of three hundred thousand — subtracting the forty thousand Artabazos took with him in his flight — of the remainder not three thousand men survived. Of the Lacedaemonians from Sparta, ninety-one were killed in battle; of the Tegeans, sixteen; and of the Athenians, fifty-two.

chapters.title: Book IX — Calliope, Chapter 71
